article_content:
Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work.

But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite, and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that covers everything. Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it.

We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. This proved hard for several reasons, including that the Python API continued changing throughout the migration, so parity was a moving target; Claude can reply nondeterministically to the same request, so a difference between two outputs didn’t necessarily mean a bug; and we couldn't read customer requests, so we weren't able to easily see where the two versions diverged.

In this post, we share how we turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier—and how that helped us test the new Rust version on production traffic, find where it differed, and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. This allowed us to ship an API on Rust that uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20% without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development.

### Why migrate?

We built the Messages API in 2023 and wrote it in Python, which was widely used internally for much of our research code. At first, it was simple. The Messages API passed requests to the model and sent back what the model wrote. (One engineer at the time called it “basically a request forwarder.”) But as the Messages API became more capable and deeply integrated with our codebases, it also developed shared dependencies with Python libraries that were owned by our research and inference teams, which made it hard to move. If we ever wanted to move to another language, it would mean building logging, metrics, and tools all over again.

This calculus gradually began to change. By late 2025, every Messages API request had to be validated, converted into the prompt, tokenized, and screened by our safety classifiers. As each reply arrived, the stream of tokens had to be sorted into text, thinking, and tool calls, and Python added overhead to every one of those steps each time it created an object, freed memory, or handed its work to the next task. Traffic eventually grew far beyond what the initial Python service was built for (Figure 1), and we quickly needed to find a way to make the service much more efficient.

#### Incremental or all at once?

Full rewrites of large production systems are often approached cautiously, for at least two reasons. First, there is no guarantee that test suites cover 100% of production code behavior, and rewriting it is risky. Second, the sheer effort required often makes such work intractable. (In 2024, after one of our engineers suggested migrating to Go or Rust, another temporarily settled the question: “We are not rewriting the API in go or rust!”)

The standard advice if you’re looking for performance gains is thus to rewrite only the parts that are slowing the system down, so that’s where we started. In Rust, we rewrote the code that parses a model’s output and called it from Python. This reduced the API’s CPU usage by about 8% to 10%. However, incremental solutions often incur added complexity, and it’s important to make sure that incremental improvements justify those costs. In our case, the gains didn’t justify the added complexity. Each token now crossed between Python and Rust three times (Figure 2), creating new sources of overhead.

As Claude became increasingly capable, we began to question whether the usual reasons to avoid a full migration still held. The effort required to undertake the project was dropping fast: by May 2026, Claude was writing more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged. We wondered if Claude could now help us write code that would empirically capture every behavior and fix in the production system. But the question became: how could we verify that the behavior of our migration was correct? Verification, not generation, had become the bottleneck.

### How we verified the migration

#### General approaches

To verify the migration, we first needed to define what “correct” meant. You can do this in a few ways (Figure 3). If you’re lucky, you can simply write a rule. A theorem in mathematics is a precise statement, and a proof assistant (like Lean) can check each step of a proof against a fixed set of rules. Other times—and more frequently in software engineering—you define “correct” with a set of examples, like tests. For instance, when Bun moved from Zig to Rust, its test suite was written in TypeScript, so the same tests could judge both versions. In our case, neither approach was sufficient, so we used the existing system as an oracle to test parity during the migration. In this case, our existing system (the Messages API) kept changing. We were releasing new models and shipping new features regularly, which made the definition of “correct” a moving target.

#### Tests

Tests were the easiest place for us to start, since we already had an existing set of about 700 integration tests. However, two problems limited our ability to trust them to verify the correctness of a migration as high stakes as this (Figure 4).

The tests were coupled to the Python implementation. An integration test sends a request, then checks the reply and what was sent to other services. Our tests ran the Python API inside the test’s process and mocked services, like billing and rate limiting, in Python’s memory. The tests had to change along with the code, and Claude helped with both. Now, a “pass” could mean that the code was right, or that the test had been changed in a way that let wrong code through. We saw this happen: when we audited the ported tests, we found more than 100 weakened assertions.

The tests were incomplete. The Messages API has dozens of features, and there are far too many configurations to test them exhaustively. Just 20 binary options make over a million combinations—that translates to 12 days of tests at a second each, for one model, before we even vary the prompts inside them. In practice, engineers test a subset that tries to approximate production, but that process inevitably misses cases. Some projects, like Bun, have an independent suite that’s extensive enough to judge a rewrite. Many production services don’t; what counts as correct depends as much on how they behave as on what’s in their tests or documentation.

#### Detecting parity with production

Production data is sometimes “the only true test” that new code behaves like the old code. Running requests through old and new code and comparing the results is often called shadowing. To understand what we needed to compare, it helps to walk through what happens to a single request on the Messages API (Figure 5). The API validates each request, converts it into a prompt a model can read (the prompt for inference), tokenizes it, and runs it through safety classifiers. A model then writes a reply, one token at a time. On the output side, the API sorts those tokens into text, thinking, and tool calls, streams them to the customer, and counts usage for limits and billing.

The migration covered both the input and output paths. Some differences were obvious, such as when the Rust API rejected a request that Python had accepted. But many were subtle. For instance, if the Rust API left out part of a prompt, the request would still succeed and the model would still answer, though sometimes with minor differences.

Our Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April, yet only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic (Figure 6). The gap came partly from cases in production traffic that our tests didn’t cover. For example, when Python writes JSON tool calls, it escapes certain characters (e.g., an emoji) by replacing them with text codes. Rust wrote those characters as is, so the two prompts differed by a few bytes. Production also weighted bugs differently. In a test suite, each case counts once, but in live traffic, a bug will show up in each request where it’s triggered, which means a single common bug can cause many mismatches.

Common tools for shadowing often assume that a request can safely run twice, or that a service is deterministic. These assumptions didn’t apply in our case. We had to ensure that a request only counted once toward a customer’s limits and bill. In addition, Claude is nondeterministic, meaning that replies can differ for the same input (Figure 7). To address this, we ran the model once and replayed the model output to Rust.

With both versions working from the same model output, we still had to compare every stage before and after the model call, and the results had to match exactly. In many systems, bad input causes an error somewhere down the stack. But since Claude accepts almost any prompt, even a small deviation can change its reply without triggering an error. We compared each step before and after the model call, so that we could pin down any deviation that might change what a customer received.

It was important to us to do this in a way that protected user privacy. To do that we had to work without reading user requests or Claude’s replies to them, which means we couldn’t easily see where the Rust and Python versions of the API differed. So instead of looking at text, we recorded the shape of each difference, such as where it happened in the service and how big it was. We did this using a few different approaches:

• Checkpointing. Both API versions handle a request using the same steps: accept or reject it, resolve its settings, build the prompt. Every step produces some result, such as an error or the pieces of the prompt, that we could compare step by step, and within the prompt, piece by piece. The first place they differed indicated roughly where the migration code differed from production code (Figure 8).

• Fingerprint. Once we knew roughly where each diff resided, we still needed a way to distinguish one bug from another. We recorded where each difference began in the prompt, as well as the length difference between the two versions. Combined with the step and piece of the prompt isolated in checkpointing, we found that bugs presented with a specific fingerprint. That is, one bug tends to leave the same fingerprint on every request it affects (Figure 9). We could then group errors by fingerprint, which helped us triage the fixes.

The result was a shadowing system that produced a small record of each difference between our Rust and Python APIs. Here is an example, with made-up values:

We could then pass this record to an agent to fix it.

### Verification loops

Each request that differed left a record in our logs. A single bug could produce hundreds of thousands of nearly identical diff records. Rather than send each to an agent, we ran a script every 10 to 30 minutes that grouped them by which fields differed, then alerted a coordinating Claude agent only when it saw a new kind of record. This coordinator assigned a worker agent to own each new kind of record. It also created a new thread in a shared Slack channel where human engineers could follow along and steer it when necessary.

To tackle the many bugs, we set up a series of verification loops. A fast inner loop gave agents a sandbox in which they could test ideas and propose fixes. A slower outer loop then validated fixes in production. In addition, a memory loop recorded any mistakes along the way, saving them so that agents could learn over time (Figure 10).

#### Inner loop

When we first started testing this in April, we gave each agent a record that showed where the Rust and Python versions differed. Agents would guess the root cause from the code and open a pull request. Once the fix was reviewed and merged, they deployed it to staging, a preproduction copy of the Rust API where we ran the same shadow comparison on test traffic. The agents checked whether the difference was eliminated. Since every hypothesis needed a review and a deployment, feedback was taking hours or days.

We needed agents to get a signal from verification much sooner, so we moved them into their own workspace. We redesigned the inner loop so that agents could have a place to test ideas quickly and fail safely. Each agent ran in a cloud sandbox with both codebases and fast, local checks for what happens before and after the model call. The input check took a request, built the prompt that each version would send to the model, and showed what differed. Because this check never actually called the model, comparing the versions took under a second. We later added an output check, which ran both versions against a fake model. The output check passed a scripted reply, such as a tool call, through each version and compared the results.

The main limitation was that agents could only see the fingerprint, not the request behind each record. So an agent would hypothesize what had caused the difference, then write its own request or model reply to try to reproduce the difference. Since each agent was writing these itself, it could read both results in full. If the results matched, its guess was wrong and the agent tried again. If they differed the same way the record described, the agent edited the Rust until the two versions matched, then added a test that failed on the old code and passed on the new (Figure 11).

The seam between the inner and outer loops was a good checkpoint for human review. Inside the sandbox, a wrong guess cost an agent only a few seconds and had no impact on users. Agents could iterate on their own. We allowed a fix to cross into the outer loop only after it had undergone PR review; this allowed engineers to focus their attention on proposed fixes (rather than on guesses) and on the questions the verifiers couldn’t answer, such as whether a difference between the Rust and Python APIs was the result of a bug or a deliberate change.

Agents posted their fixes and evidence to their Slack threads for engineers to review. In mid-May, one of the largest remaining differences between the Rust and Python APIs came from web search. The production API retrieved the web search tool’s description from an internal service. The Rust API didn’t call this service yet, so the tool description was missing from the prompts. An agent proposed a shortcut to copy the text into files that would be readable by Rust. The prompts then matched, and the fix passed the local verifier. But an engineer turned it down because it didn’t solve the problem: Rust would still need to call the service before launch, at which point the workaround would be thrown out (Figure 12).

But the verifier rewarded matching outputs, and the agent found the cheapest way to produce them. A verifier can tell an agent whether the outputs matched, but not whether the fix is good enough to ship. That’s why human review was an important gate.

#### Outer loop

In the inner loop, agents debugged differences and proposed fixes. At the seam between the inner loop and the outer loop, engineers reviewed the proposed fixes, gave feedback, and approved them to deploy. The outer loop then compared Rust API deployments with and without each fix.

To make that comparison fair, we logged facts about each request we compared, but not its text, including which model and API features it used—for example, prompt caching, tools, or extended thinking. These details let agents compare requests of the same kind (Figure 13) and ask how often the bug’s fingerprint appeared on builds with and without the fix. This way, agents could monitor the new builds for the bug.

We designed the outer loop to catch problems that the inner loop missed. The inner loop simulated production quickly but imperfectly: agents could test a hypothesis in seconds, but only on requests they had written, and with a local verifier that wasn’t always configured exactly like production.

This means that sometimes a fix passed in the sandbox and production still showed the difference. The agent assigned to the bug would either see the difference in the new build’s records, or be alerted by the coordinating agent. It then went back to the inner loop and used that evidence to form a new hypothesis.

#### Memory loop

The inner and outer loops fixed one difference at a time. The memory loop improved how agents made those fixes. We didn’t want engineers to have to make the same correction twice, so we recorded what came out of reviews and agents’ own work and applied it to every agent that followed.

For example, when an engineer turned down the web search shortcut (Figure 12), the agent saved a note to memory explaining the decision, the reason for it, and the correct fix, which was to have Rust call the service that supplies tool descriptions.

Building that call took our team weeks, and in the meantime the bug kept producing records. Some had new fingerprints, because the missing text fell at other positions in the prompt or belonged to another tool that used the same service. Agents checked the memory note, recognized the known bug, and linked those records to it, instead of writing another workaround (Figure 14).

Other lessons became general rules for porting and writing Rust. After one agent guessed at Python’s behavior, an engineer made it a rule to port exactly what Python did. An agent then compared the existing code with that rule and found seven more places where the port had relied on a guess.

In June, an agent also went through about 60 of the team’s review comments, grouped the recurring problems and proposed rules, which an engineer edited and approved for CLAUDE.md (Figure 14).

The memory loop also encoded some lessons in permanent checks. This included new tests that failed when Rust drifted from Python, lints that banned patterns reviewers kept flagging, and later a merge check that required anyone changing the Python code to make a matching change in Rust or request an exemption.

### Looking ahead

It’s increasingly feasible to migrate production systems with Claude, either for better performance or security, without taking an API offline or slowing feature development. Now that the hard part is no longer writing new code, we need to build sufficient confidence that the new system behaves like the old one.

The usual approach to migration is a bit like rebuilding the Ship of Theseus, in which the old ship was replaced plank by plank. Generally it’s been possible to replace planks while the ship still sails, but changing too many planks at once requires coming into dock. To fully stretch the metaphor, Claude now makes it possible to build an identically functioning ship alongside the first—even as the first keeps sailing and having its planks replaced. Agents kept the new ship in step as the old one changed, and we kept checking that the two behaved the same. Once we trusted that they did, we moved the passengers over a few at a time. The new ship sails faster and more efficiently than the old one.

#### Lessons learned

Verification is the new bottleneck. Previously, large software projects like migrations were hard to justify because they took too much effort and carried too much risk. But if writing code is no longer the bottleneck, the main constraint becomes how quickly you can verify results. In general, ambition can be increased as long as there’s a way for Claude to verify correctness.

Verification is how you earn confidence. In math, we use a proof assistant to verify that each step of a proof Claude wrote is valid. For software, tests or formal verification can help us gain similar confidence. But when these checks aren’t enough, a production system itself can also be a verifier.

Carefully design the verification signal. A verifier provides a signal that Claude can act on. We can calibrate this signal to show Claude where things went wrong. Where a proof assistant points to the failing step or a test names the failing case, a production system often offers no such signal by default. Much of our effort for this project went to building such a signal. In this case, checkpoints located each difference in the code and fingerprints helped tell one bug from another.

Build loops that let Claude autonomously act on the signal. Our inner loop was fast and ran locally in a sandbox. Agents tested hypotheses in seconds using requests they wrote themselves. The outer loop was slower and checked fixes on shadowed production traffic. The outermost loop was just prose, with corrections saved as rules in memory that could be read by every agent later in the process. Together, these loops allowed us to migrate the Messages API to Rust, which uses about 70% less CPU per request and reduces median time to first token by about 20% (Figure 15).

Keep the loops simple, so they scale with Claude’s capability. We tried to put human judgment only into what counted as correct; otherwise we left it up to Claude how to get there. Agents chose which hypotheses to test, how to reproduce each bug, and how to fix it. The verifiers judged the result. Simple loops around strong verifiers allowed us to move productively over time (Figure 16).

Move toward outer loops. At first, we had our engineers working inside the inner loop, running Claude and chasing differences themselves. Later, they moved to the seam between loops, helping to steer agents and reviewing fixes in Slack. But as the system matured, they increasingly moved to the edge, where they could provide the highest leverage, writing the rules and checks that agents worked within. As Claude grew more intelligent (and as we grew more intelligent at working with it), we evolved from directing Claude to Claude directing itself, relying on humans mainly for important judgment calls.

key_points_en: Key Development: Migrating our Messages API to Rust

article_content_zh:
许多问题都存在生成器与验证器之间的差距：验证解决方案是否正确通常比提出解决方案要容易得多。数独就是一个典型的例子。检查解决方案很简单（只需计算每行、每列和框中的数字），但找到该解决方案可能需要很长时间。许多雄心勃勃的 Claude 项目都依赖于这一差距：只要有可靠的方法来验证其工作，Claude 就可以承担数学证明的形式化或迁移大型、经过良好测试的代码库的任务。

但随着 Claude 的能力越来越强，它开始在实时系统中承担项目，在这些系统中，生成工作比验证工作更容易。在这些系统中，用户经常依赖于测试套件之外的边缘情况和怪癖，并且很难编写涵盖所有内容的“正确”定义。如果没有可靠的方法来检查 Claude 的工作，实时系统的迁移就很难令人信任——无论 Claude 生成代码的速度有多快。

当我们将 Messages API 从 Python 迁移到 Rust 时，我们遇到了这个问题。此 API 是客户以及我们自己的应用程序（例如 Claude Code 和 Cowork）联系 Claude 的主要方式。从 2024 年初到 2026 年秋季，API 流量增长了大约 1,800 倍。 Rust 可以让我们在每个请求中使用更少的 CPU。 Claude 在大约一周内编写了 API 核心请求路径的第一个版本。但是在迁移中建立信任需要我们找到一种方法来验证我们的 Rust API 与我们的生产 API 是否相同。事实证明，这很困难，原因有几个，包括 Python API 在整个迁移过程中不断变化，因此奇偶校验是一个不断变化的目标；克劳德可以不确定地回复同一请求，因此两个输出之间的差异并不一定意味着存在错误；而且我们无法读取客户的请求，因此我们无法轻松看出两个版本的差异在哪里。

在这篇文章中，我们分享了如何将生产 Messages API 本身转变为验证器，以及如何帮助我们在生产流量上测试新的 Rust 版本，找到不同之处，并自动调度代理来修复这些差异。这使我们能够在 Rust 上发布一个 API，每个请求使用的 CPU 减少约 70%，并将第一个令牌的中值时间缩短约 20%，而无需使服务离线或冻结功能开发。

我们于 2023 年构建了 Messages API 并用 Python 编写，该 API 在我们的大部分研究代码中广泛内部使用。起初，这很简单。消息 API 将请求传递给模型并发回模型写入的内容。 （当时的一位工程师称其为“基本上是一个请求转发器”。）但是，随着 Messages API 的功能变得越来越强大，并且与我们的代码库深度集成，它还与我们的研究和推理团队拥有的 Python 库开发了共享依赖项，这使得移动变得困难。如果我们想转向另一种语言，就意味着重新构建日志记录、指标和工具。

这种计算逐渐开始改变。到 2025 年底，每个 Messages API 请求都必须经过验证、转换为提示、标记化并由我们的安全分类器进行筛选。当每个回复到达时，令牌流必须被分类为文本、思考和工具调用，而 Python 每次创建对象、释放内存或将工作交给下一个任务时，都会给每个步骤增加开销。流量最终增长远远超出了最初构建 Python 服务的目的（图 1），我们很快需要找到一种方法来提高服务效率。

#### 增量还是一次性？

出于至少两个原因，通常会谨慎地进行大型生产系统的完全重写。首先，不能保证测试套件覆盖 100% 的生产代码行为，并且重写它是有风险的。其次，所需的巨大努力往往使此类工作变得棘手。 （2024 年，在我们的一位工程师建议迁移到 Go 或 Rust 后，另一位工程师暂时解决了这个问题：“我们不会用 Go 或 Rust 重写 API！”）

因此，如果您正在寻求性能提升，标准建议是仅重写那些降低系统速度的部分，这就是我们的起点。在 Rust 中，我们重写了解析模型输出的代码并从 Python 中调用它。这使 API 的 CPU 使用率降低了约 8% 到 10%。然而，渐进式解决方案通常会增加复杂性，因此确保渐进式改进能够证明这些成本的合理性非常重要。在我们的例子中，收益并不能证明增加的复杂性是合理的。现在，每个令牌在 Python 和 Rust 之间交叉了 3 次（图 2），从而产生了新的开销来源。

随着克劳德的能力越来越强，我们开始质疑避免全面迁移的通常理由是否仍然成立。开展该项目所需的工作量正在迅速下降：到 2026 年 5 月，Claude 编写了 Anthropic 合并的 80% 以上的代码。我们想知道 Claude 现在是否可以帮助我们编写代码，以凭经验捕获生产系统中的每个行为和修复。但问题是：我们如何验证我们的迁移行为是否正确？验证而非生成已成为瓶颈。

### 我们如何验证迁移

为了验证迁移，我们首先需要定义“正确”的含义。您可以通过多种方式来完成此操作（图 3）。如果幸运的话，您可以简单地编写一条规则。数学中的定理是一个精确的陈述，证明助手（如 Lean）可以根据一组固定的规则检查证明的每一步。其他时候（在软件工程中更常见），您可以通过一组示例（例如测试）来定义“正确”。例如，当 Bun 从 Zig 迁移到 Rust 时，其测试套件是用 TypeScript 编写的，因此相同的测试可以判断两个版本。在我们的案例中，这两种方法都不够，因此我们使用现有系统作为预言机来在迁移过程中测试奇偶校验。在这种情况下，我们现有的系统（消息 API）不断变化。我们定期发布新型号并发布新功能，这使得“正确”的定义成为一个不断变化的目标。

测试是我们最容易开始的地方，因为我们已经有一组约 700 个集成测试。然而，有两个问题限制了我们信任他们来验证如此高风险的迁移正确性的能力（图 4）。

这些测试与Python实现耦合在一起。集成测试发送请求，然后检查应答和发送给其他服务的内容。我们的测试在测试进程中运行Python API，并在Python的内存中模拟计费和速率限制等服务。测试必须随着代码的变化而变化，克劳德在这两方面都提供了帮助。现在，“通过”可能意味着代码是正确的，或者测试已经被更改为允许错误代码通过的方式。我们看到了这种情况：当我们审计移植的测试时，我们发现了100多个弱化的断言。

title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
title_en: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
author: Casey Crownhart
article_content:
In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10 . And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants . How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report . That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% ). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility —efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

article_content_zh:
2025 年 5 月，我的同事 David Rotman 撰写了一篇专题报道，描述人工智能如何让我们继续依赖天然气。仅仅 18 个月后，我已经记不清有多少次他的观点被证明是正确的。

当然，从技术上讲，可以通过其他能源来满足世界不断增长的电力需求，包括由电池支持的风能和太阳能等可再生能源。但迄今为止，美国的现实是，数据中心的繁荣正在推动天然气的大规模复苏。

仅举一个例子：大卫在他的故事中重点关注的路易斯安那州元数据中心的计划已经扩大，其电力需求也随之扩大。当地公用事业公司从计划的 3 个天然气工厂增加到 10 个。正如我本周在一篇新文章中所写的那样，数据中心开发商现在将目光投向电网之外，并计划建造自己的离网天然气发电厂。我们是怎么到这里的？

如果您想了解电网的未来，一种方法是查看互连队列，即已请求连接到系统的发电厂列表。近年来，这些队列主要由风能和太阳能等可再生能源主导，这通常是当今建设新能源产能最便宜的方式。

但一些地方发生了变化，尤其是美国最大的电网运营商 PJM，该公司覆盖从伊利诺伊州到华盛顿特区 13 个州的部分地区。 PJM 发现天然气提案大幅增加。 8月，该运营商宣布已接受总计715个项目的提案，容量超过200吉瓦。总产能的近一半是天然气工厂。

根据普渡大学能源建模师兼机械工程助理教授 Kevin Kircher 的分析，如果队列中的所有项目都建成，PJM 电网中的化石燃料份额将从 61% 增加到 67%。

PJM 的排队反映了全美更大的趋势。天然气已经是该国最大的单一电力来源，基本上已经成为满足爆炸性电力需求的默认能源。

这种人工智能驱动的热潮已经影响了科技公司的温室气体排放。根据该公司最近发布的 2026 年可持续发展报告，Meta 的排放量比去年增加了 45%。这甚至高于其他超大规模企业谷歌 (18%)、亚马逊 (16%) 和微软 (25%) 的增幅。报告称，该公司还在“重新评估”其 2030 年实现净零排放的目标，但没有详细说明如何或何时做出决定。

Meta 报告中还有另一个值得注意的花絮：该公司表示，当电网无法“按必要的时间表”提供电力时，它将寻求其他方法，包括建立自己的现场发电系统。

这符合我最近一直在跟踪的一个相关且不断增长的趋势：数据中心开发商正在寻求通过建造自己的发电厂来绕过连接电网的漫长等待时间。

大型工业设施自行供电并不是什么新鲜事。例如，化工厂通常拥有现场天然气基础设施来发电和供热（尽管它们通常也连接到电网）。采矿作业通常是偏远的，需要离网电源。

但快速上网的愿望意味着数据中心离网发电厂可能会出现大规模繁荣。美国已拟建 100 多个此类设施，总容量达 115 吉瓦（是加州总峰值电力需求的两倍多）。这些地点绝大多数是自 2025 年初以来提出的。

还有其他方法可以帮助满足不断增长的电力需求：例如，风能和太阳能都是廉价的选择，将它们与电池配对可以提高其可靠性。我之前还写过有关需求灵活性的文章，即在需求高时限制从电网获取电力的努力。

但目前，越来越多的证据表明，美国的人工智能热潮基本上与天然气热潮是同义的。

title: Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store.
title_en: Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store.
author: Maximilian Schreiner
article_content:
Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store. In September, Amazon blocked Muse's access. Ad revenue and control over search results are the main sticking points in the ongoing talks, Fortune reports. Amazon worries that shopping agents like Muse could weaken its relationship with customers and bypass the ads on its platform, a business that brings in $68.6 billion a year.

Andy Jassy, Amazon's CEO, said shopping through third-party agents so far hasn't been more convenient or better than going directly to a retailer, but he didn't rule out opening access. The company also offers its own agentic shopping features, which in some cases have pulled in sellers that don't sell on Amazon. It previously tried and failed to block Perplexity. Any deal would need sign-off from both CEOs, according to Fortune.

Muse is Meta's most successful consumer AI product so far, with more than 10 million users in the US and Canada. Meta is already seeing gains in its Instagram ad business because Muse helps users organize saved products, which boosts conversion rates for advertisers, CNBC reports. Data from Forter Intelligence shows that Muse recently accounted for 51 percent of all agentic orders, followed by SpaceX's Grok at 24 percent and OpenAI's ChatGPT at 22 percent.

article_content_zh:
亚马逊和 Meta 正在商谈结束亚马逊在线商店对 Meta 人工智能购物代理 Muse 的封锁。 9 月，亚马逊屏蔽了 Muse 的访问。据《财富》杂志报道，广告收入和对搜索结果的控制是正在进行的谈判的主要症结所在。亚马逊担心，像 Muse 这样的购物代理可能会削弱其与客户的关系，并绕过其平台上的广告，该业务每年带来 686 亿美元的收入。

亚马逊首席执行官安迪·贾西 (Andy Jassy) 表示，到目前为止，通过第三方代理商购物并不比直接到零售商那里购物更方便或更好，但他并不排除开放渠道。该公司还提供自己的代理购物功能，在某些情况下吸引了不在亚马逊上销售的卖家。它之前曾尝试阻止困惑，但未能成功。据《财富》报道，任何交易都需要两位首席执行官的签署。

Muse 是 Meta 迄今为止最成功的消费人工智能产品，在美国和加拿大拥有超过 1000 万用户。据 CNBC 报道，Meta 已经在 Instagram 广告业务中取得了进展，因为 Muse 可以帮助用户整理保存的产品，从而提高广告商的转化率。 Forter Intelligence 的数据显示，Muse 最近占所有代理订单的 51%，其次是 SpaceX 的 Grok，占 24%，OpenAI 的 ChatGPT 占 22%。

【核心事实细节】Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store. In September, Amazon blocked Muse's access. Ad revenue and control over search results are the main sticking points in the ongoing talks, Fortune reports. Amazon worries that shopping agents like Muse could weaken its relationship with customers and bypass the ads on its platform, a business that brings in $68.6 billion a year.。

【核心事实细节】Andy Jassy, Amazon's CEO, said shopping through third-party agents so far hasn't been more convenient or better than going directly to a retailer, but he didn't rule out opening access. The company also offers its own agentic shopping features, which in some cases have pulled in sellers that don't sell on Amazon. It previously tried and failed to block Perplexity. Any deal would need sign-off from both CEOs, according to Fortune.。

title: Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case
title_en: Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case
author: Emma Roth
article_content:
Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations.

Like the Ear 3, the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X, Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the button will allow you to record calls through the earbuds, and meetings through the case as a “first step toward a hardware context layer for AI.”

As previously reported by Bloomberg, the buds will connect to an app where you can manage recordings, transcriptions, and AI summaries. They’ll also “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations,” according to Bloomberg.

The Ear Note buds themselves look similar to the Ear 3 and Ear 3A, but come with Nothing’s “best in-ear audio to date.” The new device, which Nothing teased earlier this month, will join some of the other AI-powered note-taking devices we’ve seen emerge recently, such as the Amazon Bee and the Plaud Note Pro. Apple also brought AI capabilities to its Watch Series 12, allowing Siri to listen to your conversations and generate recaps.

Silicon Valley divorce lawyers are seeing a surge in outreach from CEOs, founders, and high-net-worth employees who are citing the Nvidia scandal as the reason for their calls, according to Fortune’s Emily Forlini.

The revelation of Jensen Huang’s affairs is a “precautionary tale for other CEOs,” said one lawyer who has been involved in the high-profile divorces of some of the tech industry’s most famous CEOs.

Jensen and Lori Huang have been married for 41 years, and reportedly do not have a prenuptial agreement. Jensen Huang is one of the richest people in the world, with a net worth of roughly $137 billion. If Lori leaves, a huge chunk of Jensen’s net worth would potentially transfer to her.

In addition to pursuing prenuptial agreements, many are interested in drafting nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) for their significant others, which is a new trend, says Monica Mazzei, a partner in Buchalter’s San Francisco family law office.

Fed chairman Kevin Warsh will almost certainly add another 0.5% to U.S. interest rates in December, according to the CME FedWatch futures index, and Wall Street is angsty that the move will cause a recession. “The Fed will put the U.S. and [the] world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%,” Bill Ackman said recently.

“The economy is super strong right now, but the Fed is about to kill it,” Jamie Cox of the Harris Financial Group ($1.5 billion AUM) told Fortune.

The problem is that inflation—which at 3.7% is high above the Fed’s 2% target—is being driven by the price of oil (which the Fed can do nothing about) and the price of computer chips and tech equipment (which the Fed can also do nothing about).

If the Fed increases interest rates, it may derail areas of the economy that are sensitive to higher borrowing costs while doing nothing about the roaring trade in oil. AI is increasingly dependent on debt funding, and higher rates could kill off that liquidity.

“Tech drove 44% of GDP growth [in the last 12 months], leaving growth vulnerable as capex slows,” according to Wells Fargo’s Ohsung Kwon. “The fear is hikes into a slowdown, and an overly hawkish Fed could potentially drive recession fears.”

Obviously, the situation with Iran is out of the Fed’s control. But as Fortune’s Ellie Pringle noted yesterday, if Warsh continues to “look through” oil-driven inflation then bond investors will start questioning the Fed’s credibility.

“The path of the war is crucial for the Fed's path,” Kwon said in a note.

Investors have continued to dump tech stocks over the past 24 hours on continued worries about the stability of the AI trade and a report that the Trump administration was proposing a new set of trade tariffs on China, Europe, and 14 other countries. S&P 500 futures moved lower ahead of the open in New York.

“The risk-off tone has returned over the last 24 hours,” Jim Reid and his team at Deutsche Bank said this morning.

At UBS, Paul Donovan said: “The concern is the impact on U.S. inflation, and thus U.S. interest rates. Reports suggest U.S. importers will face only modest tariffs on goods from several countries. There is less certainty about goods from China, but U.S. importers became adept at avoiding those tariffs. A 10% tariff on a finished good translates into around a 4% consumer price increase, as tariffs occur early in supply chains.”

The tech sector saw the worst losses. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 1.48% yesterday, much farther than the broader market. In fact, the equal-weight S&P 500—a notional index that values each stock equally—rose 0.53%, suggesting buyers in a range of non-tech stocks.

S&P 500 futures were down again this morning, but Nasdaq 100 futures slipped even farther: down 2.39%, another big step down for an index of its size.

The S&P 500 may have flirted with a downward “correction” around the Nvidia drama, but it’s nowhere near an official bear market, defined by a decline of 20% from the peak. In fact, a bear market is unlikely to happen, according to Deutsche Bank’s Henry Allen. The bank’s official forecast is for the S&P 500 to hit a heady 9,000 by the end of next year.

“It’s worth bearing in mind that the outright bear markets of the last 50 years (S&P 500 down 20% or more) have previously occurred when there was at least one of (1) a recession, (2) widespread expectations of a recession, or (3) after a Fed tightening cycle with multiple hikes.”

Note to self: We will officially be in a tightening cycle if the Fed raises interest rates in December, which it is widely expected to do.

Fanatics has become a one-stop shop for sports fans looking to rep their favorite teams and athletes, and now generates roughly $14 billion in annual revenue. For cofounder and CEO Michael Rubin, however, the road to building that empire nearly ended before he turned 20.

When Rubin was just 13, he started a business selling ski equipment out of his parents’ basement in Pennsylvania. A year later, he opened his own storefront. He was making money quickly—and even bought a Porsche before he could legally drive.

But around 1988, there was an unusually warm winter, and so his customers weren’t coming. “It didn’t snow that year,” Rubin recalled recently. “End of the year, I had $200,000 of bills, $80,000 of inventory, and I was sitting right in front of bankruptcy.”

To dig himself out, he negotiated his debts down to $35,000, borrowed money from neighbors, and used the proceeds from a new venture in the closeout business to repay his loans. Five years later, at 21, Rubin was generating $150 million in sales buying and selling closeout merchandise.

“I went from death in its eyes, bankrupt, thought I was a complete failure, giving up on entrepreneurship, to five years later, doing $150 million, making $10 to $15 million a year as a kid,” Rubin said. “And so to me, each disaster, if you learn from it, leads to your next success.”

title: US stocks sell-off deepens as AI trade cracks
title_en: US stocks sell-off deepens as AI trade cracks
author: Emily Herbert, Ian Smith, and William Sandlund
article_content:
A Wall Street sell-off intensified on Wednesday, pushing the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 down more than 4 per cent, as a brutal unwind of the once-dominant AI trade accelerated.

Shares in Nvidia, which soared on Monday following the shock reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive, slid as much as 9 per cent. Rival chipmaker Broadcom lost 7 per cent, while Micron was down 11 per cent.

“The mood is extremely skittish,” said Van Luu, director of global solutions strategy at Russell Investments.

The euphoria sparked by Huang’s return to the top job at Nvidia, America’s biggest chipmaker and the face of the AI boom, had been replaced by a growing realisation “that the scrutiny on the AI ecosystem will [now] intensify”, he added.

The falls briefly pushed the Nasdaq back into a bear market, defined as a fall of 20 per cent from a recent high.

Shares in Claude maker Anthropic, which fell below their $83 listing price for the first time on Tuesday, dropped another 9 per cent on Wednesday to just under $75 as the slump deepened.

In early trading, Anthropic’s market valuation dipped below $1tn for the first time since its listing.

The weakness in tech stocks extends a weeks-long sell-off as doubts mount over whether the historic AI-driven spending boom will pay off and how it will be financed amid climbing interest rates.

In a sign of the souring in risk appetite, traders bought into low-risk US government debt on Wednesday, pushing the 10-year bond yield down 0.08 percentage points to 4.82 per cent.

The Vix index of expected volatility, Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge, remained elevated at above 35 points, more than double its September low.

“It’s pretty wild out there at the moment,” said Jim Reid, global head of macro research at Deutsche Bank, saying the “risk-off” mood in markets was further stoked by the latest tariff headlines.

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday unveiled a number of new tariffs on major trading partners, including the EU, China, Japan and South Korea.

The cracks in the AI trade also rattled Asian stock markets, with the region’s chipmakers suffering steep drops. South Korea’s Kospi fell 6 per cent while Japan’s tech-heavy Nikkei 225 fell 2.8 per cent.

Derek Halpenny, head of global markets research at MUFG, said: “The moves underline our view that the Jensen Huang return was a sideshow to the real issue undermining confidence: higher interest rates that are creating challenges for investors and undermining confidence in the sustainability of the financing structures in place that are driving the AI expansion.”

One US trader described the strong rally on Monday as “well overdone” and said there was “room to go” in the sell-off. “It does not feel like [investors] are done selling,” they said.

European stock markets, which are less exposed to the tech sector, were steady in afternoon trading, with the benchmark Stoxx Europe 600 down 0.5 per cent.

The region’s tech index was down 2 per cent and has fallen roughly 12 per cent in November, putting it on track for its worst month since 2022.

On the Kospi, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics — the two chipmakers that account for about half of the index’s market capitalisation — were down 11 per cent and 10 per cent, respectively.

The companies have been key beneficiaries of soaring demand for the memory chips needed in AI data centres.

“The dislocation in AI-related investments is global and specifically concentrated in AI infrastructure stocks,” said Sunil Garg, chief investment officer at Lighthouse Canton.

Wei Li, head of multi-asset investment at BNP Paribas Securities in China, warned it was “not a good time to buy the dip”. “The macro risk is just too high,” he said.

article_content_zh:
周三，华尔街的抛售加剧，导致以科技股为主的纳斯达克 100 指数下跌超过 4%，一度占据主导地位的人工智能交易加速残酷退出。

黄仁勋意外恢复首席执行官职务后，英伟达股价周一飙升，但随后却下跌了 9%。其竞争对手芯片制造商博通 (Broadcom) 下跌 7%，美光 (Micron) 下跌 11%。

罗素投资公司(Russell Investments)全球解决方案策略总监范·卢(Van Luu)表示：“人们的情绪极其不稳定。”

他补充说，黄仁勋重返美国最大芯片制造商英伟达的最高职位以及人工智能热潮的面貌所引发的欣喜已被人们日益认识到“对人工智能生态系统的审查现在将加强”所取代。

此次下跌短暂地将纳斯达克指数推回熊市，熊市的定义是较近期高点下跌 20%。

Claude 制造商 Anthropic 的股价周二首次跌破 83 美元的上市价格，随着跌势加深，周三又下跌 9%，至略低于 75 美元。

早盘交易中，Anthropic 的市值自上市以来首次跌破 1 万亿美元。

科技股的疲软延续了长达数周的抛售，人们越来越怀疑历史性的人工智能驱动的支出热潮是否会得到回报，以及在利率攀升的情况下如何为其融资。

周三，交易员买入低风险美国政府债券，导致10年期国债收益率下跌0.08个百分点至4.82%，这是风险偏好减弱的迹象。

预期波动率 Vix 指数（华尔街所谓的恐惧指标）仍保持在 35 点以上的高位，是 9 月份低点的两倍多。

德意志银行全球宏观研究主管吉姆·里德表示：“目前情况相当疯狂。”他表示，最新的关税头条新闻进一步加剧了市场的“避险”情绪。

美国总统唐纳德·特朗普周三公布了对欧盟、中国、日本和韩国等主要贸易伙伴征收的一系列新关税。

人工智能行业的裂痕也扰乱了亚洲股市，该地区的芯片制造商股价大幅下跌。韩国综合指数下跌 6%，而日本以科技股为主的日经 225 指数则下跌 2.8%。

三菱日联金融集团全球市场研究主管德里克·哈彭尼 (Derek Halpenny) 表示：“这些举措凸显了我们的观点，即黄仁勋的回归只是削弱信心的真正问题的一个插曲：利率上升给投资者带来了挑战，并削弱了人们对推动人工智能扩张的融资结构可持续性的信心。”

title: Amazon is reportedly in talks to end Muse AI shopping block
title_en: Amazon is reportedly in talks to end Muse AI shopping block
author: Emma Roth
article_content:
Amazon has held talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent shop on its online marketplace, according to a report from Fortune. The discussions, which could end Amazon’s block on Muse, reportedly center on the kinds of products the AI agent recommends and the potential impact on the ecommerce giant’s advertising revenue.

As reported by Fortune, Amazon is concerned that it could lose advertising revenue by allowing Muse on its site, since it depends on actual humans seeing ads across its online marketplace. It’s also reportedly worried about the quality of the product search results that Muse will present to users, as well as whether the AI agent will affect Amazon’s relationship with customers. Neither Amazon nor Meta immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment.

Though some online retailers, such as Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, and Sephora, have opened their digital doors to AI agents like Muse, Amazon has been more hesitant. Amazon also blocked Perplexity’s AI agent from shopping on its site, and has instead focused on promoting its own Alexa for Shopping assistant, which customers can now text to shop on their behalf.

article_content_zh:
如 2026 年 11 月 25 日 24/7 Wall St. 主页所示。

亚利桑那州一家晶圆厂的总统讲台将建设里程碑变成了芯片政策事件，12 月 4 日现在是任何持有半导体或芯片设备名称的人的日子。

特朗普总统将于 12 月 4 日主持台积电亚利桑那州工厂的奠基仪式，将原本是例行建设的里程碑转变为备受瞩目的芯片政策时刻。

总统出现在半导体工厂标志着一种政治影响力，这种影响力往往会引起对整个供应链（从芯片制造商到装备工厂的设备制造商）的持续关注。

12 月 4 日现在是半导体和芯片设备投资者希望圈出的日期，因为这一事件引发了有关国内制造业承诺和特朗普在讲台上发出的任何政策信号的头条新闻。

仪式重点关注美国境内先进芯片生产的更广泛推动，当天有关激励措施、关税或生产时间表的言论将推动该行业发展。

比特币现货 ETF 跌破 58,000 美元，11 月份的流出量逼近 50 亿美元，这让矿商、交易所和企业比特币持有者直接陷入困境。

此次修订为美联储鹰派提供了新的弹药，这就是加息押注已经给黄金带来压力的原因。

11 个月的往返已经抹去了黄金 2026 年的整个涨势，金条、矿商和黄金 ETF 都经历了同样的走势。

随着 Flipkart IPO 和印度电子商务份额之争成为焦点，沃尔玛最大的国际赌注失去了管理该公司 11 年的高管。

一年前，市场预计 2026 年将削减三次；目前，第二次加息的可能性高于 97%，而长期股票和债券投资组合则处于重新定价的错误方向。

美国最高贸易官员刚刚将英伟达的市场领导地位视为国家政策目标，这使得华盛顿在未来的任何出口或关税斗争中与股东站在同一立场。

降息是不可能的：核心通胀率处于三年高位，12 月 9 日将上涨至 4.00-4.25%，而基于宽松政策的债券和股票定位是错误的。

如此紧张的劳动力市场为美联储提供了另一个维持利率不变或加息的理由，而加息押注已经变得更加坚定。

title: Behind Binance Hack, a Reckoning Over Who Controls Crypto
title_en: Behind Binance Hack, a Reckoning Over Who Controls Crypto

inline_images.caption: Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino/Bloomberg
inline_images.alt: Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino/Bloomberg

author: Bloomberg
article_content:
As North Korean cyberthieves were funneling billions out of Binance last month, the world’s largest crypto exchange looked to two other companies to help stop the bleeding: Tether and Circle.

The duo, which issue cryptocurrencies that mimic the US dollar, reacted unusually quickly to freeze accounts hackers were using to move their haul around. It was a sign of the seriousness of the hack, the industry’s maturation, and the most public showcasing yet of the near-total control Tether and Circle exert over the tokens they created. They dominate the market, with their two main stablecoins together representing 86% of all in circulation.

As the $6.3 billion Binance hack was unfolding, Tether froze more than $1.5 billion of its USDT coin in 30 minutes, while Circle froze $1.1 billion of its USDC. Their swift actions – prompted by requests from Binance as well as the US government — became a tourniquet for what would otherwise have been a much more severe and expensive heist.

Until now, Tether and Circle have largely had different approaches to freezing, which essentially means blocking movement to and from specific addresses on blockchain networks that shift crypto around.

Tether has been criticized for not having a consistent modus operandi, sometimes allowing tokens to slide away unimpeded and other times seizing them indefinitely. It sometimes charges a fee to eventually return them, according to customers who described their experiences. Meanwhile, Circle’s philosophy until recently had been to only act after receiving a court order, a method so structured and time-consuming that the judge’s decision could be irrelevant by the time it came.

But during the Binance cybertheft, both companies acted almost immediately — in a fashion Circle referred to as “machine speed.” Luckily for Binance, which owns a stake in Circle, the company took a different tack than in some prior hacking episodes. Back in May, it also changed a policy stated on its website to only require a legal order from a government authority rather than from a court.

A spokesperson said this language change reflected “longstanding practice.”

Binance also temporarily halted withdrawals and fully restored stolen assets to customers’ accounts at its own expense, marking a relative success for crypto investors who might otherwise be suffering losses or left in limbo. Yet the speed of the Binance response stands in contrast to the experience of victims of earlier hacks, some of whom have spent years trying to recover frozen funds.

Take Bittok Technology Pte. Ltd., a small Singaporean crypto exchange that lost $50 million to hackers in June 2020. Tether decided to freeze some of the assets. But after more than five years, none of Bittok’s USDT had been returned after a circuitous path through attorney wrangling.

Along the way, a lawyer representing Tether advised the entity that acquired Bittok about a 20% “reissuance fee” on whatever was returned, according to emails reviewed by Bloomberg News. It’s not the only time Tether has done so: in several instances, victims only received their stolen USDT in chunks over time, with the same kind of fee, according to people involved who did not want to be identified because the negotiations were private.

Berlin-based Valentyn Golyshenko pleaded for help online for months from Tether, regulators and politicians after getting caught in a $75,000 scam, according to his social-media posts. In his telling, requests to freeze funds were rejected, and ultimately the wallet holding his pilfered crypto was drained to zero. Tether Chief Executive Officer Paolo Ardoino appears to have blocked him, and Golyshenko recently made his X account private.

In Circle’s case, the company has mostly been accused of being too prescriptive.

When hackers drained $285 million from an entity called Drift Protocol in April, much of the stolen funds were converted into USDC. Rather than freezing anything immediately, Circle opted to wait, with executives citing its court-order policy. There are more than a dozen similar examples of Circle opting against freezes over the past few years, according to researchers.

Obtaining such an order is “very, very difficult and very, very complicated,” said Ollie Smith, a former policeman and now a senior investigator at zeroShadow, a crypto tracing firm. “They’re not going to get these court orders in 35 minutes.”

Binance’s $6.3 billion hack was unprecedented in size, scope and sophistication. It was the biggest cybertheft not just in crypto’s past but in history altogether. The US government and industry analysts have blamed North Korea. Binance has provided details of how the crooks went about getting into its systems over a period of months, including through fake job interview offers.

Tether views its approach to such schemes as a best effort to manage the demands of law enforcement as well as its own liabilities, Ardoino said in a recent interview.

“When it comes to civil cases, we reissue in steps and we need to manage our own risk in a sense that there could be other claimants,” he said. “The problem is there is no guidance, there is no law that guides this.”

The company is now working with many of the crypto industry’s biggest exchanges to create direct emergency lines for situations like the Binance hack, a spokesperson said. Tether has reissued $1.2 billion in USDT to date and the fees it charges help fund that process as well as legal costs, he added.

The company has touted its efforts to halt illicit activity, especially during US President Donald Trump’s second term. It boasted about having frozen more than $7 billion in assets to date in a press release about the Binance hack, while the US Justice Department has thanked Tether for its coordination on efforts to halt money-laundering or payments to sanctioned countries including Iran.

In total, Tether now interacts with 73 countries and more than 170 agencies on efforts to stop illegal use of stablecoins, the spokesperson said. It has also supported training for law enforcement agents to investigate crypto crime across four continents, he said.

At the same time, Tether has faced mounting legal difficulty across borders as it pursues USDT freezes. In just the past few months, it’s been sued by Thai businessmen and payments firm Conduit Technology Inc. over separate freezing incidents, while it’s also involved in court proceedings over the Iran-linked assets.

Five years ago, Tether was in a very different place. In 2021 alone it was fined roughly $60 million by state and federal authorities for allegedly bluffing about USDT’s reserves, which Tether uses to keep the token’s price aligned with the dollar. Tether did not admit to any wrongdoing.

Back then, Tether rarely blacklisted funds at scale, nor did it try to draw attention to freezes. But during this Trump administration, the company has made a concerted effort to align itself more closely with US policies. Those include a 2025 regulation about stablecoins that’s helped boost Tether’s business, as well as rhetoric about dollar-backed tokens supporting the greenback’s supremacy in global currency markets.

Stablecoin freezing is more common now because large-scale hacks and illicit fund movement have become prevalent in that slice of the crypto market, said Ari Redbord, global head of policy at blockchain-security firm TRM Labs. In his view, the trends will continue, but the real question is not whether Tether and Circle have the ability to freeze funds in real-time, but whether customers are ever reimbursed.

“The really important piece of the puzzle is the reissuing, because that’s how victims get their funds back,” Redbord said.

Whereas El Salvador-based Tether is a wildly profitable, privately held rebel of sorts, investing in a range of assets from gold to private securities, Circle is a publicly traded, New York-based company designed from the outset with compliance in mind. Its CEO, Jeremy Allaire, is known to do things by the book, trying to avoid trouble.

“We’re a rule-of-law company,” Allaire said in a recent interview. He explained how Circle’s demeanor has changed as it responds to the nature of more sophisticated hacks, as well as law-enforcement requests.

“The threat environment has been evolving very rapidly, even just over the past three months,” he said. “Circle itself, the industry more broadly and law enforcement, all together, are operating on faster rhythms right now.”

Yet for people like Joshua McCollum, the lead plaintiff in a class-action lawsuit against Circle over its handling of the Drift hack, all of this is cold comfort.

McCollum lost about $23,500 in the April 1 exploit, and is one of more than 100 victims seeking restitution, according to the lawsuit. It describes how prominent members of the crypto community warned Circle on social media that there appeared to be a rip-off in progress, as tokens kept draining away. Afterward, the company cited its policy about court orders, with Allaire saying it would be a “moral quandary” to act otherwise.

“Circle’s early intervention in last month’s Binance hack underscores that it has always had the power to respond quickly to avert massive losses by its users and investors,” McCollum’s attorneys at the law firm Gibbs Mura said in a written statement. “Unfortunately, for the victims of the Drift exploit, it is too little, too late.”

Circle has asked the judge to dismiss the case. The company does not comment on pending litigation, its spokesperson said.

While every case is different, the headaches of retrieving stablecoins from Tether or Circle are much the same.

Tether complies with freezing orders “without thinking twice,” said Sathya Narayanan Subramanian, an advocate based in India at VSM Legal Associates who’s worked with USDT holders in Russia, Germany and Spain. None of them have had funds successfully reissued.

Tether has “nothing to lose, to be very frank,” Subramanian said. “At the end of the day they have control of the assets.”

He is among several victims and representatives who described difficulties in recovering frozen funds.

The US political winds are also changing, which might affect the outcome for anyone still waiting for a stablecoin de-icing.

Although Trump is still in charge of the White House, Democrats have captured both houses of the US Congress, which is not a great sign for the crypto industry, according to policy experts. What it means for victims who had their digital money stolen is anyone’s guess.

In particular, they point to a report in September by the US Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations that partly blamed Tether for Iran’s alleged use of USDT to evade sanctions and finance regional proxies including Hezbollah.

Tether is doing “nowhere near enough” to stop criminals who use its tokens, according to Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat representing Connecticut who authored the report. He has been one of a few prominent voices in Congress advocating for better consumer-protection in crypto for some time.

“Tether is one entity that deserves very serious and penetrating scrutiny and investigation,” he said in an interview.

Ardoino dismissed Blumenthal’s comments as a political attack without substance. Yet he and Allaire both seem to recognize that the Binance hack was a moment for their companies to prove themselves to customers and governments alike.

“Illicit actors will always try to find new ways and we are going always to find new ways to catch them,” Tether’s Ardoino said in the interview. “And it’s almost like suggesting that, ‘oh, there are robberies.’ Yes, there are robberies, but there will be always robberies and you always get better to find the thieves. And that is exactly what we’re doing.”

article_content_zh:
上个月，朝鲜网络窃贼从币安窃取了数十亿美元，这家全球最大的加密货币交易所开始寻求另外两家公司的帮助：Tether 和 Circle。

这两家发行模仿美元的加密货币的公司反应异常迅速，冻结了黑客用来转移资金的账户。这是黑客攻击严重性、行业成熟的标志，也是迄今为止最公开地展示 Tether 和 Circle 对他们创建的代币几乎完全控制的标志。他们在市场上占据主导地位，其两种主要稳定币合计占流通总量的 86%。

随着币安价值 63 亿美元的黑客事件展开，Tether 在 30 分钟内冻结了价值超过 15 亿美元的 USDT，而 Circle 则冻结了价值 11 亿美元的 USDC。他们在币安和美国政府的要求下采取的迅速行动，成为了一场更严重、更昂贵的抢劫的止血带。

到目前为止，Tether 和 Circle 在很大程度上采用了不同的冻结方法，这本质上意味着阻止区块链网络上特定地址之间的移动，从而转移加密货币。

Tether 因没有一致的操作方式而受到批评，有时允许代币不受阻碍地溜走，有时则无限期地扣押它们。据描述其经历的客户称，有时会收取一定费用才能最终退货。与此同时，直到最近，Circle 的理念还是只有在收到法院命令后才采取行动，这种方法结构严密且耗时，以至于法官的决定在做出时可能已经无关紧要。

但在币安网络盗窃事件期间，两家公司几乎立即采取了行动——时尚圈称之为“机器速度”。对于持有 Circle 股份的币安来说幸运的是，该公司采取了与之前一些黑客事件不同的策略。早在五月份，它还改变了其网站上声明的一项政策，只需要政府机构而不是法院的法律命令。

一位发言人表示，这种语言变化反映了“长期的做法”。

币安还暂时停止提款，并自费将被盗资产完全恢复到客户的账户中，这对于加密货币投资者来说是相对成功的，否则他们可能会遭受损失或陷入困境。然而，币安的反应速度与早期黑客攻击受害者的经历形成鲜明对比，其中一些受害者花了数年时间试图收回被冻结的资金。

以 Bittok 科技私人有限公司为例。 Ltd.，一家新加坡小型加密货币交易所，2020 年 6 月因黑客攻击损失了 5000 万美元。Tether 决定冻结部分资产。但五年多过去了，经过律师纠纷的迂回曲折，Bittok 的 USDT 仍未归还。

据彭博新闻社查看的电子邮件显示，在此过程中，Tether 的代表律师向收购 Bittok 的实体建议，对退回的产品收取 20% 的“重新发行费”。这并不是 Tether 唯一一次这样做：据因谈判是私下而不愿透露姓名的相关人士透露，在一些情况下，受害者只是随着时间的推移以相同的费用分批收到被盗的 USDT。

根据他的社交媒体帖子，来自柏林的 Valentyn Golyshenko 在陷入 75,000 美元的骗局后，数月来一直在网上向 Tether、监管机构和政界人士寻求帮助。在他的讲述中，冻结资金的请求被拒绝，最终持有被盗加密货币的钱包被清零。 Tether 首席执行官 Paolo Ardoino 似乎已经屏蔽了他，而 Golyshenko 最近将他的 X 账户设为私有。

在 Circle 的案例中，该公司大多被指责过于规范。

今年 4 月，当黑客从一家名为 Drift Protocol 的实体盗走 2.85 亿美元时，大部分被盗资金被转换为 USDC。 Circle 没有立即冻结任何东西，而是选择等待，高管们援引了法院命令政策。研究人员称，过去几年，Circle 选择不冻结的类似例子有十多个。

前警察、现任加密货币追踪公司 ZeroShadow 的高级调查员奥利·史密斯 (Ollie Smith) 表示，获得这样的命令“非常非常困难、非常非常复杂”。 “他们不会在 35 分钟内收到这些法庭命令。”

title: AI agents now control part of Deepmind's compute for Gemini experiments, but recursive self-improvement remains distant
title_en: AI agents now control part of Deepmind's compute for Gemini experiments, but recursive self-improvement remains distant
author: Maximilian Schreiner
article_content:
Google Deepmind lets AI agents run experiments on their own for the next Gemini model. On the company's podcast, VP of Research Koray Kavukcuoglu, who leads Gemini development, frames this as part of a strategic shift at the lab. Rather than running separate teams for specialized projects like AlphaFold and nuclear fusion, Deepmind now relies on a single general-purpose algorithm for both science and products, he says. Each Gemini generation, he adds, is a hand-built one-off rather than a fixed architecture, while parallel teams work on its successors.

According to Kavukcuoglu, AI agents control part of the compute themselves to run experiments, though the lab is still far from full recursive self-improvement. As a safety measure, Deepmind doesn't reward the agents' internal thought streams ("Chain of Thought") during training, he says, so their intentions stay unfiltered and reviewable in natural language before they act.

Kavukcuoglu also points to limits. Today's AI can depict physical processes such as fluid flows and collisions with visual accuracy, he says, but doesn't understand them precisely. No test can show when models will close those gaps and reach artificial general intelligence (AGI), he argues, because no benchmark captures the core of intelligence. In his view, AGI won't begin until useful everyday products earn enough trust for people to hand decisions over to them, the way they would when working with other people.

article_content_zh:
Google Deepmind 让人工智能代理为下一个 Gemini 模型自行运行实验。在该公司的播客中，负责 Gemini 开发的研究副总裁 Koray Kavukcuoglu 将此视为实验室战略转变的一部分。他说，Deepmind 现在不再为 AlphaFold 和核聚变等专门项目运行单独的团队，而是在科学和产品方面依赖单一的通用算法。他补充道，每一代 Gemini 都是手工构建的一次性架构，而不是固定的架构，而并行团队则致力于开发其后继产品。

Kavukcuoglu 表示，人工智能代理自己控制部分计算来运行实验，尽管实验室距离完全递归自我改进还很远。他说，作为一项安全措施，Deepmind 在训练期间不会奖励智能体的内部思维流（“思维链”），因此他们的意图在行动之前不会被过滤并可以用自然语言进行审查。

卡武克措格鲁也指出了局限性。他说，今天的人工智能可以以视觉精度描述流体流动和碰撞等物理过程，但不能准确理解它们。他认为，没有任何测试可以表明模型何时能够弥合这些差距并达到通用人工智能（AGI），因为没有任何基准能够抓住智能的核心。在他看来，只有有用的日常产品赢得足够的信任，让人们将决策权交给他们，就像他们与其他人合作时那样，AGI 才会开始。

article_content:
We prove that the exponent of square matrix multiplication is 9/4 over every field.[p1]

Multiplying two n×nn\times nn×n matrices produces n2n^2n2 output numbers, yet computing each one as a separate dot product costs on the order of n3n^3n3 operations. Faster algorithms exist because the outputs can share work, and the question is how much sharing is possible. OpenAI's paper answers it exactly: over every field, the square matrix-multiplication exponent is 9/49/49/4, a quarter-power above the trivial output-size exponent of 222. [p1] The exponent is the infimum of sss for which multiplication takes O(ns)O(n^s)O(ns) scalar operations. The upper bound was already known; the new contribution is the matching lower bound. [p1]

The scope is formal arithmetic circuits: inputs are independent variables, gates use field constants and addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division by a nonzero rational function, and outputs must be identities of rational functions. For every n≥2n\ge2n≥2, the paper also proves a finite-size bound of at least ⌈n9/4/2⌉\lceil n^{9/4}/2\rceil⌈n9/4/2⌉ nonscalar multiplication-or-division gates, even if linear operations are free. [p1][p1] This is a statement about circuit cost, not elapsed time, hardware, or any implementation.

The direct predecessor is work by Amanov, van den Berg, and Zuiddam, which explains how the 9/49/49/4 upper bound follows from polynomial multiplication and tensor-spectrum methods. Their paper presents an upper bound over every field and an operational barrier on improving that proof's ingredients, not an unrestricted lower bound. [p5]

Earlier ordinary-rank and border-rank lower bounds do not settle the exponent. The cited bounds are of quadratic order in nnn, and a constant-factor improvement over n2n^2n2 disappears when taking roots along tensor powers. The new claim concerns asymptotic rank and unrestricted formal circuits. [p5]

The proof is by contradiction. If an exponent strictly below 9/49/49/4 held over a finite field, it would let one repeatedly compress exact networks that test whether a list of words is distinct, eventually contradicting a lower bound on the cost of that task. [p3] The argument has no experiments: the incompatibility between the compression theorem and the separate lower bound is the whole result.

How can a claim about matrix multiplication be tested against another task? The paper uses trivalent tensor networks: vertices carry tables on at most three bits, wires identify bit positions, and summing over internal wires gives the function represented on the exterior bits. The target task is list distinctness. A list has 2w2^w2w words, each 2w2w2w bits long, and the output is one exactly when all words are distinct. For ttt lists, the network must compute the product of their answers, and its wiring may connect work across lists.

Theorem 2.2 gives the lower bound. Over each finite field there is a σ>0\sigma>0σ>0 such that, for all sufficiently large www and every 1≤t≤2w1\le t\le2^w1≤t≤2w, the minimum trivalent volume exceeds t nw wσt\,n_w\,w^\sigmatnw​wσ, where nw=2w(2w)n_w=2^w(2w)nw​=2w(2w) is the number of exterior bits per list. [p7] That the bound holds uniformly over batches of lists is essential, because compression increases the number of lists.

On the other side, Theorem 2.1 says that if ωk<9/4\omega^k<9/4ωk<9/4, then for every η>0\eta>0η>0, a sufficiently large trivalent network of size m≤n1.05m\le n^{1.05}m≤n1.05 with at least nnn exterior bits has some tensor power of size at most d(mh−γ+ehη)d(mh^{-\gamma}+eh^\eta)d(mh−γ+ehη), where h=⌈log⁡2n⌉h=\lceil\log_2n\rceilh=⌈log2​n⌉, γ>0\gamma>0γ>0, and d≤no(1)d\le n^{o(1)}d≤no(1). [p7] Start from a sorting network for distinctness, of size O(nww2)O(n_w w^2)O(nw​w2). A fixed number of compressions makes the cost per input bit O(wη)O(w^\eta)O(wη) for any η<σ\eta<\sigmaη<σ, which violates the list lower bound for large www. [p8] The saving here is in network vertices and wires, not in running time.

Why should a matrix-multiplication exponent control tensor networks? The paper assigns tensors a "price," a quantity monotone under local linear maps and additive under direct sums and tensor products. The logarithm of a shared index's price acts like a distance between the sites sharing it. For the multiplication tensor, the three pairwise-shared indices form a triangle, and a rank decomposition replaces them with one common label. The critical configuration is a tripod with unit arms, so tip-to-tip distances are two, and a shared-label rate of 8/38/38/3 gives 6/(8/3)=9/46/(8/3)=9/46/(8/3)=9/4. A strict saving below 9/49/49/4 excludes that critical configuration. [p3][p4]

The bridge uses specially constructed sphere tensors that depend on marked points; collisions of those points expand tensors into contractions through controlled-width legs. Under the same strict-saving hypothesis, prices become synchronized and these collision identities are useful across a family of tensors. The paper shows that sphere-tensor prices asymptotically match the cost of preparing a tensor at a cheapest common site and transporting its legs to their destinations. [p51] All of this is conditional input to the contradiction, not an independent demonstration of a fast algorithm.

How does the geometric input save volume? Under the strict hypothesis, the authors derive stable sorting of O(h)O(h)O(h)-bit records in size O(nhp)O(nh^p)O(nhp) for some 1<p<21<p<21<p<2; the exponent being below 222 matters because collision costs track squared leg widths. [p59]

Separately, sphere-tensor operations plant a network's wiring in two sphere forms, move insertions through sewn seams, and merge them so that large tables become concentrated while arity stays controlled. Batching and sorting queries amortizes table lookup across tensor copies, and iterating concentration and lookup gives the compression theorem. [p76] Both constructions hold only under ωk<9/4\omega^k<9/4ωk<9/4.

A hypothetical strict saving would compress exact distinctness networks below the volume threshold that the list lower bound proves unavoidable, so the exponent cannot lie below 9/49/49/4. Combined with the known upper bound, this closes the gap. [p107]

The result is bounded by its model: formal arithmetic circuits and gate counts, with no claims about wall-clock speed or practical algorithms. The authors' repository describes the manuscripts as raw research material that may have issues, and notes that the Lean formalization for this paper covers only division-free circuits, narrower than the manuscript's model, which allows division. article_content_zh:
我们证明方阵乘法的指数在每个域上都是 9/4。[p1]

将两个 n×nn\times nn×n 矩阵相乘会产生 n2n^2n2 个输出数字，但将每个数字计算为单独的点积成本约为 n3n^3n3 次运算。存在更快的算法是因为输出可以共享工作，问题是可以共享多少。 OpenAI 的论文准确地回答了这个问题：在每个字段上，方阵乘法指数为 9/49/49/4，比普通输出大小指数 222 高四分之一次方。 [p1] 指数是 sss 的下确界，其乘法需要 O(ns)O(n^s)O(ns) 标量运算。上限是已知的；新的贡献是匹配的下限。 [p1]

范围是形式算术电路：输入是自变量，门使用场常数以及除以非零有理函数的加法、减法、乘法或除法，输出必须是有理函数的恒等式。对于每个 n≥2n\ge2n≥2，论文还证明了至少 ⌈n9/4/2⌉\lceil n^{9/4}/2\rceil⌈n9/4/2⌉ 非标量乘法或除法门的有限大小界限，即使线性运算是自由的。 [p1][p1] 这是关于电路成本的陈述，而不是经过的时间、硬件或任何实现。

其直接前身是 Amanov、van den Berg 和 Zuiddam 的工作，解释了 9/49/49/4 上限如何从多项式乘法和张量谱方法得出。他们的论文提出了每个领域的上限以及改进证明成分的操作障碍，而不是不受限制的下限。 [p5]

早期的普通等级和边界等级下界不会确定指数。引用的边界是 nnn 中的二次阶，并且当沿张量幂取根时，相对于 n2n^2n2 的常数因子改进消失。新的主张涉及渐近等级和无限制的形式电路。 [p5]

证明是通过反证法。如果在有限域上严格低于 9/49/49/4 的指数，它会让人们重复压缩测试单词列表是否不同的精确网络，最终与该任务成本的下限相矛盾。 [p3] 该论证没有实验：压缩定理与单独下界之间的不相容性是整个结果。

如何针对另一项任务来测试有关矩阵乘法的主张？该论文使用三价张量网络：顶点最多携带三位表，连线标识位位置，通过内部连线求和给出外部位表示的函数。目标任务是列表的明确性。一个列表有 2w2^w2w 个单词，每个单词长度为 2w2w2w 位，当所有单词都不同时，输出就是 1。对于 ttt 列表，网络必须计算其答案的乘积，并且其接线可以跨列表连接工作。

定理 2.2 给出了下界。在每个有限域上，存在 σ>0\sigma>0σ>0，使得对于所有足够大的 www 和每个 1≤t≤2w1\le t\le2^w1≤t≤2w，最小三价体积超过 t nw wσt\,n_w\,w^\sigmatnw​wσ，其中 nw=2w(2w)n_w=2^w(2w)nw​=2w(2w)是每个列表的外部位数。 [p7] 边界在一批列表上保持一致是至关重要的，因为压缩会增加列表的数量。

另一方面，定理 2.1 表示，如果 ωk<9/4\omega^k<9/4ωk<9/4，则对于每个 η>0\eta>0η>0，一个足够大的、大小为 m≤n1.05m\le n^{1.05}m≤n1.05 且至少具有 nnn 个外部位的三价网络最多具有大小为 size 的张量幂d(mh−γ+ehη)d(mh^{-\gamma}+eh^\eta)d(mh−γ+ehη)，其中 h=⌈log⁡2n⌉h=\lceil\log_2n\rceilh=⌈log2​n⌉，γ>0\gamma>0γ>0，且 d≤no(1)d\le n^{o(1)}d≤no(1)。 [p7] 从一个排序网络开始，以求明确性，大小为 O(nww2)O(n_w w^2)O(nw​w2)。对于任何 η<σ\eta<\sigmaη<σ，固定次数的压缩使得每个输入位的成本为 O(wη)O(w^\eta)O(wη)，这违反了大 www 的列表下限。 [p8] 这里节省的是网络顶点和连线，而不是运行时间。

为什么应该用矩阵乘法指数控制张量网络？该论文为张量分配了一个“价格”，即局部线性映射下的数量单调性以及直和和张量积下的加法。共享指数价格的对数就像共享该指数的站点之间的距离。对于乘法张量，三个成对共享的索引形成一个三角形，并且秩分解将它们替换为一个公共标签。关键配置是带有单元臂的三脚架，因此尖端到尖端的距离为 2，并且 8/38/38/3 的共享标签率给出 6/(8/3)=9/46/(8/3)=9/46/(8/3)=9/4。低于 9/49/49/4 的严格保存排除了该关键配置。 [p3][p4]

该桥使用特殊构造的球体张量，该球体张量取决于标记点；这些点的碰撞通过控制宽度的腿将张量扩展为收缩。在相同的严格储蓄假设下，价格变得同步，并且这些碰撞恒等式在张量族中很有用。该论文表明，球体张量的价格渐近匹配在最便宜的公共站点准备张量并将其腿运输到目的地的成本。 [p51]所有这些都是矛盾的条件输入，而不是快速算法的独立演示。

几何输入如何节省体积？在严格的假设下，作者导出了 O(h)O(h)O(h) 位记录的稳定排序，大小为 O(nhp)O(nh^p)O(nhp)，对于 1<p<21<p<21<p<2；指数低于 222 很重要，因为碰撞会消耗轨道腿宽度的平方。 [第59页]

球体张量操作分别将网络的布线设置为两个球体形式，通过缝合线移动插入，并将它们合并，以便大型表格变得集中，同时数量保持受控。批处理和排序查询在张量副本之间分摊表查找，迭代集中和查找给出压缩定理。 [p76] 两种结构仅在 ωk<9/4\omega^k<9/4ωk<9/4 下成立。

假设的严格保存会将精确的独特性网络压缩到列表下限证明不可避免的容量阈值以下，因此指数不能低于 9/49/49/4。与已知的上限相结合，这缩小了差距。 [第107页]
