author: Matthias Bastian
article_content:
AI models keep getting better, but putting them to work mostly creates friction, a new Anthropic report finds. Review bottlenecks, employee pushback, security risks, and outdated custom tools are dragging down many enterprise projects.

Anthropic's researchers conducted 66 in-person interviews at 58 US companies for the qualitative study, from AI startups to established firms in law, construction, finance, medicine, and manufacturing. The authors note that the sample isn't representative because every participant is an Anthropic customer. Still, it offers a detailed look at nearly 300 real-world AI deployments.

The findings from the "Working with AI"report amount to a reality check for anyone expecting quick efficiency gains. Respondents say 55 percent of the deployments studied produced higher output or better quality. But almost one in five (19 percent) still delivers no business value. Those deployments get stuck in internal bottlenecks (6 percent), lose their time savings to review work (5 percent), or have unclear effects (8 percent).

External hurdles like regulation (4 mentions) and skeptical customers (13 mentions) barely came up. The real pain happens inside the companies themselves, according to the report.

### AI output overwhelms reviewers and sparks workplace friction

The most common obstacle cited in Anthropic's full report (PDF) is the volume of AI output that humans still need to check (49 mentions). Employee resistance (43 mentions) and required expert reviews and testing (42 mentions) rank close behind. In one case, an AI agent added one stray "S"to an API call and derailed a carefully planned software release.

AI also tends to speed up only parts of a workflow while other departments fall behind (20 mentions). One industrial equipment maker found that AI could translate its product interface text into 10 languages with ease. The company shut the feature back down because nobody on staff could field customer support calls in those languages.

That uneven pace breeds day-to-day conflict as power users flood coworkers with AI-generated text. The report mentions "Claude grenades"and "Claude cannons,"as when an employee casually sends IT seven pages of AI-written instructions.

Skeptics push back and refuse to read AI-written emails at all. One frustrated executive put it bluntly, saying, "A mediocre engineer with an AI is a menace to society."

Anthropic's findings echo the broader "workslop"debate. In a survey by BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab, 40 percent of US workers said they regularly receive shallow AI content from colleagues. Workers spend an average of nearly two hours dealing with each incident, and the survey found that trust within teams takes a hit.

### Job fears drive quiet resistance among employees

Employee resistance is the second most common obstacle in Anthropic's study, with 43 mentions. Pushback is most visible when companies roll out AI from the top down to automate entire workflows.

Only two of the 58 companies reported direct layoffs tied to AI automation, and five dismissed workers who refused to use AI. But the hiring impact is already visible. Two-thirds of the companies surveyed are hiring fewer people because of AI. Nine firms also cut outside contractors, mostly offshore roles in software development, customer support, design, and legal services.

That creates a dilemma for skilled workers, the report says. They're asked to use their knowledge to build and review the very AI systems that could make their own jobs obsolete. "If I'm open to this, I'm essentially building my own coffin,"one employee told the researchers. One manager said she woke up at 3 a.m. worried about her career and asked Claude how she could protect herself from being replaced.

In practice, that fear triggers both open and quiet pushback. When one company tried to speed up application reviews with AI so it could skip 90 percent of its planned hires, human reviewers dragged their feet. Some still took more than 10 minutes per case when two minutes would have been enough.

At one law firm, conflict staff pushed back against an AI workflow that left them to handle complex potential conflicts previously passed to attorneys. The firm shelved the agent and returned to its old process.

### Workers pocket time savings as top-down automation stalls

Other employees keep AI-driven time savings for themselves, the report says. In roughly a tenth of the cases studied, the benefits went directly to workers in the form of more pleasant work or simply less of it. Another frustrated executive said their employees deliberately hide AI gains. "They don't want you to know, because they want to use those 10 hours a week to go walk their dog,"the executive said.

Workers also worry about tighter monitoring. Several companies use AI to track staff closely, with daily reports on hourly throughput and error rates, for example, or automated scoring of customer calls. One executive called it a "panopticon effect"in an interview.

Many top-down automation projects also turn out to be brittle. Expensive custom tools often become obsolete within months as AI models improve rapidly, or they end up as rarely used "zombie"apps. "It's almost like we're trying to throw darts at a spinning dart board,"one executive said of those investments.

### Employee-built AI apps turn into maintenance and security traps

Handing employees AI tools and counting on grassroots initiative only goes so far, Anthropic's researchers say. Nontechnical staff do report impressive wins from "vibe coding,"building their own tools with plain-language prompts. One accountant built an app to automate an 80-hour audit of workplace retirement plan contributions.

But standalone projects like that often fall apart in the last mile. Months later, the accountant's prototype still wasn't in production because an outside contractor had to build the final version. Companies frequently lack stable technical infrastructure (21 mentions) and staff for maintenance and support (20 mentions). The operations lead at a large law firm considered building custom recruiting dashboards but said off-the-shelf software at $30 to $100 a month is less work to maintain.

Security risks are also growing (18 mentions). "Every single employee now is a developer… creating additional attack surface every day,"one data security chief warned. Individual workers usually lack the authority to change how work is divided across a company.

### Gains stay small unless companies restructure how they work

Anthropic's data shows a clear link between bigger organizational changes and higher self-reported value from AI. Simple tools that fit into daily work without structural changes, such as presentation tools and quick data queries, often bring only small gains, respondents said.

The report outlines three ways companies are reshaping their organizations around AI. Some broaden job roles so individuals or small teams own entire workflows, cutting coordination overhead.

Others shift employees toward tasks AI can't handle, like strategic decisions, customer relationships, and quality review. Still others build shared, secure data and IT infrastructure so nontechnical staff can work with clean data instead of drowning in a mess of it (21 mentions).

Even this approach doesn't guarantee against job losses, Anthropic's researchers acknowledge. Across all three strategies, though, the report's central finding holds: the biggest pain points in AI adoption don't come from weak technology but surface where companies try to force new tools into old structures.

Our "AI Radar #2"report on why AI productivity disappears between benchmarks and balance sheets shows how individual time savings and measurable productivity gains can diverge. Workers who use generative AI save an average of 5.4 percent of their work time, according to that analysis. It's still not clear whether or when that potential will show up in measured productivity data, the authors note.

article_content_zh:
一份新的 Anthropic 报告发现，人工智能模型不断变得更好，但将它们投入使用大多会产生摩擦。审查瓶颈、员工抵制、安全风险和过时的自定义工具正在拖累许多企业项目。

Anthropic 的研究人员对 58 家美国公司进行了 66 次面对面访谈，进行定性研究，这些公司涵盖人工智能初创公司、法律、建筑、金融、医药和制造领域的老牌公司。作者指出，该样本不具有代表性，因为每个参与者都是 Anthropic 客户。尽管如此，它还是详细介绍了近 300 个现实世界的人工智能部署。

对于任何希望快速提高效率的人来说，“与人工智能合作”报告的调查结果相当于一次现实检验。受访者表示，55% 的研究部署产生了更高的产量或更好的质量。但几乎五分之一（19%）仍然没有提供任何商业价值。这些部署陷入内部瓶颈（6％），浪费了审查工作所节省的时间（5％），或者效果不明确（8％）。

监管（4 次提及）和持怀疑态度的客户（13 次提及）等外部障碍几乎没有出现。报告称，真正的痛苦发生在公司内部。

### 人工智能输出压倒审稿人并引发工作场所摩擦

Anthropic 完整报告 (PDF) 中提到的最常见障碍是人类仍需要检查的人工智能输出量（49 次提及）。员工抵制（43 次提及）和所需的专家评审和测试（42 次提及）紧随其后。在一个案例中，人工智能代理在 API 调用中添加了一个杂散的“S”，从而破坏了精心计划的软件发布。

人工智能还往往只加快部分工作流程，而其他部门则落后（20 次提及）。一家工业设备制造商发现人工智能可以轻松地将其产品界面文本翻译成 10 种语言。该公司重新关闭了该功能，因为员工中没有人可以用这些语言接听客户支持电话。

当高级用户向同事发送人工智能生成的文本时，这种不平衡的节奏会滋生日常冲突。该报告提到了“克劳德手榴弹”和“克劳德大炮”，就像一名员工随意向 IT 发送七页人工智能编写的指令一样。

怀疑论者反驳并拒绝阅读人工智能编写的电子邮件。一位沮丧的高管直言不讳地说：“拥有人工智能的平庸工程师对社会是一种威胁。”

Anthropic 的发现呼应了更广泛的“workslop”争论。 BetterUp 实验室和斯坦福社交媒体实验室的一项调查显示，40% 的美国员工表示，他们经常从同事那里收到浅层人工智能内容。员工平均要花费近两个小时来处理每个事件，调查发现团队内部的信任受到了打击。

### 对工作的恐惧引发了员工的悄悄反抗

在 Anthropic 的研究中，员工抵制是第二个最常见的障碍，共被提及 43 次。当公司自上而下推出人工智能以自动化整个工作流程时，阻力最为明显。

58 家公司中，只有两家公司报告了与人工智能自动化相关的直接裁员，还有五家公司解雇了拒绝使用人工智能的员工。但招聘的影响已经显而易见。三分之二的受访公司因人工智能而减少了招聘人员。九家公司还削减了外部承包商，其中大部分是软件开发、客户支持、设计和法律服务领域的离岸职位。

报告称，这给技术工人带来了困境。他们被要求利用自己的知识来构建和审查可能会让他们自己的工作变得过时的人工智能系统。 “如果我对此持开放态度，那么我实际上是在建造自己的棺材，”一名员工告诉研究人员。一位经理表示，她凌晨 3 点醒来，担心自己的职业生涯，并询问克劳德如何保护自己不被取代。

【核心事实细节】人类研究表明，在工作中采用人工智能最困难的部分与学习工具无关。
【行业研判】Anthropic 的研究人员对 58 家美国公司进行了 66 次面对面访谈，以进行定性研究。

title: Back-to-back cyber incidents at US financial investigators and spy agencies follow a string of federal hacks and outages
title_en: Back-to-back cyber incidents at US financial investigators and spy agencies follow a string of federal hacks and outages
author: Maximilian Schreiner
article_content:
The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) took systems offline as a precaution after unauthorized access. Hours earlier, reports emerged of a separate breach at the CIA and other US intelligence agencies that may have involved an AI tool.

FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident. The Verge reported that the agency announced on Tuesday that a limited portion of its systems had been accessed without authorization.

While FinCEN didn't disclose the scope or cause of the incident, it took some systems offline as a precaution. FinCEN's mission is to protect the financial system from illegal activity such as money laundering and terrorist financing. It also manages financial transaction data for law enforcement and collects suspicious activity reports from banks under the Bank Secrecy Act.

Banks can still file suspicious activity reports online, FinCEN says, though some services may face delays. Its telephone hotline for financial institutions isn't affected, the agency says.

### Separate breach hits US spy agencies' open-source intelligence system

The New York Times reported a breach at several US intelligence agencies just hours before FinCEN's announcement, citing US officials and others familiar with the matter. According to the Times, the intrusion hit the CIA, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA), and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI).

The report said intruders broke into an analysis system for open-source intelligence that searches publicly available, unclassified information to produce intelligence. That includes commercially available datasets, social media content, satellite imagery, and other online material, according to the report. Even though much of this data is freely available or sold by data brokers, it can be revealing when combined, the Times noted.

It's still not clear what specific data was accessed or taken. Classified information wasn't at risk, sources told the Times. One person familiar with the matter said the issue has since been resolved, and an ODNI representative said critical capabilities weren't affected.

### Attackers may have used Artex, a repurposed AI defense tool

Multiple sources told the New York Times that investigators suspect the attackers behind the intelligence breach used Artex, an AI hacking tool. A Chinese engineer released the tool in July to help organizations defend against cyberattacks. US officials and security experts say attackers have since repurposed it for offensive use.

Cybersecurity researchers have linked Artex to dozens of attacks on companies worldwide since its release, including in Japan and South Korea. Investigators haven't yet determined who was behind the US intelligence breach. Early indicators, including the use of Artex, point to possible Chinese involvement, according to two people familiar with the matter. Western officials have accused Chinese intelligence services and a network of contractors of cyberattacks on US agencies and companies for years, allegations Beijing routinely denies.

### A string of federal hacks and outages has left the US public uneasy

These reports come during a stretch of frequent technical outages and security incidents across federal agencies. Attacks aren't always the cause, and in some cases, fear of an attack triggered the disruptions. US officials told the New York Times that AI had uncovered software flaws that needed to be patched quickly. A few of those efforts produced errors.

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) reported a security incident just last week and took several internal applications offline, Nextgov said. President Donald Trump confirmed a hack of the FBI's National Crime Information Center on Saturday during a phone interview with Fox News. CNN had earlier reported the breach of the nationwide database, which law enforcement agencies use to share information on suspects. The FBI is investigating.

Other disruptions, which officials and companies say weren't caused by cyberattacks, have added to public concern. Those include a multi-day outage of the NSA's internal classified network last week and a nationwide ground stop this month that officials blamed on router maintenance issues.

Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence who Trump recently tapped as acting cyber director, tried to reassure the public on several US news shows on Sunday. Speaking on ABC's "This Week,"Clayton said cyber espionage and security incidents have long been part of American business and daily life.

article_content_zh:
美国财政部的金融犯罪执法网络 (FinCEN) 在发生未经授权的访问后将系统关闭以作为预防措施。几个小时前，有报道称中央情报局和其他美国情报机构发生了一起可能涉及人工智能工具的数据泄露事件。

FinCEN 正在调查一起网络安全事件。据 The Verge 报道，该机构周二宣布，其系统的有限部分在未经授权的情况下被访问。

虽然 FinCEN 没有透露事件的范围或原因，但作为预防措施，它关闭了一些系统。 FinCEN 的使命是保护金融体系免受洗钱和恐怖主义融资等非法活动的影响。它还为执法部门管理金融交易数据，并根据《银行保密法》从银行收集可疑活动报告。

FinCEN 表示，银行仍然可以在线提交可疑活动报告，但某些服务可能会面临延迟。该机构表示，其金融机构的电话热线不受影响。

### 美国间谍机构的开源情报系统遭遇单独违规

《纽约时报》援引美国官员和其他知情人士的话说，就在 FinCEN 宣布这一消息的几个小时前，报道了美国多家情报机构的数据泄露事件。据《泰晤士报》报道，这次入侵袭击了中央情报局、国家地理空间情报局（NGA）和国家情报总监办公室（ODNI）。

报告称，入侵者闯入了开源情报分析系统，该系统搜索公开可用的非机密信息以产生情报。报告称，这包括商业数据集、社交媒体内容、卫星图像和其他在线材料。 《泰晤士报》指出，尽管其中大部分数据可以免费获取或由数据经纪人出售，但将其合并后可能会揭示真相。

目前尚不清楚哪些具体数据被访问或获取。消息人士告诉《泰晤士报》，机密信息并未面临风险。一位知情人士表示，问题已得到解决，国家情报总监办公室的一名代表表示，关键功能没有受到影响。

### 攻击者可能使用了 Artex，一种经过改造的人工智能防御工具

多位消息人士告诉《纽约时报》，调查人员怀疑情报泄露背后的攻击者使用了人工智能黑客工具 Artex。一名中国工程师于 7 月发布了该工具，以帮助组织防御网络攻击。美国官员和安全专家表示，攻击者此后已将其重新用于进攻用途。

自 Artex 发布以来，网络安全研究人员已将 Artex 与全球数十起针对公司的攻击联系起来，其中包括日本和韩国。调查人员尚未确定谁是美国情报泄露事件的幕后黑手。据两位知情人士透露，包括 Artex 的使用在内的早期迹象表明，中国可能参与其中。多年来，西方官员一直指责中国情报部门和承包商网络对美国机构和公司进行网络攻击，但北京方面经常否认这一指控。

### 一连串的联邦黑客攻击和服务中断让美国公众感到不安

这些报告是在联邦机构频繁发生技术中断和安全事件期间发布的。攻击并不总是原因，在某些情况下，对攻击的恐惧引发了中断。美国官员告诉《纽约时报》，人工智能发现了需要快速修补的软件缺陷。其中一些努力产生了错误。

Nextgov 表示，美国农业部 (USDA) 上周报告了一起安全事件，并下线了多个内部应用程序。唐纳德·特朗普总统周六在接受福克斯新闻电话采访时证实，联邦调查局国家犯罪信息中心遭到黑客攻击。美国有线电视新闻网 (CNN) 早些时候曾报道全国数据库遭到破坏，执法机构利用该数据库共享嫌疑人信息。联邦调查局正在调查。

title: Top Nvidia chips still for sale in China, despite U.S. ban
title_en: Top Nvidia chips still for sale in China, despite U.S. ban

inline_images.alt: Top Nvidia chips still for sale in China, despite U.S. ban

author: Joshua Yang
article_content:
SHENZHEN, China — Sellers at Huaqiangbei market, a sprawling electronics bazaar, hawk smartwatches, consumer drones, motherboards — and cutting-edge Nvidia chips supposedly barred from China by the U.S. Commerce Department.

This open defiance of U.S. export controls is in evidence in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, just a few miles from the state villa where President Donald Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping last week and hailed him as a “friend.”

During a recent visit, one vendor in a corner of Huaqiangbei at first denied that he knew where to find high-end Nvidia chips. Then, he relented.

The day's top stories, curated by Washington Post editors. Sign up for free

After making a few calls to suppliers, he quoted a price of 20 million renminbi — around $3 million — for a server containing eight Blackwell B300s, the most advanced Nvidia chips produced.

The traders of Huaqiangbei form part of a vast effort in China to secure vaunted Nvidia chips and keep up with the United States, which China lags in the artificial intelligence race. In recent weeks, that effort has only grown more urgent as the U.S. tightens its export controls following an alleged Chinese espionage plot targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who was forced by his board to step down before a whiplash return on Monday.

In a sign that their supply networks are coming under strain from the fast-moving events in the U.S., Huaqiangbei vendors said that the prices of Nvidia chips have risen drastically in the past few weeks.

Two months ago, a Blackwell B300 server was priced at just $2 million, according to Wu, a vendor who spoke on the condition that he be identified only by his last name for fear of official scrutiny. “If U.S. authorities or Nvidia restrict the supply, the price will rise,” Wu said. “But of course, after a certain point, the demand will be very low. It’s not good for our business.”

The prices in Huaqiangbei, which fluctuate as market conditions change, illustrate a complex and ever-evolving battle between Beijing, Washington and Nvidia to widen or narrow the supply of U.S. chips available to China.

Nvidia chips are the “decisive factor” in the AI competition between the U.S. and China, Chan said. “Who can get access to the best Nvidia chips matters tremendously.”

Finding U.S.-restricted Nvidia chips to buy in Shenzhen is simply a matter of asking the right person.

Vendors across multiple buildings of Huaqiangbei market quoted prices of $3 million to $3.4 million for a single B300 server with eight graphics processing units, or GPUs. Development of a cutting-edge AI model can require tens of thousands of these B300 GPUs.

Since Nvidia introduced its Blackwell series of chips in 2024, the U.S. has banned their shipment to China over security concerns and a stated desire to protect the U.S. technological edge.

But in a sign of the Trump administration’s shaky approach to enforcement — including sporadic waivers of the rules — Blackwells are available in Shenzhen, along with other export-controlled Nvidia chips critical for developing the most advanced artificial intelligence models. It is not illegal under Chinese law for vendors to sell chips, regardless of U.S. law.

“If I ever wanted to be a big [Chinese AI developer] and I needed a bunch of Blackwells, I would just go to Huaqiangbei and work out a deal,” said Joshua Woodard, founder of the Sparrows, a Shenzhen-based supply chain consultancy.

The stalls tend to attract a mix of fledgling start-ups, independent developers and foreign customers, vendors said.

For the past four or five years, Russians and Iranians have come to buy Nvidia chips at Jason Cheng’s stall, he said.

“We don’t care which country a customer comes from, as long as they can pay,” said Cheng, who spoke on the condition that he be identified only by his English name to avoid drawing the attention of authorities.

The Washington Post was not able to verify the authenticity of the proffered Blackwells, which are stored in off-site warehouses — some in Shenzhen, others in nearby Hong Kong, according to the vendors, who requested up-front deposits to view the chips in person.

One vendor, whom The Post contacted online, shared a photo of a sealed crate in a Shenzhen warehouse, saying that it contained Blackwell B300s.

Other chips were easier to track down. In his stall, Wu openly displayed what appeared to be Nvidia RTX 5090 chips and said he also had RTX PRO 6000 chips in stock. Both are significantly cheaper than the Blackwells but can be used in AI development and remain restricted for export from the U.S.

Wu’s chips are usually sourced from Hong Kong, he said, acknowledging their restricted status. “We’re not clear about where they are before Hong Kong. But the United States sells the 6000s to other countries in the world, don’t they?”

In an emailed statement, Liu Chang, the spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, wrote: “China’s position on U.S. chip exports to China is consistent. China opposes the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security and abusing export control measures, which disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains.”

Washington began cracking down on export control violations earlier this month in response to the revelation first reported by the New York Times that Nvidia’s Huang had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a customer of the company and an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. (The two are not related.)

The affair set off alarms in Washington, but even during the 11-day period of Huang’s ouster from Nvidia, scrutiny around the California-based tech company continued. For U.S. policymakers, Huang’s affair broadened into a wider issue: “Whether Nvidia was either knowingly or unknowingly allowing for its chips to eventually be accessed by Chinese companies,” Chan said.

Most high-end Nvidia chips have been under U.S. export controls since 2022, but the products nevertheless have made their way into China, according to Trump administration officials.

China also made little effort to conceal that it was getting the chips. Procurement records for Chinese research institutes and universities, which are public, list acquisitions of export-restricted Nvidia chips through 2025 and 2026, including as recently as last month.

Nvidia has denied it knowingly defied bans to sell chips to China, though it carried out a years-long lobbying campaign in Washington to loosen the restrictions.

Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

In Washington, the flow of the chips was aided by disagreements within the Trump administration on how stringently to enforce the export controls, which fall under the purview of the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS).

This month, that infighting spilled into public view as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for turning a blind eye to Nvidia chips slipping into China.

Leadership was lacking “from day one,” said a former BIS official who served in the second Trump administration, speaking on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. “There was no direction on what to do and no help on what to do.”

The former BIS official, along with another former senior administration official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share sensitive details, said enforcement was slowed by the stipulation that Jeffrey Kessler, the head of BIS, had to personally approve many routine actions. That included traveling overseas and contacting other parts of the U.S. government to investigate alleged violations, the former BIS official said. “Everything was having to go across his desk for an action to be taken. He has been hands on and gumming up the works for so much of this.”

The Commerce Department and BIS did not respond to requests for comment.

Uneven enforcement aside, the Commerce Department at times authorized the sale of restricted chips. Earlier this year, it approved a plan to sell nearly 580,000 export-controlled Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, two of which are linked to the country’s military, according to documents released last week by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

U.S. authorities have since pledged to tighten rules around export controls, including closing the loophole on Chinese firms “renting” the computing power of Nvidia chips stationed outside China.

But it remains to be seen whether Lutnick enforces the export controls, Chan said. “They might go along with the letter of the law, but are they going to go along with the spirit of the rule and really take it all the way?”

Lutnick and Nvidia now face a bipartisan reckoning in Washington. Democratic members of Congress and Trump administration officials alike have called for deeper scrutiny into Nvidia’s business practices and the Commerce Department’s handling of the scandal, with some Democrats urging Lutnick’s ouster.

For all their shaky implementation, U.S. export controls were monitored by Chinese officials with growing concern — and defiance.

“Experience has shown us that we cannot be choked by ‘chokeholds,’” Xi said in a speech last December, referring to Washington’s effort to halt China’s inflow of Nvidia chips.

But in Beijing, policymakers disagreed over whether Chinese companies should continue procuring Nvidia chips or whether the country should lean on homegrown chipmakers to reduce reliance on its chief geopolitical rival.

China’s Ministry of Commerce is generally believed to favor importing Nvidia chips, while the National Development and Reform Commission, a powerful macroeconomic planning body, seeks to build up domestic chipmaking capacity, Chan said.

The closest Nvidia competitor in China is tech juggernaut Huawei, which is behind the Ascend line of chips intended for use in AI model development. Huawei’s chips fall well short of Nvidia’s, however, and the latest Chinese AI models, including those released by DeepSeek, relied at least partially on Nvidia chips, analysts say.

“It’s a question right now about whether the really big models … can be trained on purely Huawei chips,” Chan said. Training a model entirely on domestic technology, he said, “would mark a huge milestone for China’s chip industry and AI industry.”

Meanwhile, China’s AI industry faces broader obstacles. Aside from difficulties in securing enough Nvidia chips to train new models, Chinese companies — many of which offer free access to their models — are still struggling to find ways to turn a profit.

Wu, the Shenzhen vendor, thought the scramble in China to snap up Nvidia chips was overblown. He said he knew U.S. AI companies have shaky financials — but unlike their Chinese counterparts, the Americans could buy Nvidia chips without a black-market markup and charge for user subscriptions. “If you use such high-end equipment, at such a high cost, to offer models for free, how long can you support this enterprise?” he said.

The Chinese AI industry “is in a very tough place,” Chan said. Its revenue is “just far, far lower than what you would see from OpenAI or Anthropic.”

(The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.)

Still, amid the industry’s pessimism, Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s chief executive on Monday came as a bright spot for the vendors of Huaqiangbei.

“We all support Jensen Huang. He is a standard-bearer of Nvidia,” Cheng said. “When he was replaced, we were concerned that GPU prices would keep rising. Now that he is back, we have more confidence that GPU prices will stay relatively stable.”

Isaac Arnsdorf in Washington and Lyric Li in Seoul contributed to this report.

article_content_zh:
中国深圳——华强北市场上的卖家，这是一个庞大的电子市场，售卖的是 hawk 智能手表、消费级无人机、主板——以及据说被美国商务部禁止进入中国的尖端英伟达芯片。

这种对美国出口管制的公然蔑视在中国南方城市深圳显而易见，距离唐纳德·特朗普总统上周会见中国领导人习近平并称他为“朋友”的国家别墅仅几英里。

在最近的一次采访中，华强北一个角落里的一个小贩起初否认他知道在哪里可以找到高端的英伟达芯片。后来，他心软了。

当天的头条新闻，由《华盛顿邮报》编辑策划。免费注册

在给供应商打了几次电话后，他对一台包含八个 Blackwell B300（Nvidia 生产的最先进芯片）的服务器的报价为 2000 万元人民币（约合 300 万美元）。

华强北的交易员是中国为获得引以为傲的英伟达芯片并追赶美国而做出的巨大努力的一部分，而中国在人工智能竞赛中落后于美国。最近几周，随着美国加强对英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋的间谍阴谋，美国收紧了出口管制，英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋周一在董事会的压力下被迫辞职，因此这一努力变得更加紧迫。

华强北供应商表示，过去几周英伟达芯片的价格大幅上涨，这表明他们的供应网络正因美国的快速发展事件而承受压力。

据供应商 Wu 透露，两个月前，一台 Blackwell B300 服务器的售价仅为 200 万美元。由于担心受到官方审查，他只透露了自己的姓氏。 “如果美国当局或英伟达限制供应，价格就会上涨，”吴说。 “但当然，到了一定程度之后，需求就会非常低。这对我们的业务不利。”

华盛顿智库布鲁金斯学会研究员凯尔·陈 (Kyle Chan) 表示，英伟达并未公开披露其高端芯片的价格，但同等 B300 服务器在美国的零售价约为 50 万至 60 万美元。

华强北的价格随着市场条件的变化而波动，这表明北京、华盛顿和英伟达之间为扩大或缩小对中国的美国芯片供应而展开复杂且不断演变的斗争。

陈表示，英伟达芯片是中美人工智能竞争的“决定性因素”。 “谁能获得最好的 Nvidia 芯片至关重要。”

在深圳寻找美国限制购买的英伟达芯片只需询问合适的人即可。

华强北市场多座大楼的供应商对一台配备 8 个图形处理单元 (GPU) 的 B300 服务器的报价为 300 万至 340 万美元。开发尖端的 AI 模型可能需要数以万计的 B300 GPU。

自 Nvidia 于 2024 年推出 Blackwell 系列芯片以来，美国出于安全考虑和保护美国技术优势的明确愿望，禁止将其运送到中国。

title: Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?
title_en: Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?
author: Terrence O'Brien
article_content:
The emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools like Reverse Engineer Anything has caused chaos in the music gear world, leaving companies scrambling to figure out how to respond. While some, like Roland, have remained silent for now, others have embraced the modding community. In the last several weeks, as it’s become clear that no piece of music gear is safe from Claude and a subreddit full of curious tinkerers, companies have begun making more and more of their devices open source.

The biggest name to decide “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em” is inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more. “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want,” inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell tells The Verge. That includes a recently launched SDK and several open-source devices, including the recently teased MPC Sample Key.

Akai is trying to walk a fine line, offering modders access while keeping its products reliable for professionals. O’Donnell says the company will “try to give them a reset button” so “they can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.”

Behringer has also rushed to cash in, announcing a slew of open-source devices. In just a matter of weeks, it announced a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick, a clone of the E-mu SP-1200, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller, all of which are open source. It’s unclear when any of these products might launch.

M-Vave’s FM-1 helped kick-start the whole movement. The $70 pocketable clone of the iconic Yamaha DX7 became the synth of the summer not just because of its dirt-cheap price and faithfully re-created ’80s tones, but because it also turned out to be infinitely hackable. There are well over a dozen different custom firmwares for the FM-1. M-Vave responded by releasing an open-source firmware with more features for developers to build on. The company also confirmed that a successor, the FM-2, is in development and will be open source as well.

Other companies have also embraced the modding community. Erica Synths recently released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine, but founder Ģirts Ozoliņš isn’t necessarily fully on board with vibe coding. “Inventions succeed if they solve some fundamental problems, right?” he tells The Verge. “So, I’m still wondering what fundamental problem vibe coding solves.”

“We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community.”

While he can’t imagine a producer simply stacking his studio with a bunch of hacked FM-1s running various synth engines, he’s curious to see what the community cooks up for the LXR. And he does see a benefit in making music tech a little less disposable. “What I like on the upside of this is that there is some trace of sustainability. Instead of buying five or 10 plastic boxes, you can try options on one,” he says, though he’s under no illusions about the environmental impact of vibe coding. “Of course it by far does not offset data center impact on the planet and on ecology and stuff like that.”

Polyend has also gotten on board, open-sourcing its line of Tracker grooveboxes. The Polish company’s decision to open its arms to vibe coders isn’t too much of a surprise. Last year it released the Endless guitar pedal, which lets users vibe-code their own effects. Opening its other instruments to AI tinkering feels like a natural extension.

Elektron is less thrilled about the emergence of vibe-coded mods. The company banned links to custom firmware from its official forums, saying, “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them (potentially rendering them unusable), prevent future updates, affect warranty coverage.”

Elektron’s CPO Christian Alsing told YouTuber EZBOT that he was sympathetic to the hacker community and that the company has roots there with its first instrument, the Sidstation (based on the iconic SID sound chip from the Commodore 64). He also said that he believes users have a right to modify their devices as they see fit. But he pushed back on the idea that Elektron is “withholding features,” an accusation that Akai also faced.

Ģirts also defended Elektron, saying, “people tend to blame the company, saying they are hiding features ... you design an instrument, you have a specific concept in mind, and you cannot foresee millions of possibilities ... it’s not about hiding features; it’s more about having an idea of how an instrument should look and work.”

Other major music manufacturers, like Roland, Korg, Arturia, and Novation – all of whom did not comment for this story – have yet to issue any public statements about the explosion of AI-aided custom firmwares.

key_points_zh: 主体与场景：Terrence O'Brien在全球大模型开源社区与技术研发一线
核心事实：Vivi 编码是否已使开源成为合成器的新常态？
动因背景：超算集群极速扩张面临区域电网承载与清洁能源供应瓶颈，倒逼科技巨头深度布局专用能源基础设施以保障算力生命线。
key_points_en: Key Development: Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?

article_content_zh:
强大的振动编码代理和逆向工程等工具的出现在音乐装备世界中造成了混乱，使公司忙于找出应对方法。虽然像罗兰这样的一些人目前保持沉默，但其他人已经拥抱了模组社区。在过去的几周里，随着克劳德和充满好奇的修补匠的 Reddit 子版块显然没有任何音乐设备是安全的，公司已经开始将越来越多的设备开源。

决定“如果你不能打败他们，就加入他们”的最响亮的名字是 inMusic，它是 Akai、Moog、Native Instruments 等公司的母公司。 inMusic 首席执行官 Jack O’Donnell 告诉 The Verge：“我们将向社区提供一个工具箱，我们将提供 MPC 或 Sample 等的内部运作方式，以便人们可以做他们想做的事情。”其中包括最近推出的 SDK 和多个开源设备，其中包括最近发布的 MPC Sample Key。

Akai 正在努力走一条微妙的路线，为改装者提供访问权限，同时保持其产品对专业人士的可靠性。奥唐纳表示，该公司将“尝试给他们一个重置按钮”，这样“他们就可以进行试验，然后就不会失去他们所拥有的东西。”

贝林格 (Behringer) 也急于获利，推出了一系列开源设备。短短几周内，它就宣布推出售价 150 美元的 MPC One 克隆版 Kick、E-mu SP-1200 克隆版、Anima DJ 控制器、Ignite 音序器和 Polykeys 61 MIDI 控制器，所有这些都是开源的。目前尚不清楚这些产品何时推出。

M-Vave 的 FM-1 帮助启动了整个运动。这款价值 70 美元的便携式克隆标志性 Yamaha DX7 成为今年夏天的合成器，不仅因为其极其便宜的价格和忠实地再现了 80 年代的音色，还因为它还具有无限的可破解性。 FM-1 有十多种不同的定制固件。 M-Vave 对此做出了回应，发布了开源固件，其中包含更多功能供开发人员构建。该公司还确认，后续产品 FM-2 正在开发中，并且也将开源。

其他公司也加入了改装社区。 Erica Synths 最近发布了其 LXR-02 鼓机的源代码，但创始人 Ģirts Ozoliņš 不一定完全支持氛围编码。 “如果发明能够解决一些基本问题，那么它们就会成功，对吗？”他告诉The Verge。 “所以，我仍然想知道氛围编码解决了什么基本问题。”

“我们将为社区提供一个工具箱。”

虽然他无法想象制作人会在自己的工作室中简单地堆放一堆运行各种合成器引擎的被黑客入侵的 FM-1，但他很想知道社区为 LXR 准备了什么。他确实看到了让音乐技术不再那么一次性的好处。 “我喜欢它的好处是它有一些可持续性的痕迹。你可以尝试购买一个塑料盒，而不是购买 5 个或 10 个塑料盒，”他说，尽管他对氛围编码对环境的影响不抱任何幻想。 “当然，到目前为止，它并不能抵消数据中心对地球、生态等的影响。”

Polyend 也加入进来，开源了其 Tracker 凹槽盒系列。这家波兰公司决定向氛围编码员张开双臂，这并不令人意外。去年，它发布了 Endless 吉他踏板，让用户可以对自己的效果进行振动编码。向人工智能开放其他工具感觉像是一个自然的延伸。

Elektron 对振动编码模组的出现并不那么兴奋。该公司禁止在其官方论坛上提供自定义固件的链接，并表示：“我们始终会警告不要对我们的固件和/或机器进行修改，因为这些修改可能会导致固件和/或机器变砖（可能导致它们无法使用）、阻止未来的更新、影响保修范围。”

Elektron 的 CPO Christian Alsing 告诉 YouTuber EZBOT，他对黑客社区表示同情，并且该公司的第一款仪器 Sidstation（基于 Commodore 64 的标志性 SID 声音芯片）就扎根于此。他还表示，他相信用户有权根据自己的需要修改他们的设备。但他反驳了 Elektron“保留功能”的观点，Akai 也面临着这一指控。

Ģirts 还为 Elektron 进行了辩护，他说：“人们倾向于责怪该公司，说他们隐藏了功能……你设计了一款仪器，脑子里有一个特定的概念，但你无法预见数百万种可能性……这不是隐藏功能；更多的是了解仪器应该如何外观和工作。”

其他主要音乐制造商，如 Roland、Korg、Arturia 和 Novation，都没有对本文发表评论，但尚未就人工智能辅助定制固件的爆炸式增长发表任何公开声明。

article_content:
Walmart-backed fintech major PhonePe has revived its IPO plans and restarted discussions with investment bankers, targeting a March 2027 listing at a valuation of $12 Bn to $15 Bn, sources told Inc42.

The Bengaluru-based company plans to file updated IPO papers by December-end for an offer for sale of up to ₹12,000 Cr ($1.3 Bn). Notably, PhonePe was valued at $14.5 Bn during General Atlantic’s $600 Mn secondary investment in 2025. Sources said PhonePe expects greater clarity by December-end on two regulatory issues affecting the company’s business – the merchant discount rate (MDR) framework for UPI transactions and the 30% market-share cap for third-party UPI apps. A possible extension or relaxation of the cap could ease a regulatory overhang ahead of the proposed listing, the sources said. PhonePe declined to comment on the IPO development. The Economic Times first reported on the revival of its listing plans. The renewed push comes after PhonePe paused its IPO plans in March, citing geopolitical uncertainty and volatility in global capital markets. At the time, the company said it would restart the process once markets stabilised.

The rally in Indian equities and foreign portfolio investors’ return to net buying appear to have given PhonePe greater confidence to revive its listing plans.

PhonePe is seeing stronger growth in lending and operating revenue, the sources said. The company’s lending business has grown around 100%, while operating revenue has increased 35%-40% QoQ. The company is also expected to report a net profit, they added. This would mark a turnaround from FY26, when PhonePe reported a net loss of ₹2,792 Cr. Operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr from ₹7,105 Cr in FY25.

The lending business offers PhonePe a route to diversify revenue beyond its core payments operations. Its growth and contribution to profitability will be relevant to the company’s pitch to public market investors.

Beyond financial performance, the regulatory outlook remains central to PhonePe’s IPO preparations.

Introducing MDR on select UPI transactions could create an additional revenue stream for payment companies. However, whether such charges will be introduced remains uncertain.

The other issue is the National Payments Corporation of India’s (NPCI) 30% cap on UPI transaction volumes handled by individual third-party application providers (TPAPs). NPCI had extended the compliance deadline for existing apps exceeding the cap to December 31, 2026.

PhonePe operates above the threshold, making any further extension or relaxation significant for its growth plans ahead of the proposed public market debut.

Its renewed listing push also coincides with IPO preparations at payments infrastructure major Razorpay.

Razorpay has received SEBI’s approval for its proposed ₹5,000 Cr–₹6,000 Cr public offering. It is targeting a valuation of around $5 Bn (₹47,000 Cr), with a listing likely between January and March 2027, sources previously told Inc42. The timeline could put its debut ahead of PhonePe’s proposed March listing.

article_content_zh:
消息人士告诉 Inc42，沃尔玛支持的金融科技巨头 PhonePe 已恢复 IPO 计划，并重新启动与投资银行家的讨论，目标是 2027 年 3 月上市，估值为 120 亿至 150 亿美元。

这家总部位于班加罗尔的公司计划在 12 月底之前提交更新的 IPO 文件，并提出出售高达 12,000 卢比（13 亿美元）的要约。值得注意的是，在 General Atlantic 于 2025 年进行 6 亿美元二次投资期间，PhonePe 的估值为 145 亿美元。消息人士称，PhonePe 预计到 12 月底，影响该公司业务的两个监管问题将更加明确——UPI 交易的商家折扣率 (MDR) 框架和第三方 UPI 应用程序 30% 的市场份额上限。消息人士称，可能延长或放宽上限可能会缓解拟议上市之前的监管压力。 PhonePe 拒绝就 IPO 进展发表评论。 《经济时报》首先报道了其重启上市计划的消息。 PhonePe 在 3 月份以地缘政治不确定性和全球资本市场波动为由暂停了 IPO 计划后，又重新推出了这一举措。当时，该公司表示，一旦市场稳定，将重新启动该流程。

印度股市的反弹和外国投资组合投资者恢复净买入，似乎让PhonePe更有信心重启其上市计划。

消息人士称，PhonePe 的贷款和营业收入增长强劲。该公司的贷款业务增长约100%，营业收入环比增长35%-40%。他们补充说，该公司预计还将报告净利润。这将标志着 2026 财年出现好转，当时 PhonePe 报告净亏损 2,792 卢比。营业收入从 2025 财年的 7,105 印度卢比增长 11.5% 至 7,920.5 印度卢比。

贷款业务为 PhonePe 提供了一条在核心支付业务之外实现收入多元化的途径。它的增长和对盈利能力的贡献将与该公司向公开市场投资者的推销相关。

除了财务业绩之外，监管前景仍然是 PhonePe IPO 准备工作的核心。

在选定的 UPI 交易中引入 MDR 可以为支付公司创造额外的收入来源。不过，是否会征收此类费用仍不确定。

另一个问题是印度国家支付公司 (NPCI) 对个别第三方应用程序提供商 (TPAP) 处理的 UPI 交易量设置 30% 的上限。 NPCI 将超出上限的现有应用程序的合规期限延长至 2026 年 12 月 31 日。

PhonePe 的运营高于门槛，因此任何进一步的延期或放松对其在拟议的公开市场首次亮相之前的增长计划都具有重要意义。

其重新上市的努力也与支付基础设施巨头 Razorpay 的 IPO 准备工作同时进行。

Razorpay 的 5,000 Cr 至 6,000 Cr 公开发行计划已获得 SEBI 批准。消息人士此前告诉 Inc42，该公司的估值目标约为 50 亿美元（47,000 印度卢比），可能于 2027 年 1 月至 3 月期间上市。其上市时间可能会早于 PhonePe 计划于 3 月份上市的时间。

title: PrismML shrinks a 54 GB language model to 5.9 GB by reducing every weight to just three possible values
title_en: PrismML shrinks a 54 GB language model to 5.9 GB by reducing every weight to just three possible values
author: Jonathan Kemper
article_content:
Startup PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an updated version of its aggressively compressed language model. It's based on Qwen3.8-27B and takes up just 5.9 GB of memory, same as its predecessor. That's possible because of ternary quantization, where each weight can only be one of three values (−1, 0, or +1) instead of the usual 16-bit storage. At full precision, a model this size would need about 54 GB.

Bonsai 2.5 is designed to perform more reliably on agentic tasks that involve long chains of tool calls. It needs fewer passes and tokens than Bonsai 2, and it's less likely to get stuck in loops or spiral into drawn-out reasoning phases.

The benchmark numbers reflect the improvement. On SWE-bench Verified, the score jumps from 60.8 to 75.6 percent. The full Qwen model hits 80.6. On AppWorld, an agent benchmark, Bonsai leaps from 51.2 to 90.5, landing just behind the base model. On LiveCodeBench v6, the new version scores slightly lower than its predecessor.

On an RTX 4090, the model generates about 204 tokens per second using multi-token prediction. The weights are available under an Apache 2.0 license and run via llama.cpp on Nvidia and Intel GPUs, as well as through MLX on Mac, iPhone, and iPad. PrismML grew out of a research team at Caltech and is backed by Khosla Ventures, Google, and Samsung, among others. The company first introduced Bonsai 27B in July, built on an older Qwen model. Its smallest variant needed less than 4 GB of memory, small enough to run directly on an iPhone.

title: ‘Rejection Will Have Consequences’: Inside Trump’s Demands to Another Chips CEO
title_en: ‘Rejection Will Have Consequences’: Inside Trump’s Demands to Another Chips CEO
author: Noah Shachtman
article_content:
The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.

Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”

Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”

Days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”

President Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.

Fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the company’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.

It’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official says. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”

Documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.

“The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.

“It's just straight-up coercion,” says Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The company starts making decisions not based on what's best for the company in the short or long term, what's best for shareholders, but what's best for politics and what the government is demanding.”

“That's not what you want from any company,” he adds. “When you're talking about the world's most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that's a huge problem.”

Representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

The parallels between Nvidia’s government-assisted autogolpe and Intel’s alleged forced sale aren’t exact. In the Intel case, Trump all but accused the company’s boss of being compromised by Beijing; in the Nvidia situation, the president reportedly dismissed concerns from his own intelligence agencies about the executive’s connections to China. But both instances show a growing fusion of private enterprise and public office.

During the Biden administration, Intel won awards for up to $11 billion in government grants and contracts, much of it under the CHIPS Act, which was meant to help build semiconductor manufacturing and assembly plants in America and bolster domestic research.

At the time, there was some grumbling inside the Commerce Department, which administered the CHIPS and Science Act grants, about funding what was seen as a “failing incumbent” in the semiconductor space, says the former official. (Intel had, in recent years, fallen on hard times.) But by March 2025, Intel had received about $2.2 billion of the grants. That’s when President Trump told Congress that the CHIPS Act was “a horrible, horrible thing.” The rest of Intel’s money was put on hold, tied to hitting certain milestones, while the administration said it was renegotiating the deals.

The same month Lip-Bu Tan was hired as Intel’s new CEO. Soon after, his ties to China made him a Trump target, when Reuters reported that Tan had invested in “hundreds of Chinese tech firms,” some with connections to Beijing's military. Tan’s former firm, Cadence Design Systems, pleaded guilty to violating US sanctions by selling semiconductor designs to a restricted Chinese military university, and agreed to pay more than $140 million in fines. Tan was never personally charged, but the violations happened while he was the CEO.

Two weeks later, the president was watching Maria Bartiromo’s show on the Fox Business Network. It mentioned a letter a senator had sent Intel about the China ties. Trump posted, "The CEO of INTEL is highly CONFLICTED and must resign, immediately. There is no other solution to this problem."

Tan went to the Oval Office on August 11 to see if there was, in fact, another solution. He got 40 minutes with the president, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Tan claimed his experience in China was a strength, not a detriment. According to the book Regime Change, Tan argued that there was no way he could’ve known about every one of the deals his many companies made; Trump, who had his own sprawling business empire, surely knew what that was like. Tan promised to give up his holdings in China, according to a letter Tan shared with Intel’s board, and put any proceeds into a blind trust.

“The primary goal was to eliminate any worries about Lip-Bu himself, his Cadence background and his investments with China,” according to a source with knowledge of the matter. But there were major financial concerns for Intel, too. “We had declining revenues and needed money.”

Neither Tan’s letter, excerpted in the complaint, nor Trump’s social media posts praising the CEO after the meeting mentioned anything about giving the government a chunk of the company. Yet Trump later insisted that a deal had been cooked up right then and there. “He came in, he saw me, we talked for a while. I liked him a lot, I thought he was very good,” the president told the Wall Street Journal. “I said, ‘You know what? I think the United States should be given 10% of Intel.’ And he said, ‘I would consider that.’”

“I should’ve asked for more. It was so easy,” Trump later recalled.

According to the court filing’s review of Intel’s internal documents, Shapiro—a former partner at the New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz—made a verbal offer on August 18. Ultimately, in exchange for the cut of Intel, the Trump administration would free up the $8.9 billion US government grants that it had already won. They wanted about a tenth of the company’s stock for free, in exchange for Washington keeping the commitment it had already made.

Then came the call in which Shapiro insisted there was no room for negotiation. “The board needs to consider,” he said, according to Intel’s summary of his remarks included in the court documents, the “benefits of having a friend in this administration and what the administration can do to help Intel (including with customers).”

Intel’s board met, and decided they hated the deal. “The economic terms that had been

proposed [by] the Administration were not, in their current form, attractive to the company,” minutes of the meeting, reprinted in the lawsuit, noted.

But they went ahead with it anyway. Paisner’s lawyers say in the court documents the board took the offer thrust forward by the administration. Intel’s attorneys disagree, arguing in their motion to dismiss that there was some back-and-forth deal-making, and it made the agreement more favorable to the company. The grants became “immediately available” while “strategically aligning the interests of Intel’s stockholders and the US Government.”

On August 25, Lutnick released a video with Tan, sitting side-by-side on cushioned chairs. “I really look forward to have the US government be my shareholder,” Tan turned to Lutnick and said. “And we can work together and make Intel great again.”

Inside the company, the video was “a surprise to everyone,” according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter. Some employees joked that it was reminiscent of a “hostage video.”

Not long after that, Nvidia—led by Tan’s friend Jensen Huang—made a $5 billion investment in Intel. “I love seeing their stock price go up, making the USA RICHER, AND RICHER,” Trump posted. “Who would not want to make deals like that?”

Deals, plural. On the day Tan was hauled to the Oval Office, Trump announced that his administration had been negotiating separately with Huang. The Nvidia leader was beyond eager to sell more of his semiconductors to China. “And I said, if I'm going to do that, I want you to pay us as a country something,’” Trump said. They settled on 15 percent of all sales of the H20 model chip. Months after that, they cut a second deal: a 25 percent bounty on sales of Nvidia’s even-more advanced H200 chips.

In their lawsuit against Nvidia, Paisner’s attorneys argue the surcharges amount to “unlawful taxes,” and that the board’s “decisions to enter into such agreements are the product of mismanagement and breaches of fiduciary duty.”

In court, NVIDIA’s lawyers insisted that the company “did not enter into any illegal ‘agreement’ with the government but instead engaged with the government and stated that it would comply with federal regulations.” Moreover, the attorneys say Paisner is trying to make a political point, rather than a legal one. “When asked about his purpose in bringing this action,” they write, “Paisner was candid: ‘It’s to make a public point of how NVIDIA conducts itself.’”

The attorneys wrote this in May, months before Nvidia’s and Huang’s recent drama. Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said on the company’s quarterly earnings call that it did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” citing his “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” (Not to mention mounting evidence that the company’s most sophisticated chips were making their way to China, in violation of US law.) But, according to The New York Times, after days of pressure from top administration officials, the company and the government essentially struck a deal Sunday night to reinstate Huang.

“Don’t think for a second that politics ever play a role in this company, not even a little bit,” Huang said during his first company-wide meeting after rejoining the company, WIRED reported. “We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”

Additional reporting by Lauren Goode.

article_content_zh:
特朗普政府向世界领先的半导体公司之一传达的信息很明确：向美国政府提供您公司的一部分股份。现在。否则。

根据联邦诉讼中包含的公司电话内部记录，商务部律师戴维·夏皮罗 (David Shapiro) 在 2025 年 8 月告诉英特尔公司首席财务官，“不要错误地认为这是一场谈判”。 “总统预计周五将就这些条款宣布达成协议。”

根据夏皮罗为英特尔董事准备的讲话摘要，他承认“董事会可以选择不接受这一提议”。但特朗普政府官员“指出，拒绝将产生[夏皮罗]无法预测的后果。”

几天后，董事会满足了政府的要求。唐纳德·特朗普在其社交平台上发帖称：“我非常荣幸地宣布，美国现在完全拥有并控制英特尔 10% 的股份。” “美国没有为这些股份支付任何费用，这些股份现在的价值约为 110 亿美元。这对美国来说是一笔很棒的交易。”

特朗普总统周一也同样兴高采烈，宣布他已“说服”英伟达董事会重新聘请首席执行官黄仁勋。这一宣布引起了震惊。但这并非完全没有先例。

法庭文件称，十五个月前，特朗普政府干预了另一家主要芯片制造商的领导决策。当时和现在一样，有关该公司首席执行官与中国关系过于密切的指控层出不穷。当时和现在一样，特朗普政府关心的是该公司的财务未来。

商务部的一位前成员告诉《连线》杂志，这是整个政府、特别是商务部内部更广泛转变的一部分。这位前特朗普政府官员表示，旧的指标“比如创造就业机会或美国更具竞争力或拥有更多市场份额”已经过时了。在与私营企业打交道时，最重要的一个问题是：“你们会以现金形式回馈政府吗？”

作为股东对英特尔董事会提起诉讼的一部分，未经编辑的文件显示出政府为了得到自己想要的东西愿意付出多大的努力。 WP Intelligence 此前曾报道过该诉讼的指控。

诉讼称，“委员会在总统威胁的阴影下运作，屈服于政府的勒索。”同一股东理查德·佩斯纳 (Richard Paisner) 在 4 月份对 Nvidia 提起了第二起诉讼，要求提供内部记录。

“这只是直接的强制，”自由主义卡托研究所副所长斯科特·林西科姆说。 “公司开始做出决策时，不是基于短期或长期对公司最好的事情、对股东最好的事情，而是基于对政治最好的事情以及政府的要求。”

“这不是你想从任何公司得到的，”他补充道。 “当你谈论世界上最具创新性的公司和这些不仅具有巨大经济影响而且还具有国家安全影响的尖端技术时，那就是一个大问题。”

英特尔代表拒绝对此事发表评论。白宫、商务部和英伟达没有回应置评请求。

英伟达政府资助的 autogolpe 与英特尔所谓的强制出售之间的相似之处并不确切。在英特尔案中，特朗普几乎指责该公司老板受到北京方面的妥协；据报道，在英伟达事件中，总统驳回了他自己的情报机构对该高管与中国的关系的担忧。但这两个例子都表明私营企业和公职部门日益融合。

在拜登执政期间，英特尔获得了高达 110 亿美元的政府拨款和合同，其中大部分是根据《CHIPS 法案》获得的，该法案旨在帮助在美国建立半导体制造和组装工厂，并支持国内研究。

author: Wall Street Journal
article_content:
The Nvidia soap opera took another wild turn Monday when its board announced Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. Investors loved it, and sent Nvidia’s shares up more than 30% while other AI stocks pared losses from last week’s rout. Call it the Donald Trump market put, but his extraordinary political intervention will have legal and political costs.

Mr. Trump proudly claimed credit for the board’s decision to bring Mr. Huang back less than two weeks after he was pushed out. “I convinced them,” he told CNBC. “I made the deal.” The board “did ask for assurance on the national security threat,” he added. “And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot.”

While analysts view Huang's return as largely positive for Nvidia and the broader AI trade, some say the AI chipmaker is not out of the woods yet.

Huang will appear before Congress committees for questioning on Dec. 1.

Retail sentiment for NVDA dipped to 'bullish' from 'extremely bullish.'

As Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Congress hearing looms, President Donald Trump has said his government could potentially pardon him if he is indicted, while adding that he didn't think such an act would be necessary.

The President even said he has thought about having the U.S. government take a stake in Nvidia, similar to its stake in Intel in 2025, saying "it's probably not too late," according to comments made to the New York Post.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Huang, one of the most prominent figures in the AI industry, was reinstated by Nvidia's board on Monday in a reversal after Trump intervened on his behalf.

Trump told the Post that it was his understanding that Huang had not had affairs with other women linked to Beijing and that he did not know how many affairs Huang had acknowledged.

NVDA stock rallied 31.5% the same day, but the rally lost steam. Shares dipped nearly 6% in Tuesday's session and another 2.2% in overnight trading.

While Huang's return as Nvidia chief is a major shot in the arm for the company and the broader AI trade, some commentators say the AI chipmaker is not out of the woods yet.

On Dec. 1, Huang will appear for a closed-door meeting with the House Foreign Affairs, China Select, and Intelligence committees on topics including his affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, and his company's security protocols. He will testify before the Senate Banking Committee later that week.

Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers from both parties sharply criticized Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang, saying Congress should tighten restrictions on China's access to the company's advanced AI chips and scrutinize the circumstances surrounding Huang's return, Reuters reported.

Still, some remain confident for Nvidia, given the record demand for AI servers and Huang's track record as an excellent leader and deal-maker.

"Even using a new formula discounting for affairs and every possible risk method and outcome. With Jensen at Nvidia. My Nvidia chips using AI analysis come up with $242 a share," Ross Gerber, CEO of investment firm Gerber Kawasaki, said in an X post, signaling a 56% upside.

Timothy Teter, Nvidia's general counsel, sold $4.5 million worth of company shares, according to an exchange filing on Tuesday. The divestiture was through several trades made on Nov. 19.

On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for NVDA dipped to 'bullish' from 'extremely bullish' as of late Tuesday, and message volume dipped to 'high' from 'extremely high.'

"$NVDA The most profitable AI company, with a CEO backed by the president of the US who needs him to succeed... and at a discount. What else do we need?" said a trader.

Another, with a contrarian view, wrote: "$NVDA Trump can only shield him for one more month .Come January Dems are gonna expose him as a traitor . This goes under $125 easy."

Year-to-date, NVDA stock is down 16.5%.

article_content_zh:
周一，英伟达肥皂剧再次发生疯狂转变，董事会宣布黄仁勋恢复首席执行官职务。投资者很喜欢它，英伟达的股价上涨了 30% 以上，而其他人工智能股票则收复了上周暴跌带来的损失。称之为唐纳德·特朗普市场看跌期权，但他非凡的政治干预将带来法律和政治成本。

特朗普自豪地宣称，董事会在黄先生被赶出不到两周后就决定让他重新回归。 “我说服了他们，”他告诉 CNBC。 “我达成协议了。”他补充说，董事会“确实要求就国家安全威胁做出保证”。 “我们至少用我们所知道的一切向他们保证，而且我们知道很多。”

虽然分析师认为黄仁勋的回归对英伟达和更广泛的人工智能行业来说基本上是积极的，但一些人表示这家人工智能芯片制造商尚未摆脱困境。

黄将于 12 月 1 日在国会委员会接受质询。

NVDA 的零售情绪从“极度看涨”降至“看涨”。

随着英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋的国会听证会临近，唐纳德·特朗普总统表示，如果他被起诉，他的政府可能会赦免他，同时补充说他认为没有必要这样做。

根据《纽约邮报》的评论，总统甚至表示，他已经考虑过让美国政府入股英伟达，就像 2025 年入股英特尔那样，并称“可能还不算太晚”。

黄仁勋是人工智能行业最著名的人物之一，在特朗普代表他进行干预后，英伟达董事会于周一恢复了黄仁勋的职位。

特朗普告诉《华盛顿邮报》，据他了解，黄没有与其他与北京有关的女性发生过婚外情，而且他不知道黄承认了多少婚外情。

虽然黄仁勋重新担任英伟达首席执行官对该公司和更广泛的人工智能行业来说是一剂强心剂，但一些评论人士表示，这家人工智能芯片制造商尚未摆脱困境。

与此同时，据路透社报道，美国两党议员严厉批评英伟达让黄仁勋复职的决定，称国会应加强对中国获取该公司先进人工智能芯片的限制，并仔细审查黄仁勋回归的情况。

title: Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long
title_en: Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long
author: Aarian Marshall
article_content:
In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.

Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?

Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.

Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.

“Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” says Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”

This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.

But just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring new hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.

In September, the National Science Foundation announced a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a new center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.

“Turbulence is the reason we don’t have fusion energy yet,” says Murillo, who heads up the new center, called Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence, or Tempest. The chaotic swirling of superhot plasma inside a reactor allows heat to leak out, preventing the material from reaching the temperatures needed to allow nuclei to fuse. The US federal government wants to get closer to figuring that out.

“Closer,” because turbulence is impossible to perfectly predict, scientists say. For one thing, turbulence occurs at many different, small scales at the same time. Air swirling around an airplane breaks into eddies, then smaller eddies, and then even smaller eddies, with each interacting with each other—too many variables, happening too quickly, to mathematically account for. For another, tiny changes—wind speed, temperature—can eventually dramatically alter air movement, suddenly altering the turbulence once predicted. To make perfect forecasts, one would need a perfect picture of exactly what’s going on in the atmosphere at all times.

But increasing sophisticated applications of machine learning could allow scientists to get closer to knowing what’s going to happen when, says Murillo. And while brute, computational force can’t solve the turbulence problem, AI agents might give the effort a boost. OpenAI’s blockbuster announcement this fall that it had resolved the Navier-Stokes problem—equations that are the beginning of all turbulence models—suggests LLMs could help.

“Turbulence has been a problem only human minds could work on; as of this year, that's no longer true,” says Murillo.

To make flying better, the aviation industry doesn’t necessarily need to solve turbulence. It needs to get better at knowing what sort of conditions create it and not send airplanes there.

One company in Tel Aviv, SkyPath, uses those in-plane iPads and their accelerometers to collect and share crowdsourced data between different airplanes, even if they don’t fly for the same airline. (This sort of dating sharing can be a sensitive topic for competing companies; SkyPath says it assuages these concerns by ensuring that data is anonymized before it’s shared.) More than 40,000 of these devices have SkyPath installed on them, says CEO Maya Shpak; the company says that several major airlines, including American, use the technology. SkyPath combines that collected data with additional information, including weather forecasts, and uses machine intelligence to make predictions about the future state of the air. The app helps pilots avoid turbulent air and warn passengers and crew members that choppiness is coming, 10 to 15 minutes before it happens.

One pilot named Eric who uses SkyPath, who asked WIRED not to use his full name because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said the app is a helpful tool that allows him to warn passengers what to expect. His issue is the same as those studying turbulence: One can’t take measurements everywhere all at once.

“It’s like any crowdsourced software,” says the pilot. “It only works if everyone uses it, and no one wants to use it until everyone else is.” Today, several large operators are using the app, which makes it especially useful in areas with lots of flights, he says.

Cornman, the physicist, wants to keep all these advances in perspective. “No matter what people say, we’re not getting close to 100 percent, 90 percent, 80 percent [predictive accuracy] anytime soon,” he says. “It’s too complicated a problem.” Smoother skies, if not perfect ones, are ahead.

article_content_zh:
1500 年代初，一位名叫莱昂纳多·达·芬奇 (Leonardo da Vinci) 的意大利博学家对一种现象进行了很好的研究，这种现象让紧张的飞行员恐惧地抓紧飞机座位，空乘人员匆忙地将推车推回厨房：湍流。

达芬奇对混乱的水涡流着迷，其运动如此复杂，以至于他根据自己的观察结果画了数百幅图画。到底为什么水——实际上是任何液体，无论是大气还是心脏中的血液——会以这种方式移动？

现在世界有了 ChatGPT、自动驾驶汽车和太阳能发电厂，但仍然不完全了解湍流是如何运作的。密歇根州立大学理论与计算物理学教授迈克尔·穆里略（Michael Murillo）表示：“这是经典物理学中最难解决的问题，也是我们需要解决的问题。”

现在，大量数据驱动的预测和避免湍流的努力可以让乘客更接近平稳飞行。根据国际航空运输协会的数据，飞机发动机在一小时的商业飞行中会产生 20 TB 的数据，飞机在飞行途中还会广播更多数据：GPS 位置、高度、速度。 “电子飞行包”基本上是一个专门的iPad，配备了导航图和手册，只要飞机的互联网连接配合，就可以传输自己的信息。卫星观察并收集这一切。

美国国家科学基金会国家大气研究中心的物理学家拉里·科曼（Larry Cornman）几十年来一直在研究湍流，他说：“空中交通量增加了，通信成本和在飞机上安装计算机的成本都下降了。” “现在是时候致力于这些事情了，因为我们可以做到。”

这对于航空安全来说是个好消息。根据美国联邦航空局的数据，2009 年至 2023 年间，美国飞机上有 200 多人在与湍流相关的事件中受重伤。湍流也越来越严重。气候变化改变了世界急流周围的大气条件，产生了不稳定的风切变。从飞机的驾驶舱来看，这会转化为突然的、晴空的湍流，难以看到或预测。从历史上看，飞行员避免湍流的唯一方法是听取那些在他们之前不小心经历过湍流的人的警告，并希望一切都没有改变。

但就在过去两年，科曼在湍流领域数十年的研究成果以前所未有的方式投入到该领域，这是美国联邦政府和航空业协调的几个项目的一部分。当科曼和美国联邦航空局空中交通管制员确定联邦要求的飞机位置、高度和速度广播可以用来发现意外的湍流时，一个突破出现了，而不需要机上安装新的硬件或软件。研究人员可以利用这些众包的公共数据来预测湍流何时何地会出现。

9 月，美国国家科学基金会宣布向九所大学提供 3000 万美元的资助，以建立一个新的中心，致力于预测空气中的湍流、聚变反应堆内的带电粒子以及横跨太空的气体云中的湍流。

“湍流是我们还没有聚变能的原因，”穆里略说，他是这个新中心的负责人，该中心名为多物理和科学湍流工程的变革性探索，或称暴风雨。反应堆内超热等离子体的混乱旋转会导致热量泄漏，从而阻止材料达到原子核聚变所需的温度。美国联邦政府希望进一步解决这个问题。

科学家表示，“更接近”是因为湍流不可能完美预测。一方面，湍流同时在许多不同的小尺度上发生。围绕飞机旋转的空气会分裂成漩涡，然后是更小的漩涡，然后是更小的漩涡，每个漩涡之间相互作用——太多的变量，发生得太快，无法用数学来解释。另一方面，微小的变化——风速、温度——最终可能会极大地改变空气运动，突然改变曾经预测的湍流。为了做出完美的预测，人们需要一幅关于大气中任何时候正在发生的事情的完美图片。

但穆里洛表示，日益复杂的机器学习应用可以让科学家更接近地了解何时会发生什么。虽然简单的计算力无法解决湍流问题，但人工智能代理可能会推动这一努力。今年秋天，OpenAI 重磅宣布它已经解决了纳维-斯托克斯问题（该方程是所有湍流模型的开端），这表明法学硕士可以提供帮助。

“湍流一直是一个只有人类大脑才能解决的问题；截至今年，情况已不再如此，”穆里略说。

为了让飞行变得更好，航空业不一定需要解决湍流问题。它需要更好地了解什么样的条件会造成这种情况，而不是将飞机派往那里。

特拉维夫的一家公司 SkyPath 使用这些机内 iPad 及其加速计来收集和共享不同飞机之间的众包数据，即使它们不执飞同一家航空公司。 （这种约会共享对于竞争公司来说可能是一个敏感话题；SkyPath 表示，它通过确保数据在共享之前进行匿名化来缓解这些担忧。）首席执行官 Maya Shpak 表示，其中超过 40,000 台设备安装了 SkyPath；该公司表示，包括美国航空在内的几家主要航空公司都使用该技术。 SkyPath 将收集到的数据与包括天气预报在内的附加信息相结合，并使用机器智能来预测未来的空气状况。该应用程序可帮助飞行员避开湍流，并在风浪即将来临前 10 到 15 分钟警告乘客和机组人员。

title: The secretive Iranian cyber unit behind Europe’s freezer hacks
title_en: The secretive Iranian cyber unit behind Europe’s freezer hacks

inline_images.caption: A notice informing customers that refrigerators are out of service at a Delhaize Shop & Go near Brussels © Stephanie Lecocq/Reuters
inline_images.alt: A notice informing customers that refrigerators are out of service at a Delhaize Shop & Go near Brussels © Stephanie Lecocq/Reuters

author: Tom Wilson
article_content:
One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history: cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food.

Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command.

The group, which often goes by the online persona CyberAv3ngers, has a history of targeting critical infrastructure. In 2023 and 2024, it hacked Israeli-made industrial control devices inside water, manufacturing and transportation systems across several US states. Operational disruption was minimal, but the attackers left a message each time: “Every equipment ‘made in Israel’ is CyberAv3ngers legal target.”

State-backed Iranian hackers have rarely targeted Europe in this way, however. October’s hacks, experts say, mark an escalation in the Islamic republic’s cyber warfare strategy and a new willingness to hit European infrastructure.

“Iran has very clearly messaged that the global economy will be disrupted as a consequence of it being shut out from the world,” said Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations.

While France and other European countries have largely stayed out of the US and Israel’s campaign against Iran, which started in February, the Islamic republic increasingly views all Nato countries as legitimate targets, she continued. “This is about sowing panic in Europe and increasing that global pain threshold.”

Similar attacks were staged this month against supermarkets in 10 other countries across Europe, though no group has yet been blamed.

Iran has denied any role in the freezer hacks, but France is seeking international arrest warrants for three Iranians allegedly involved: Hamid Reza Lashgarian, believed by US intelligence to be head of the Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command, and two Shahid Kaveh leaders, 37-year-old Mahdi Lashgarian and 35-year-old Reza Salarvand. Both Lashgarians were placed under US sanctions in 2024.

Often staffed with young engineers and software developers, the Revolutionary Guards’ cyber units have developed formidable skills in espionage and cyber warfare.

“Iran is a country of engineers, and people continue to underestimate its capabilities,” said Sanam Vakil, Middle East director at Chatham House think-tank. “It has a long history of successful cyber operations,” she added, noting that Iran had learnt through its own experience of cyber attacks, most notably the Stuxnet assault on its nuclear programme by the US and Israel in 2009.

French intelligence agencies have said the group used a Chinese-made scanning tool to scour the public internet for connected refrigeration units. Infrastructure linked to the group also conducted reconnaissance using Modbus, a digital language widely used to control industrial machinery — a technique Shahid Kaveh has employed since at least April, according to the authorities.

The modus operandi described by the French authorities was consistent with the Iranian attacks in the US in 2023 and 2024, said Cynthia Kaiser, former deputy cyber director at the FBI. Near-identical hacks to those have taken place this year, though CyberAv3ngers did not claim responsibility and US authorities stopped short of explicitly blaming Iran.

Kaiser said it was also possible that a third state could have contracted Shahid Kaveh to conduct the European attacks. “Even if Iranians were behind the keyboard, these attacks really appear more consistent with Russian-type targeting,” she said. “It wouldn’t surprise me if we eventually uncovered collaboration behind the scenes.”Russia, like Iran, has sophisticated cyber capabilities and has shown increasing willingness to use them against Europe.

Vakil at Chatham House acknowledged Russian involvement remained a possibility, noting that the strength of the relationship between the two countries was often under-appreciated by western officials. “Their ties have grown through the context of these wars,” she said, referring to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and Iran’s conflict with the US and Israel. In March, Russian state-sponsored hacking group NoName claimed responsibility for a series of attacks on Israeli targets.

Whether or not Shahid Kaveh was working on behalf of Moscow or another power, the operation would have to be sanctioned by the senior leadership of the IRGC, according to Gil Messing, chief of staff at Israeli cyber security group Check Point Software.

Cyber weapons have a limited shelf life, as once a specific software or hardware vulnerability has been exploited, it tends to be almost immediately patched by other potential targets.

“The decision to make such a thing and burn out this capability is something that would have to be authorised by senior levels,” Messing said. “This is not a very sophisticated attack, but it sends a very strong message.”

article_content_zh:
十月的一个晚上，黑客发动了历史上最不寻常的网络攻击之一：提高了法国数百家超市制冷系统的温度，并毁坏了数百万欧元的食品。

黑客之前曾针对商用冰箱和冰柜进行过攻击，但从未达到如此规模，也从未在欧洲中心地区进行过攻击。这次无耻的攻击让网络专业人士不确定是谁执行了如此疯狂的行动。但法国情报机构在数字线索中发现了波斯语痕迹和其他线索，指向伊斯兰革命卫队的精英黑客部队。

据称此次黑客攻击的幕后黑手沙希德·卡维 (Shahid Kaveh) 已经为西方情报机构所熟知。它以在 20 世纪 80 年代两伊战争中阵亡的伊朗指挥官马哈茂德·卡维 (Mahmoud Kaveh) 的名字命名，是革命卫队网络电子司令部监管的几个黑客单位之一。

该组织通常以网络角色 Cyber​​Av3ngers 为目标，有着针对关键基础设施的历史。 2023 年和 2024 年，它入侵了美国多个州的供水、制造和运输系统内的以色列制造的工业控制设备。运营中断很小，但攻击者每次都会留下一条信息：“‘以色列制造’的每台设备都是 Cyber​​Av3ngers 的合法目标。”

然而，国家支持的伊朗黑客很少以这种方式针对欧洲。专家表示，十月份的黑客攻击标志着伊斯兰共和国网络战战略的升级，以及攻击欧洲基础设施的新意愿。

欧洲外交关系委员会的艾莉·格兰马耶表示：“伊朗非常明确地传达了这样的信息：如果伊朗被排除在世界之外，全球经济将受到扰乱。”

她继续说，虽然法国和其他欧洲国家基本上没有参与美国和以色列自二月份开始的针对伊朗的行动，但伊朗伊斯兰共和国越来越多地将所有北约国家视为合法目标。 “这是为了在欧洲播下恐慌并提高全球的痛苦阈值。”

本月，欧洲其他 10 个国家的超市也遭受了类似的攻击，但尚未有任何组织受到指责。

伊朗否认与冰箱黑客攻击有任何关系，但法国正在寻求对三名涉嫌参与的伊朗人发出国际逮捕令：美国情报机构认为是伊朗卫队网络电子司令部负责人哈米德·礼萨·拉什加里安 (Hamid Reza Lashgarian)，以及两名沙希德·卡维 (Shahid Kaveh) 领导人，即 37 岁的迈赫迪·拉什加里安 (Mahdi Lashgarian) 和 35 岁的礼萨·萨拉万德 (Reza Salarvand)。两名拉什加人均于 2024 年受到美国制裁。

革命卫队的网络部队通常配备年轻的工程师和软件开发人员，他们在间谍活动和网络战方面拥有强大的技能。

“伊朗是一个工程师的国家，人们仍然低估了它的能力，”查塔姆研究所智囊团中东主任萨南·瓦基尔说。她补充说：“伊朗拥有成功的网络行动的悠久历史。”她指出，伊朗已经从自己的网络攻击经验中吸取了教训，其中最著名的是 2009 年美国和以色列对其核计划发起的 Stuxnet 攻击。

法国情报机构表示，该组织使用中国制造的扫描工具在公共互联网上搜索联网的制冷设备。与该组织相关的基础设施还使用 Modbus 进行侦察，Modbus 是一种广泛用于控制工业机械的数字语言，据当局称，Shahid Kaveh 至少从 4 月份起就开始使用这种技术。

FBI 前网络副主任辛西娅·凯泽 (Cynthia Kaiser) 表示，法国当局描述的作案手法与 2023 年和 2024 年伊朗对美国发动的袭击一致。今年发生了与这些几乎相同的黑客攻击，尽管 Cyber​​Av3ngers 没有声称对此事负责，而且美国当局也没有明确指责伊朗。

凯撒表示，第三个国家也有可能与沙希德·卡维签订合同来发动欧洲袭击。 “即使伊朗人在键盘后面，这些攻击确实看起来更符合俄罗斯式的目标，”她说。 “如果我们最终发现幕后合作，我不会感到惊讶。” 俄罗斯和伊朗一样，拥有先进的网络能力，并且越来越愿意利用它们来对抗欧洲。

title: Asia Data Centers Sound Out US Clients to Replace China Demand
title_en: Asia Data Centers Sound Out US Clients to Replace China Demand

inline_images.caption: New US AI chip rules against China threaten Southeast Asia’s data centers
inline_images.alt: New US AI chip rules against China threaten Southeast Asia’s data centers

author: Bloomberg
article_content:
Washington has spent years stopping advanced AI chips from physically reaching China. It turns out the chips never had to travel at all.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department issued a rule aimed at Chinese companies that tap high-end AI hardware sitting in data centers outside China. The move lands hardest on Southeast Asia, a region that has been building server farms at a brisk clip.

The rule comes from the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS. It is an interim final rule, with an effective date of approximately November 16, 2026.

Its core target is remote access. A Chinese firm does not need to own an Nvidia or AMD chip to use one. It can simply rent compute from a facility abroad and run its workloads over the internet.

The rule also reaches data centers directly. Any facility providing significant compute to Chinese entities needs a license and must carry out enhanced due diligence once it crosses a threshold of over 12 million aggregate TPP.

Operators get a 90-day compliance window after the rule takes effect. Those that miss it may face future restrictions.

There is one notable carve-out. US-headquartered operators are exempt from certain licensing requirements, though they must submit monthly compliance reports.

We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.

The rule is largely a response to the scandal around Nvidia and Megaspeed, a data center operator. Megaspeed spent at least $4.6 billion on Nvidia servers between 2023 and 2025.

The controversy centers on allegations that chips were diverted and that major Chinese clients, including Alibaba, gained remote access to compute. Those are allegations, not findings, but they were enough to push regulators into action.

Markets responded quickly. Shares of Southeast Asian companies linked to data centers fell after the announcement, with some dropping by as much as 20%.

The timing invites some awkward comparisons. In early 2026, nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips had been approved for export to Chinese companies, including some with military connections.

So the same government that cleared a large volume of chips for direct sale is now tightening the screws on rented access abroad.

For the region’s operators, the immediate issue is friction. Licensing, due diligence and customer screening all take time and money, and firms tied to these data centers could face delays and higher operating costs.

The competitive picture may also tilt. Because US-headquartered providers are exempt from certain licensing requirements, they could become the preferred option for large compute buyers in the region.

Brazil’s inclusion is worth noting too. The list is not purely a Southeast Asia story, which suggests BIS is mapping where compute could flow to China rather than drawing a regional boundary.

For investors, the key dates sit on the calendar. The rule’s effective date of approximately November 16, 2026, and the 90-day window that follows, mark the period when operators must show they can comply.
