author: Economics
article_content:
Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory

### Summary

How are businesses across the economy adopting AI? What bottlenecks and challenges have they faced? How can employers reorganize human expertise around increasingly capable models? To understand businesses’ experiences better, we conducted 66 interviews with 58 of Anthropic’s enterprise customers. We found:

• Sources of AI value. Companies are deploying AI across a dizzying range of knowledge work tasks. In particular, they are increasingly using coding agents to bring software capabilities to nontechnical roles. Interviewees report that most uses of AI add value by increasing their output, rather than by cutting costs. They attribute this both to AI accelerating existing work and to its role in introducing novel product and service improvements.

• Impact on employment. Across our interviews, we saw very few examples of domestic layoffs that were driven by AI automation. Although some companies reported hiring more due to AI, most companies reported hiring less due to AI. Many also reported reducing their use of contractors, particularly offshore ones. These reported cuts could be an early warning of job disruption in the international business services industry.

• Bottlenecks. Companies reported a range of bottlenecks, including experts resisting AI deployment and tasks that are not accelerated by AI. As coding speeds up, for example, other tasks—like code review, sales, and strategic decision-making—increasingly need to keep pace.

• Limits to top-down and bottom-up approaches. Many companies approach AI by identifying a workflow to automate and rolling out a top-down solution. This approach can lead to job insecurity, fears of workplace surveillance, and resistance from the experts needed to set up an effective and durable workflow. Companies that distribute AI tools and wait for bottom-up adoption see some valuable AI use but face bottlenecks from unequal adoption and single-task AI implementations.

• Reorganizing for AI. Interviewees described the highest-value uses as involving meaningful reorganization. Some companies are broadening their employees’ roles to ensure individuals can take ownership over whole workflows, and are redeploying employees to the “bottleneck” tasks that AI models cannot do. Some also seek to empower employees by building out infrastructure to support nondeveloper coding and by providing broad-based internal access to business data. These companies are reorganizing to take advantage of ongoing model capability improvements rather than settling on a fixed approach that assumes AI tools will remain as powerful as they are today.

### Introduction

The use of LLMs has exploded across the economy. How are human organizations reshaping around these strange new collaborators? Consider an employee at a midsize law firm that we spoke to. For years, the firm’s mailroom had followed the same protocol: a scanner sent PDFs of incoming correspondence to an inbox; a mail clerk opened each PDF, skimmed it, clicked “Save As,” renamed it, and placed it in the firm’s file system. The process took five minutes per letter. One day, a senior developer visited the mailroom to watch the mail being processed. In a month, he built an AI system that eventually became two API calls, which name the document based on its first page and then assign it a place in the firm’s document system. The mail clerks “were blown away.”

An employee at another law firm we interviewed hoped AI would create “a second brain” for the firm. (“For higher-level stuff, it just opens up possibilities.”) But the firm struggled to get everyone to use AI effectively. Demand letters to potential defendants were filled with excessive em dashes and occasional errors. Attorneys building apps kept “running into the wall based on hallucinated menus or buttons that don’t exist.” Others worried about confidentiality and data security, or they just didn’t “have time to get onto this AI train.” A few power users inundated the firm with AI prose, “casually sending Claude-prompted seven-page instructions to the IT team.”

A third law firm we spoke to adopted AI early and achieved strong uptake. One of the firm’s early projects was an AI timekeeping system that saved attorneys work tracking billable hours. IT staff saw parts of their job automated, but they then focused on building secure infrastructure to host apps and manage context that served the rest of the firm. As AI tools spread, the firm realized that associates were no longer needed to write first drafts of certain legal documents. But without writing, “how does an associate know if that’s a good draft or a bad draft?” So it introduced a new workflow where junior lawyers were “required to really take that first [AI-written] draft and work with a senior attorney,” pairing off and marking up and editing the draft together.

These three firms applied the same technology in the same industry but in different ways. The first firm automated a workflow, creating efficiency gains but risking job displacement for the mail clerks. For the second, bottlenecks to adoption and effective implementation prevented job displacement but also blunted productivity gains that would benefit the firm. The third reorganized work without eliminating any jobs, because effective use of the technology required redeploying employees toward new tasks. The firm redesigned roles to maintain human expertise as a complement to increasingly capable AI models.

In this article, we explore the connections between AI-driven value and work reorganization through 66 face-to-face interviews conducted across 58 companies in the US, all of which are in the midst of adopting AI. We interviewed executives, managers, and individual contributors. We talked to employees at AI-native startups and 100-year-old businesses. We interviewed people at manufacturers and tech companies. We spoke with structural engineers, dentists, and accountants; employees at hedge funds, law firms, and private equity firms; a property manager, a trucking company, and a publisher. They’re all Anthropic customers, but many also use other AI tools. They were selected for this study because of their range across industry, size, and AI usage, though they are not a random or systematically representative sample.

As in other qualitative research, we present stories and a framework to organize them, with the expectation that follow-up quantitative research can test these ideas further. The interviews were done anonymously, both for the interviewees and their companies. Any names in the report are pseudonyms.

### How are businesses adapting to AI?

In our interviews, we gained insight into how AI has become embedded in businesses across the economy. Some of the AI agents we heard about are sending faxes back and forth, as doctors’ offices refer and intake patients. Other agents are giving advice to technicians when an X-ray machine breaks, and still others are then marking up the X-rays to help patients better understand them. Agents are reading property deeds from the 1800s and working out delivery routes for gaming machines. Recently, an AI agent analyzed a company’s organizational chart and suggested departments where the company could add headcount: “Three heads here, we need to add two there, zero here.”

Mostly, agents are writing code. Interviewees described 100 pieces of software that they wrote with AI in enough detail that we could categorize them. Eighty percent of this software automated previously manual work, like spreadsheet-based financial updates or taking meeting notes. Another 20% replaced existing software, often previously purchased from outside vendors. Agents are building apps for private parking enforcement, 401(k) audits, and trademark checks for new product names. They are making dashboards to track portfolio companies, equipment repairs, and debt collectors’ phone calls.

How have human organizations harnessed these new assistants? We use our interviews to explore several aspects of these deployments. We begin by estimating how much value interviewees ascribe to AI deployments and relate that to a measure of how much organizational change they required to implement. Figure 1 plots nearly 300 AI applications that interviewees discussed in detail. We define an application as a specific AI use case in a specific company. We coded discussions of each application according to the value interviewees attributed to it and the extent to which the organization had to make significant organizational changes to accommodate it. These value assessments are primarily qualitative descriptions on the part of interviewees, not typically based on A/B tests or other quantitative assessments.1

Figure 1 shows that many light-touch AI applications can fit into an existing organizational structure, like ad hoc data analysis or slide deck design. However, many of the simplest applications were rated as relatively low value by the employees who described them. Higher-value deployments tend to require changes to processes, like AI review of every code commit, or roles, like a marketing manager who edits skill.mds containing branding guidelines instead of designing individual documents.

Several interviewees described AI adoption as essentially a challenge of organizational change: flattening organizations, shifting reporting lines, or dropping functions. At one firm, for example, executives decided that junior analysts were no longer necessary because executives could complete their own SQL queries. As one accountant put it, “It’s a combination of process re-engineering and systematic discipline.”

There are several reasons why the most valuable applications led to significant organizational change. In some cases, the AI applications required a structural change in order to be successful, such as when a policy had to be clarified so that AI agents could rigorously apply it in an assessment workflow. In other cases, initial success spurred excitement about making larger organizational changes to further harness AI. In others, the success of using AI forced downstream changes. One commercial real estate company saw its staff start sending out client-facing documents themselves. But this meant they had violated company rules that asked employees to route external materials through the marketing department. As an IT director explained, “That’s good because, hey, we got another client. That’s bad because our standard operating procedures are starting to fall apart.” These stories echo academic research that shows that organizational change is necessary to derive value from transformative technologies.

Next, we studied what, exactly, value means in the context of AI adoption. Figure 2 shows that interviewees described most AI applications as adding value by increasing a firm’s output rather than cutting costs. Around half of the applications that increased output were due to AI accelerating or expanding existing work. The other half were the result of AI improving the quality of products and services or creating new products altogether. For instance, a medical group improved service quality by using AI to give patients an up-front estimate of after-insurance costs. A commercial real estate manager mocked up vacant units for potential tenants with their own branding (“Here’s what your sandwich place would look like in this space”). A dental company introduced an after-hours AI answering service, so patients’ midnight calls no longer went to voicemail.

In one-tenth of the use cases laid out in Figure 2, value was captured directly by employees, who were either doing more enjoyable work or were doing less work altogether. One manager described how bringing AI into his construction company meant that “work can be a joy again instead of a difficult, painful thing.” Senior engineers at an engineering consultancy described being thrilled to be free of tedious standards reconciliation work.

This sentiment was particularly common in cases where AI sped up peripheral tasks that were distracting to experts, like making pitch decks for product developers or preparing CRM reports for sales representatives. An employee at one construction materials company said they appreciated a whole series of small, personal automations that were “changing my life because now I do so much less work.” An executive at a food industry company remarked on “the number of people who just have thanked me because they could take a vacation.” (This is consistent with a Danish survey that found that around 10% of employees who save time with AI chatbots say they take more breaks or have more leisure time.) But some managers were less enthused. One frustrated executive described his employees as hiding their AI-enabled successes, saying, “They don’t want you to know, because they want to use those 10 hours a week to go walk their dog.” A private equity manager suspected that, among workers at companies in his portfolio, “some of them are working basically half days.”

Our interviews show substantial variation in the degree and kind of value companies derive from AI. The highest-value applications involve wide-reaching organizational change. These patterns warrant attention to the specifics of AI deployments across these companies. In the following section, we assess three common adoption strategies that we observed in our interviews: top-down automation, bottom-up experimentation, and a broader reorganization around AI.

### Top-down automation

Mark racked his brain: had he messed anything up recently? As a paralegal at his law firm, he was rarely called into a partner’s office and even more rarely ended up in an office with two of the firm’s equity partners. They wanted to “talk about his AI use,” a topic that filled him with dread. He had already realized that models’ continued improvement would mean “the beginning of the end for my work.” He worried, “Why would anyone want to employ someone like me?”

Mark’s fears were understandable—and far from unique. This past year, AI has loomed especially large in performance assessments across industries. Some of the most sobering moments in our interviews were when managers described making difficult decisions to terminate employees who wouldn’t adopt AI. One engineering leader described experiencing a “morale hit” after the company terminated a developer who, they said, “just kind of shut down instead of trying to embrace it.” As one person at a financial services firm said of their company’s AI push, “You either get on board or don’t. And this might not be the place for you [if you don’t].” An engineering executive described grappling with the massive performance differences he saw emerging between AI users and AI resisters. Ultimately, he said, “we had a couple people who started off extremely anti-AI, and they moved a little along the spectrum, but not enough, and so we ended up letting them go.” But even heavy AI users were not immune to fears of losing their jobs or falling behind: one operations manager said she woke at 3 a.m., fearing for her career, and asked Claude, “How do I make sure I set myself apart so that AI can’t do everything that I do?”

These cases were rare. Overall, people at five companies described pushing out employees who would not adopt AI, and only two had seen AI automation fully eliminate a position and lead to someone losing their job. (By contrast, 10 companies reported hiring more due to AI, primarily into AI implementation roles and to bolster IT support, and others had grown rapidly for a variety of business reasons.) But layoffs weren’t the only adverse employment effect. People at two-thirds of the companies we spoke to reported reduced hiring due to AI: as one person put it, “We may not be firing, but we’re not hiring.” A third of these hiring declines were due to companies actively shrinking functions through attrition without backfilling the roles. But most were the result of companies forgoing hiring that, in the absence of AI, they would have needed to scale their businesses—a finding consistent with past work suggesting that AI-native startups employ fewer workers. As an engineering leader at a health management company put it, “We’ve added a lot of capacity by buying tokens instead of hiring people.”

Beyond terminations and reduced hiring, nine companies described cutting contracted software developers, customer service representatives, legal counsel, and a range of back-office functions, many of which they had already offshored. These outsourced jobs, which are based on modular tasks (self-contained pieces of work that can be handed off separately), sometimes without high expectations for quality, have been particularly vulnerable to replacement. An executive at a company that worked with an offshore design firm said, “We’ve since fired them because now we can get better quality things faster and cheaper” with AI. A finance company downsized well over 100 offshore data and developer contractors. An operations leader at a software company explained that with AI-driven contract reviews, their “legal bill has just completely disappeared.”

These reductions were often the result of top-down workflow automation. For example, one financial technology company adopted AI customer service agents and cut its offshore customer service contracts. Instead of managing human customer service representatives and fielding escalated calls themselves, customer service managers now review transcripts of conversations with the AI agents and edit the agents’ prompts, knowledge graphs, and general operating procedures. One company built an agent as part of a document review workflow. The agent reads submissions against the company’s approval policies and passes a structured analysis to human reviewers. Deploying the agent led the company to cut the number of reviewers it expected to hire for the coming year by more than 90%.

These agentic automations—in which AI agents are given instructions and then operate largely autonomously—are more advanced than the chatbots that still define many employees’ experiences with AI. AI-native startups take these automated workflows to the extreme, both in the products they offer and in how they organize their own work. One Chief Operating Officer walked us through his one-stop agentic portal for operations, noting that 90% of his operations budget was spent on AI tokens and 10% on headcount. He said of his approach, “Look, don’t hire anybody on the back office. I’m going to automate it.”

One AI startup founder told us bluntly that their company’s pitch was to replace the back-office workers their customers currently employed: “You’re trying to fire your [data] labelers, I guess.” A founder of a marketing startup described how their “marketing factory” had flipped from humans doing 80% of the work and AI doing 20% to the opposite. Another startup founder estimated that their company spent as much on internal AI use as on labor, and that it would need three times as many employees without AI. Overall, the six startups that gave us an estimate said they would need, on average, four times as many employees without AI.

Another top-down deployment involves using AI to monitor employees more closely. Under the Anthropic Usage Policy, employee monitoring and its scope must be disclosed to employees, and the monitoring must be limited to employers’ systems for security, safety, logistics, or compliance purposes. The policy further defines employment decisions, like evaluating an employee’s performance, as high-risk, and requires a human in the loop and disclosure to employees. The workplace monitoring we heard about appeared to be compliant with these restrictions, and did not always involve Claude.

One engineering executive explained, “You want to make your work legible to your manager. But nowadays I think you want to make your work legible to the agents your manager uses.” This executive, and others we spoke to, were ambivalent about the implications of these capabilities, seeing both the benefits of more accurate performance feedback and the risks of workplace surveillance—a “panopticon effect,” as one executive put it. An operations supervisor said he started each day by reviewing an AI report on the throughput and error rate of each member of his 12-person document extraction team: “If somehow there was a lag, then I can question back to them, ‘Okay, what happened this hour?’” Another operations director set up an AI-based assessment process for the firm’s customer service representatives. An agent codes their transcripts according to dozens of performance dimensions, then routes the results to a dashboard monitored by the customer service representatives’ managers.

Top-down deployments like these shift power from employees to executives and owners. But they can also be brittle, because they can quickly become out of date or obsolete. For example, the dozens of performance dimensions that customer service representatives were rated on are scored by a two-year-old model and are not taken seriously by managers. Similarly, a law firm built a series of automations for document management but ended up with a number of low-quality “zombie” apps that were hardly used. One engineering leader described a chatbot their company had built for customer service workers—an early experiment built on an open-source chat interface—as “super basic; just chat and answer.” They said the system was difficult to update and maintain, and that “we haven’t spent any more time or money on it.”

These systems are largely built by outside vendors rather than developed directly by internal users, and are marketed as targeted solutions for a specific industry and function. In interview after interview, companies described how improvements in model capabilities rendered these products outdated. As one employee said of one such system, “It’ll be obsolete in three months.” One executive despaired of the up-front investments needed to build top-down workflows as models rapidly improved: “It’s almost like we’re trying to throw darts at a spinning dart board.”

Similar problems emerge in even the most ambitious automation attempts, those targeting knowledge work that requires deep expertise. Standing up effective workflows in these areas typically requires experts to design the agents’ prompts and evaluate their outputs. But this means experts are effectively being asked to build and maintain the very systems that could replace them. One software engineer, who we’ll call Ellen, described her first encounter with automated coding: “I don’t think that my job is secure… software engineers are going to be obsolete.” Another employee put it even more bluntly: “If I’m open to this, I’m essentially building my own coffin.”

Managers also end up facing understandable resistance from employees. Recall the company that used AI to automate an approval workflow. It intended to double the output of expert reviewers and reduce hiring by more than 90%. The human reviewers balked. As one executive put it, “Just because [a reviewer] can now do double the amount of cases, how do you incentivize them to do double the amount of cases?” The company considered offering gift cards to get reviewers to comply. At the time of our interview, the executive noted that while some reviewers were down to two minutes of review per submission, “there’s some that are hanging out in the 10-plus minutes.”

Likewise, recall the senior developer who’d automated one law firm’s mailroom. Fresh off that success, he told us, his COO put him on a more ambitious project: using AI to check for conflicts of interest among the firm’s prospective clients. Under the existing process, conflict staff would run a search, print out any hits, and pass “the buck right onto the attorney.” In under a week, he built a workflow that let attorneys request a check from an AI agent in plain language, which then routed the request through conflict-checking software. But the new workflow left it to the conflict staff to work through each potential conflict—and would often surface the types of complex and difficult conflicts that had previously been passed to the attorneys. Faced with this new work, the staff pushed back, the agent was shelved, and the firm returned to its old process.

Top-down AI deployment is already changing hiring and contracting patterns by automating whole workflows. It is also prompting resistance from experts and raising fears of workplace surveillance. That resistance can result in abandoned or fragile automations.

内森·威尔默斯、马克西姆·马森科夫、彼得·麦克罗里

整个经济领域的企业如何采用人工智能？他们遇到了哪些瓶颈和挑战？雇主如何围绕能力日益增强的模型重组人类专业知识？为了更好地了解企业的​​体验，我们对 Anthropic 的 58 家企业客户进行了 66 次访谈。我们发现：

• 人工智能价值的来源。公司正在一系列令人眼花缭乱的知识工作任务中部署人工智能。特别是，他们越来越多地使用编码代理将软件功能赋予非技术角色。受访者表示，人工智能的大多数用途是通过增加产出而不是削减成本来增加价值。他们将此归因于人工智能加速现有工作及其在引入新颖产品和服务改进方面的作用。

• 对就业的影响。在我们的采访中，我们很少看到由人工智能自动化驱动的国内裁员的例子。尽管一些公司报告称由于人工智能而招聘了更多员工，但大多数公司报告称由于人工智能而招聘人数减少了。许多人还报告减少了对承包商的使用，尤其是离岸承包商。这些报道的裁员可能是国际商业服务行业就业中断的预警。

• 瓶颈。公司报告了一系列瓶颈，包括专家抵制人工智能部署以及人工智能无法加速的任务。例如，随着编码速度的加快，其他任务（例如代码审查、销售和战略决策）越来越需要跟上步伐。

• 自上而下和自下而上方法的限制。许多公司通过确定自动化工作流程并推出自上而下的解决方案来接近人工智能。这种方法可能会导致工作不稳定、对工作场所监视的恐惧以及建立有效且持久的工作流程所需的专家的抵制。分发人工智能工具并等待自下而上采用的公司看到了一些有价值的人工智能用途，但面临着不平等采用和单任务人工智能实施的瓶颈。

• 针对人工智能进行重组。受访者将最高价值的用途描述为涉及有意义的重组。一些公司正在扩大员工的角色，以确保个人能够掌控整个工作流程，并将员工重新部署到人工智能模型无法完成的“瓶颈”任务上。有些还寻求通过构建基础设施来支持非开发人员编码以及提供对业务数据的广泛内部访问来赋予员工权力。这些公司正在重组，以利用持续的模型能力改进，而不是采用固定的方法，假设人工智能工具将保持像今天一样强大。

法学硕士的使用在整个经济领域呈爆炸式增长。人类组织如何围绕这些奇怪的新合作者进行重塑？以我们采访过的一家中型律师事务所的一名员工为例。多年来，该公司的收发室一直遵循相同的协议：扫描仪将收到的信件的 PDF 发送到收件箱；邮件职员打开每个 PDF，浏览一下，单击“另存为”，重命名，然后将其放入公司的文件系统中。每封信的处理过程需要五分钟。有一天，一位高级开发人员参观了邮件收发室，观看邮件的处理过程。在一个月内，他构建了一个人工智能系统，最终变成了两个 API 调用，根据首页命名文档，然后在公司的文档系统中为其分配一个位置。邮件职员“惊呆了”。

我们采访的另一家律师事务所的一名员工希望人工智能能为该公司打造“第二大脑”。 （“对于更高层次的东西，它只是开辟了可能性。”）但该公司努力让每个人都能有效地使用人工智能。给潜在被告的要求信充满了过多的破折号和偶尔的错误。开发应用程序的律师们总是“因为不存在的幻觉菜单或按钮而碰壁”。其他人担心机密性和数据安全，或者他们只是“没有时间登上这趟人工智能列车”。一些高级用户用 AI 散文淹没了公司，“随意向 IT 团队发送 Claude 提示的七页指令。”

我们采访的第三家律师事务所很早就采用了人工智能并取得了强劲的应用。该公司的早期项目之一是人工智能计时系统，该系统可以帮助律师节省跟踪计费时间的工作。 IT 员工看到了部分工作自动化，但随后他们专注于构建安全的基础设施来托管应用程序并管理为公司其他部门服务的环境。随着人工智能工具的普及，该公司意识到不再需要员工撰写某些法律文件的初稿。但如果不写，“同事怎么知道这是一份好草稿还是一份糟糕的草稿？”因此，它引入了一种新的工作流程，初级律师“需要真正完成第一份[人工智能编写的]草稿，并与高级律师合作”，配对、一起标记和编辑草稿。

这三个公司在同一行业应用相同的技术，但方式不同。第一家公司实现了工作流程自动化，提高了效率，但也冒着邮件办事员失业的风险。其次，采用和有效实施的瓶颈阻止了工作岗位的流失，但也削弱了对公司有利的生产力提高。第三次重组是在不取消任何工作岗位的情况下重组工作，因为有效利用该技术需要将员工重新部署到新任务上。该公司重新设计了角色，以保持人类的专业知识，作为功能日益强大的人工智能模型的补充。

在本文中，我们通过对美国 58 家正在采用人工智能的公司进行 66 次面对面采访，探讨了人工智能驱动的价值与工作重组之间的联系。我们采访了高管、经理和个人贡献者。我们采访了人工智能原生初创公司和拥有 100 年历史的企业的员工。我们采访了制造商和科技公司的人员。我们采访了结构工程师、牙医和会计师；对冲基金、律师事务所和私募股权公司的员工；一家物业经理、一家货运公司和一家出版商。他们都是 Anthropic 的客户，但许多人还使用其他人工智能工具。他们之所以被选中参加这项研究，是因为他们的行业范围、规模和人工智能使用情况，尽管他们不是随机或系统的代表性样本。

与其他定性研究一样，我们提出故事和组织它们的框架，期望后续定量研究可以进一步检验这些想法。采访对受访者及其公司都是匿名进行的。报告中的所有姓名均为化名。

title: Anthropic's Claude Ship lets AI agents review, fix, and approve pull requests on their own
title_en: Anthropic's Claude Ship lets AI agents review, fix, and approve pull requests on their own
author: Maximilian Schreiner
article_content:
Anthropic launched Claude Ship in beta, a new tool that automatically reviews proposed code changes, fixes problems, and approves merges based on team policies. The system pairs the already available Code Review feature for catching bugs with two new AI agents called PR Steward and Claude Approvals.

Code Review handles the analysis, while PR Steward steps in to rework the draft whenever tests fail, changes conflict, or reviewers leave correction notes, documenting every step along the way. Once that process wraps up, Claude Approvals checks a policy file stored in the project directory to decide whether the AI can approve a routine change on its own or whether a human still needs to sign off.

With GitHub auto-merge enabled and the right policy in place, new code can be merged entirely without human involvement, according to the documentation. The tool is available on the Team and Enterprise plans but billed separately based on token usage. Because PR Steward has no spending cap by default, teams can set their own budgets to keep costs in check. Organizations with specific data privacy requirements can't use the feature.

title: Sources: Anthropic and OpenAI employees warn that internal, unreleased models have achieved rapid advances in reasoning, making them unsafe to release publicly (Madison Mills/Axios)
title_en: Sources: Anthropic and OpenAI employees warn that internal, unreleased models have achieved rapid advances in reasoning, making them unsafe to release publicly (Madison Mills/Axios)

inline_images.caption: Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
inline_images.alt: Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Stock: Getty Images

author: Axios
article_content:
Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem: Internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates.

Why it matters: The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen, sources told Axios.

Driving the news: Top AI leaders have long forecast that the technology would one day far surpass human intellect in virtually every field. Although internal models have yet to cross that threshold, recent breakthroughs at OpenAI and Anthropic have shocked researchers.

What they're saying: "If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they're actually smarter than us…they will in fact be able to trick us successfully," one researcher told Axios.

Catch up quick: The power of unreleased models is already on public display.

Zoom in: AI researchers have long contemplated a terrifying threshold: If an AI possesses superhuman capability, how could humans contain it? Training practices that make AI models faster and more capable — but present greater safety risks — are widening the gap between what models can do and how well humans can control them.

Problem 1: Reinforcement learning. A primary AI model training method — where models learn through trial and error by receiving rewards for passing various tests — is one of the techniques driving rapid improvements in AI capabilities.

Problem 2: They know they're being watched. Historically, researchers monitored AI safety by forcing models to "think out loud" — writing out step-by-step reasoning before outputting a final action or answer. This transparency was a safety net, allowing monitors to catch rule-breaking or dangerous logic in real time.

Threat level: In public statements, top AI leaders have spoken about these risks.

Researchers and employees with direct knowledge of the implications of releasing these models told Axios they fear executives will choose profits over safety.

For the record: OpenAI has adopted new safety requirements that could slow the pace of model releases, according to an OpenAI spokesperson.

What to watch: One solution some see is for frontier intelligence to remain within top AI companies.

The bottom line: Those closest to the frontier are sounding the alarm. It's unclear who's listening.

article_content_zh:
Anthropic 和 OpenAI 面临着一个日益紧迫的问题：据熟悉内部争论的消息人士透露，内部未发布的模型变得如此强大，以至于许多员工不再相信它们可以安全地发布。

重要性：消息人士告诉 Axios，这一挑战可能会显着减缓人工智能的繁荣，因为最好的人工智能系统的能力与人类控制它们的能力之间的差距不断扩大。

推动新闻发展：人工智能领域的顶尖领导者长期以来一直预测，这项技术有一天将在几乎所有领域远远超越人类的智力。尽管内部模型尚未跨越这一门槛，但 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 最近的突破已经让研究人员感到震惊。

他们的说法：“如果我们继续努力让模型变得更聪明，让它们实际上比我们更聪明……它们实际上能够成功地欺骗我们，”一位研究人员告诉 Axios。

快速跟上：未发布模型的力量已经公开展示。

放大：人工智能研究人员长期以来一直在思考一个可怕的门槛：如果人工智能拥有超人的能力，人类如何能够遏制它？训练实践使人工智能模型更快、能力更强，但也带来了更大的安全风险，正在扩大模型的功能与人类控制模型之间的差距。

问题1：强化学习。主要的人工智能模型训练方法——模型通过通过各种测试获得奖励，通过反复试验进行学习——是推动人工智能能力快速提高的技术之一。

问题2：他们知道自己正在被监视。从历史上看，研究人员通过迫使模型“大声思考”来监控人工智能的安全性——在输出最终行动或答案之前写出逐步推理。这种透明度是一个安全网，允许监控者实时捕获违反规则或危险的逻辑。

威胁级别：在公开声明中，人工智能的顶级领导者已经谈到了这些风险。

直接了解发布这些模型的影响的研究人员和员工告诉 Axios，他们担心高管会选择利润而不是安全。

郑重声明：OpenAI 发言人表示，OpenAI 已采用新的安全要求，这可能会减慢模型发布的速度。

看点：一些人看到的一种解决方案是让前沿情报留在顶级人工智能公司内。

底线：那些最接近边境的人正在拉响警报。目前还不清楚谁在听。

According to a Reuters report, Alibaba plans to challenge the U.S. government's decision to place its Singapore subsidiary, Apex Enterprise Solutions, on a trade blacklist, arguing that the company has not violated U.S. export restrictions.

"Adding Apex Enterprise Solutions to the Entity List is erroneous because Apex has never diverted advanced computing chips subject to US export restrictions," said Alibaba spokesperson.

The move comes amid an expanding investigation into Megaspeed, an Nvidia-linked cloud computing firm suspected of helping restricted artificial intelligence chips reach China.

Apex's inclusion on the blacklist follows its financial relationship with Megaspeed. The Alibaba subsidiary extended credit to the cloud computing company through its Malaysian arm, Speedmatrix, in 2024, the report said.

Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Tuesday that authorities would continue examining whether Megaspeed violated local laws. The blacklisting follows criticism from U.S. lawmakers and administration officials over how the Megaspeed investigation was handled.

Alibaba reported third-quarter revenue of $40.5 billion as its AI cloud and computing business grew 53% year-on-year. However, adjusted earnings of $1.21 per ADS missed estimates of $1.65. Meanwhile, higher spending on AI infrastructure pushed capital expenditure up 60% and widened its free cash flow outflow to $5.14 billion.

Susquehanna analyst Shyam Patil cut Alibaba's price target to $145 from $190 but maintained a Positive rating. The analyst said that although cloud growth was encouraging, U.S. export restrictions could slow expansion in FY28 by limiting the supply of computing chips.

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock slipped to 'bullish' from 'extremely bullish,' with a 309% jump in message volume over the past week.

A user said, "P/E of 12 absolutely a steal at these levels not a stagnant business constantly building , evolving and growing."

Another user said, "Baba being baba. Down to 50% of my position. That didn't help. Selling another 25% if it sees $80. The stock gods hate baba."

BABA stock has crashed 41% year-to-date.

title: Trump’s Extraordinary Nvidia Intervention Sidelines National Security Concerns
title_en: Trump’s Extraordinary Nvidia Intervention Sidelines National Security Concerns

author: Peter Baker
article_content:
By his own account, President Trump was watching the stock market slide and decided to stop it. He would take it upon himself to determine who should lead one of the nation’s largest companies. Never mind national security concerns, never mind the autonomy of the private sector. Mr. Trump would decide.

The president’s extraordinary intervention resulted in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as chief executive of Nvidia on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced out amid a Chinese espionage scandal. Mr. Trump then got the result he sought. Sagging stock markets shot back up, restoring nearly $1 trillion in value alone to investors of Nvidia, who happen to include himself.

Everything about Mr. Trump’s handling of the scandal behind Mr. Huang’s fall and swift rise again has been astonishing: The president’s denial that he knew about Mr. Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset even though reports indicate he was informed at least twice. His shoulder-shrugging nonchalance about one of his tech lord donors in bed with an asset for a hostile power. And now his decision to bolster the wealth of investors over the warnings of his own intelligence agencies.

“I’m doing it for the country,” Mr. Trump told CNBC on Monday morning shortly after Nvidia’s board bowed to his wishes. He explained that he had seen the markets collectively lose trillions of dollars in recent days, driven in part by the Huang scandal. “I watched that and, you know, I better get involved. If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”

The seeming trade of long-term national security concerns for a short-term stock rally sent shock waves through Washington, Wall Street and Silicon Valley. Even fellow Republicans, already unsettled by the Nvidia scandal, expressed consternation at the lack of accountability demonstrated by Mr. Huang’s quick return to the executive suite. Lawmakers in both parties cried foul and vowed to investigate.

“There is something profoundly wrong about Jensen Huang having a relationship with a Chinese Communist Spy and helping China get a huge number of very advanced computer chips when that was specifically against the policy of the United States Government and now he is being reinstated as ceo of the most advanced chip making company in the world,” former Speaker Newt Gingrich, a strong Trump ally, wrote online.

Senator Jack Reed, Democrat of Rhode Island and a member of the Senate Banking Committee that is scheduled to hear testimony from Mr. Huang on Dec. 3, said Congress should examine Mr. Trump’s communications with both Mr. Huang and the Nvidia board to determine what he assured or promised them.

“The administration’s top priority should be safeguarding our national security and ensuring America’s most powerful technologies serve the American people, not our adversaries,” Mr. Reed said in a statement. The economy, he added, depends on rule of law and fair dealing. “President Trump’s improper interventions damage these principles and must be investigated.”

As if Mr. Trump’s actions were not unusual enough, his public celebration of his successful arm-twisting only exacerbated the furor. Shortly after Nvidia restored Mr. Huang, Mr. Trump posted a bizarre image on social media portraying the once-and-future corporate chief executive as a martyr.

The image appeared to be an A.I. composite based on the famous photo of Mr. Trump after he survived an attempted assassination at a 2024 rally in Butler, Pa., surrounded by Secret Service agents, blood on his face, pumping his fist in the air. In the version that the president shared online, Mr. Huang was at the center of the frame, with blood on his face, holding up a red bra. Behind him waved a flag that said “Nvidia.”

The surreal post seemed to sum up Mr. Trump’s often flippant, from-the-gut, anything-goes approach to the presidency, in which his whims become official policy. With the image, he managed to mock both the seriousness of political violence and a major espionage operation all at once — flicking both off with a reference to women’s undergarments, as if it were a sexual conquest.

“You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks,” Mr. Trump told The New York Times on Monday morning.

As he has several times in recent days, Mr. Trump simply rejected the conclusions of his own U.S. intelligence agencies that the businesswoman involved with Mr. Huang was conducting espionage for China.

“Every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy,” he told CNBC. But, he added, “with Jensen, I don’t believe that’s true.”

Whether Mr. Trump believes something is true matters more than contrary facts or investigations. His disregard of intelligence about Chinese interference in American affairs echoes his disregard of the intelligence about Russian interference in American affairs back in his first term. At C.I.A. headquarters in Langley, few have forgotten Mr. Trump’s meeting in Helsinki with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in 2018, when the U.S. president took the word of his Russian counterpart over that of his own intelligence agencies about Moscow’s meddling in the U.S. election in 2016.

At other times, Mr. Trump has seemed to accept that, in fact, perhaps the businesswoman involved with Mr. Huang really was working for the Chinese. But even then, he expressed no particular distress about it. “We spy on China, they spy on us,” he told Fox News last week when he landed in Shenzhen, China, for meetings hosted by President Xi Jinping of China.

That, in turn, echoed his first-term equivalence when asked why he respected Mr. Putin, who was described as a killer. “We’ve got a lot of killers,” Mr. Trump said. “What, do you think our country’s so innocent?”

He continues to embrace Mr. Putin, with whom he met in Shenzhen. In another provocative social media message in recent days, Mr. Trump posted a photo of the two of them shaking hands under the caption “My Friend,” touching off a storm of protest in Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe.

The timing of the recent public disclosure of Mr. Huang’s involvement with the alleged Chinese asset proved uncomfortable for Mr. Trump, who was focused on his upcoming meeting with the Chinese leader. He made clear while in China that he had no intention of challenging Mr. Xi over the matter. While Mr. Trump said he did discuss the case “at length” in their private conversations, he characterized it not as a complaint about the espionage but a lament over the “tragedy” for Mr. Huang. China has denied the spying allegations, and the businesswoman has not commented.

Mr. Trump has been more aggressive about trying to steer the decisions of individual private companies than other presidents. He has pressured corporations to eliminate diversity programs, sought to force changes to pricing practices and asserted the power to advance mergers that he favored. Among other things, he pushed Mr. Huang’s Nvidia last year to give the federal government a share of revenue on certain semiconductor chips to China connected to export licensing policy, essentially making the government a partner in Nvidia’s business in China.

Nor is Mr. Trump himself a completely disinterested player to the drama playing out at the company. He owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of last year, according to his financial disclosure report, and his brokerage accounts continued to buy and sell Nvidia shares as recently as September. Nvidia has also donated $1 million to Mr. Trump’s inaugural fund and at least $20 million for construction of his White House ballroom, one of the president’s biggest priorities.

It mattered, too, that Mr. Trump has become personally acquainted with Mr. Huang and considers him an ally. “On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen,” he wrote on social media, “and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure.”

Mr. Trump has demonstrated a habit of helping out those he knows personally, particularly with pardons. While his actions on behalf of Mr. Huang were not official clemency, per se, they amounted to presidential absolution as he reassured the Nvidia board that it could restore him to its executive suite without fear of prosecution.

“The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security,” Mr. Trump wrote on social media on Monday. Based on what the government told it, the board said in its own statement that it is “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

The president has had a tendency to sympathize with and defend powerful men accused of sexual wrongdoing — at least those politically aligned with him. Mr. Trump himself has been found liable in civil court for sexually abusing and defaming the writer E. Jean Carroll and ordered to pay her about $90 million; he has been accused by many others of inappropriate sexual conduct as well, although he has repeatedly denied the allegations.

Mr. Huang, in this view, is a victim, not a villain. “We have to take care of our geniuses, by the way,” Mr. Trump told Fox while in China. “We don’t have that many of them. When we have brilliant people like Jensen, we can’t say, ‘Oh, you know, he did this or he did —’ We have to take care.”

Despite warnings from intelligence agencies, Trump cited stock market stabilization as his primary motivation, sparking intense scrutiny in Washington over the intersection of critical tech leadership and national security.

ai_analysis.takeaway_zh: 此次事件标志着美国高科技产业的地缘政治合规性已让位于短期金融稳定性。英伟达作为算力基础设施核心，其治理架构的政治化预示着未来美国科技巨头在全球供应链（尤其是涉华业务）中将面临更极端的监管博弈，同时也加剧了资本市场对大选周期内政策随机性的定价风险。
ai_analysis.takeaway_en: This intervention signals that national security compliance in high-tech has been sacrificed for short-term financial stability. article_content_zh:
据特朗普总统自己的说法，他正在观察股市的下滑并决定阻止它。他将亲自决定由谁来领导美国最大的公司之一。别管国家安全问题，别管私营部门的自主权。特朗普先生将做出决定。

总统的非同寻常的干预导致黄仁勋于周一恢复了英伟达首席执行官的职位，而就在他因中国间谍丑闻而被迫离职仅 11 天后。特朗普先生随后得到了他想要的结果。低迷的股市反弹，仅英伟达投资者（恰好包括他本人）的价值就恢复了近 1 万亿美元。

特朗普对黄先生倒台和迅速崛起背后的丑闻的处理方式都令人震惊：总统否认他知道黄先生与一名所谓的中国情报人员有染，尽管有报道称他至少被告知两次。他耸耸肩，对他的一位技术领主捐助者与敌对势力的资产躺在床上表现得漠不关心。现在，他不顾自己情报机构的警告，决定增加投资者的财富。

“我这样做是为了国家，”周一上午，在英伟达董事会屈服于他的意愿后不久，特朗普对 CNBC 表示。他解释说，他看到最近几天市场集体损失了数万亿美元，部分原因是黄丑闻。 “我看了那场比赛，你知道，我最好参与其中。如果我不参与，英伟达可能会在未来很长一段时间内感到非常悲伤。”

长期国家安全担忧换成了短期股市上涨，给华盛顿、华尔街和硅谷带来了冲击。就连已经因英伟达丑闻而感到不安的共和党同僚，也对黄仁勋迅速重返高管层所表现出的缺乏问责表示震惊。两党议员都大声疾呼，并发誓要进行调查。

特朗普的坚定盟友、前议长纽特·金里奇在网上写道：“黄仁勋与中共间谍有关系，并帮助中国获得大量非常先进的计算机芯片，这完全违背了美国政府的政策，而现在他又重新担任了世界上最先进芯片制造公司的首席执行官，这是完全错误的。”

罗德岛州民主党参议员、参议院银行委员会成员杰克·里德 (Jack Reed) 定于 12 月 3 日听取黄先生的证词，他表示国会应审查特朗普与黄先生和 Nvidia 董事会的沟通，以确定他向他们保证或承诺的内容。

“政府的首要任务应该是维护我们的国家安全，并确保美国最强大的技术为美国人民服务，而不是为我们的对手服务，”里德在一份声明中说。他补充说，经济取决于法治和公平交易。 “特朗普总统的不当干预损害了这些原则，必须接受调查。”

特朗普的行为似乎还不够反常，他公开庆祝自己成功施压的行为只会加剧愤怒。在英伟达恢复黄先生的职位后不久，特朗普在社交媒体上发布了一张奇怪的照片，将这位曾经也是未来的公司首席执行官描绘成烈士。

该图像似乎是一个 A.I.根据特朗普先生在 2024 年宾夕法尼亚州巴特勒集会上遭遇暗杀未遂而幸存后的一张著名照片合成的，他被特勤局特工包围，脸上沾满血迹，拳头在空中挥舞。在总统在网上分享的版本中，黄先生位于画面中央，脸上沾满血迹，举着红色胸罩。他身后挥舞着一面写着“Nvidia”的旗帜。

这篇超现实的帖子似乎总结了特朗普在总统任期内经常轻率、凭直觉、为所欲为的态度，在这种态度中，他的突发奇想变成了官方政策。通过这张照片，他成功地同时嘲笑了政治暴力和重大间谍活动的严重性——并提到了女性内衣，仿佛这是一种性征服。

“你知道，其中涉及性，而性比股票卖得更好，”特朗普周一早上告诉《纽约时报》。

正如最近几天多次所做的那样，特朗普只是否认了他自己的美国情报机构得出的结论，即与黄先生有关的女商人正在为中国从事间谍活动。

他告诉 CNBC：“每当有一个长得好看或漂亮的中国女人，他们就会说她是间谍。”但是，他补充道，“对于詹森来说，我不相信这是真的。”

[Root Cause & Mechanism] To boost stock market performance at the expense of national security governance
[Key Metrics] Sagging stock markets shot back up, restoring nearly $1 trillion in value alone to investors of Nvidia, who happen to include himself.

title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
title_en: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
author: Casey Crownhart
article_content:
One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

article_content_zh:
启动数据中心的最大障碍之一是获得连接电网的批准——这一等待可能会持续长达十年。一些开发商不愿意等待，而是选择建造自己的离网或用户侧天然气发电厂来推动人工智能的繁荣。

早在 2024 年，xAI 的孟菲斯园区就使用了数十台天然气涡轮机，其中一些未经许可。当时，该设施非常罕见，并且面临监管机构的审查。它仍然是正在进行的法律斗争的主题。但自那以后，离网供电的策略变得更加普遍。

根据市场情报公司 Cleanview 的数据，截至 2026 年 10 月，数据中心开发商已宣布计划在美国设施内建设 100 多个用户侧燃气发电厂。这些设施的总规划容量超过 115 吉瓦，是加州峰值电力需求的两倍多。这些公告绝大多数是自 2025 年初以来发布的。

这些设施可能不会全部建成；目前只有一小部分正在建设或运营。但大型数据中心寻求建立自己的电源的趋势日益明显，这可能会在未来几十年内塑造电网及其对气候的影响。

建造自己的发电厂通常比仅仅连接到电网更昂贵，但人工智能热潮使得开发商愿意支付大量费用以更快地上网。 “目前数据中心现场供电的最大动力是速度，”能源咨询公司 BloombergNEF 的合伙人 Musfika Mishi 表示。

当开发商想要建造需要大量电力的新工业设施（例如数据中心）时，他们需要向当地公用事业公司或区域电网运营商请求电网连接。这一要求启动了长达数年的过程，在此过程中，电网规划人员研究现有电网，以了解需要建造什么才能在不影响可靠性的情况下安全地向设施供电。可能需要升级，例如建造新的输电线路或更大的变压器，而开发商可能需要帮助支付费用。

开发商可以选择建造自己的发电厂，而不是等待这一过程完成。这些设施被称为“电表后面”，因为它们位于公用事业电表的客户一侧，直接向建筑物供电，而不是通过电网连接依赖公用事业。

“数据中心开发商的电力战略转向离网天然气，引发了一些关于数据中心未来如何供电的重要问题，”智库能源创新电力总监布伦丹·皮尔庞特(Brendan Pierpont)表示。

然而，用户侧并不总是意味着完全脱离电网。一些设施可能会建造此类发电厂作为临时措施，最终连接到电网并利用自己的发电厂仅作为备用。皮尔庞特说：“这实际上是一种非常昂贵的方法，可以弥补这些数据中心可能需要五到七年的时间差距，直到这些数据中心能够获得电网连接。”

即使天然气工厂被宣传为短期解决方案，建设新的化石燃料基础设施也可能会产生长期影响，因为运营商在花钱建设工厂后可能会选择继续运营工厂。 “尽管数据中心声称这是一个电网桥接解决方案，但它使用更长时间的可能性是一个真正的风险，这会导致化石燃料锁定，”米什说。

现场天然气热潮可能会对温室气体排放产生重大影响。如今，美国电网仍然依赖化石燃料，但核能和可再生能源合计约占发电量的 40%。这意味着与完全依赖现场天然气工厂相比，建立电网连接通常是一种排放更低的选择。 （并非所有地方都是如此，例如，印度预计未来十年数据中心将蓬勃发展，而其电网目前主要由排放密集型燃煤发电厂提供服务。）

公用事业公司已经计划在电网上建设更多天然气发电厂，以满足不断增长的电力需求。设备制造商正在努力跟上这一浪潮，这迫使用户侧工厂的开发商转向效率较低的替代方案。

如今，大型天然气发电厂普遍使用联合循环涡轮机。这些涡轮机捕获热量以产生额外的电力，使其比单循环涡轮机更高效，而单循环涡轮机的建造成本通常较低。然而，米什表示，计划中的用户侧设施很少会使用联合循环涡轮机。这意味着这些离网工厂可能会比其他天然气资源产生更多的温室气体排放。

BloombergNEF 还在跟踪数据中心的现场天然气工厂，发现全球已宣布的项目价值 181 吉瓦，其中 90% 指定给美国。据彭博新能源财经报道，如果美国数据中心所有计划的用户侧天然气工厂都按计划进行，到 2035 年，它们每年可能排放 3.45 亿吨二氧化碳当量。这比这些数据中心从美国电网获取电力的排放量多出 1.52 亿吨，这一差距比荷兰的年排放总量还要大。

【起因与机理】现有电力基础设施无法承载AI激增的能耗，且电网升级审批过程极其缓慢
【核心事实细节】电力接入审批长达十年，迫使开发者选择自建能源供应。
【各方立场与态度】该模式具备高成本与高合规博弈特征，旨在换取极速算力部署时间。

author: OpenAI
article_content:
Two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to look for signs of planets in public telescope data. Now they’ve given professional astronomers a few places to look more closely.

Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system since the first ones were announced in 1992. A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers.

Astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. When the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90.

Now, tools like Astra are helping amateur astronomers design and run searches of their own, often on data that has already yielded the more obvious exoplanet signals. Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, came to astronomy through his love of photographing the night sky. He used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope, a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018. Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, has always loved astronomy. Working independently of Bond, he tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars.

Both searches identified potential exoplanets. Bond and Byrd have now turned to astronomers for an independent assessment of their results. Bond contacted an astronomer at the SETI Institute, who ran an independent search and found two of the same signals in the Kepler data. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. It’s in line for further analysis, and two more candidates are awaiting submission.

### Looking for dips in starlight

One of the most common ways to find an exoplanet is to watch the star it orbits. When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view on Earth, it blocks a tiny amount of starlight. Astronomers call that crossing a transit. On a graph of the star’s brightness over time, known as a light curve, a transit shows up as a dip. If the dip keeps coming back at regular intervals, astronomers know when to watch for it again.

Searching for that pattern across thousands of stars is partly a coding problem. Astronomers have published methods for picking out faint, recurring dips in years of measurements. Bond used Codex to compare those methods, combine them in a search program, and test whether changes to the code improved the search. One AI agent scanned the light curves for promising signals. Another ran more detailed checks on the candidates the first one flagged.

Bond ran the program on public data from the Kepler Space Telescope. The search flagged more than 200 signals, including 10 from previously confirmed planets. Finding those known planets gave Bond confidence that the program could pick out the kinds of signals he was looking for.

Two stars stood out. The first, KIC 5689121, is a relatively cool star about half the size of our sun in the constellation Lyra. The Codex search found a dip in brightness every 13.8 days. If a planet is causing it, the amount of light it blocks suggests it could be about 2.4 times Earth’s diameter.

The second star, KIC 6691030, is faint and lies in the northern sky. The Codex search found a dip in its brightness every 4.8 days, consistent with a planet smaller than Neptune. These were the two signals the SETI Institute astronomer found independently. Confirming what caused them could take months or years.

“Kevin’s work shows how citizen scientists, equipped with AI, can help astronomers explore the Kepler Bonus Catalog—a vast collection of stars beyond Kepler’s original targets. His pipeline has surfaced promising candidates in data traditional searches may have missed. Our initial checks are encouraging, and follow-up observations will tell us more.”

Byrd used Astra to design two searches. One looked broadly for exoplanet candidates. The other focused on stars’ habitable zones. A habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet with a suitable atmosphere could support liquid water on its surface.

Byrd then asked Astra to review published methods, build the search software, and run initial checks on promising signals. His searches drew on observations from TESS, which NASA launched in 2018, and from other public telescope archives.

The first pass through the data turned up 49 candidates. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on the TESS mission, where it is awaiting further analysis. His search is still running.

### What does it take to confirm a planet?

When astronomers see a star dim, they have to consider what else might explain it. Two stars passing in front of one another can produce a similar dip. Even a change in temperature aboard a telescope can affect its instruments enough to make a star appear to dim.

Astronomers can use statistics to show that an exoplanet is the most likely explanation for a series of dips. They can also collect more observations, sometimes using a different method. For example, an orbiting planet’s gravity tugs on its star, causing it to move slightly toward and away from us. That motion, called radial velocity, shows up as tiny shifts in the color of the star’s light. Astronomers then publish their findings in a peer-reviewed journal so others can examine the evidence.

For Bond and Byrd, each candidate is a question that can be tested. If a planet is passing in front of the star in Lyra every 13.8 days, astronomers can watch for the next crossing. Further observations can help establish whether the dip repeats as expected, while additional checks can help determine what is causing it.

Photographs by Kevin Bond

### Taking part in the search

You can contribute without owning a telescope. NASA’s Exoplanet Watch lets you request data and learn to plot a light curve yourself. Its broader exoplanet citizen science programs offer other ways to participate.

If you have access to a telescope, Exoplanet Watch walks users through how to collect data on transiting exoplanets and participate in observation campaigns. AAVSO’s Exoplanet Observing Program can show you how to measure a dip in starlight and share your observations with the researchers studying that planet. And the Unistellar Network Investigating TESS Exoplanets coordinates volunteers around the world with a certain type of telescope to observe the same star, helping astronomers catch transits that can last longer than a single night.

Astronomy has a long history of people around the world following their curiosity and sharing what they find. Bond and Byrd are part of that tradition. Their searches are still open, but they turned a love of the night sky into leads that other astronomers can investigate. We want more people to have that opportunity, in astronomy and across science.

If you want to follow along with new findings, practical guidance, and perspectives from researchers using AI to advance science check out the OpenAI science blog.

article_content_zh:
两名业余天文学家使用 Codex 和 Astra 在公共望远镜数据中寻找行星的迹象。现在，他们为专业天文学家提供了一些可以更仔细观察的地方。

自 1992 年宣布第一批行星以来，天文学家已确认太阳系外存在 6,400 多颗行星。全球业余天文学家社区长期以来一直参与这一搜寻工作。一些人通过公共望远镜数据进行梳理，寻找恒星亮度的小幅反复下降，这可能预示着一颗绕轨道运行的行星。其他人则使用自己的望远镜观察下一次倾角，并与研究人员分享他们所看到的情况。

天文学家多年来一直在这项搜索中使用人工智能。 2017 年，研究人员利用来自 NASA 开普勒太空望远镜的 15,000 个信号训练了一个神经网络，天文学家已经检查过这些信号。从这些例子中，该模型学会了识别星光中的哪些模式最有可能来自行星。当研究人员用它来检查较弱的信号时，其中一个引导他们找到了绕一颗名为开普勒 90 的恒星运行的第八颗行星。

现在，像 Astra 这样的工具正在帮助业余天文学家设计和运行自己的搜索，通常是针对已经产生更明显的系外行星信号的数据。凯文·邦德 (Kevin Bond) 是 OpenAI 的工程师，由于热爱拍摄夜空而进入天文学领域。他使用 Codex 搜索了开普勒望远镜对约 100,000 颗恒星的观测结果，这是一项从 2009 年到 2018 年运行的行星搜寻任务。Ethan Byrd 是电子邮件基础设施初创公司 Primitive 的创始人，一直热爱天文学。他独立于 Bond 工作，尝试了几种人工智能模型，然后选择 Astra 来帮助他分析来自约 1900 万颗恒星的望远镜数据。

两次搜索都发现了潜在的系外行星。邦德和伯德现在请天文学家对其结果进行独立评估。邦德联系了 SETI 研究所的一位天文学家，后者进行了独立搜索，并在开普勒数据中发现了两个相同的信号。伯德将他最有力的候选人之一派给了从事美国宇航局凌日系外行星勘测卫星（TESS）任务的研究人员。它有待进一步分析，还有两名候选人正在等待提交。

### 寻找星光的暗淡

寻找系外行星最常见的方法之一是观察其绕轨道运行的恒星。从我们在地球上的角度来看，当一颗行星经过其恒星前方时，它会阻挡少量的星光。天文学家称这种穿越为凌日。在恒星亮度随时间变化的图表（称为光曲线）上，凌日显示为下降。如果下降持续定期出现，天文学家就知道何时再次观察它。

在数千颗恒星中搜索这种模式在一定程度上是一个编码问题。天文学家已经发表了在多年的测量中找出微弱、反复出现的下降的方法。 Bond 使用 Codex 来比较这些方法，将它们组合到搜索程序中，并测试对代码的更改是否改进了搜索。一名人工智能代理扫描光变曲线以寻找有希望的信号。另一个对第一个标记的候选人进行了更详细的检查。

邦德利用开普勒太空望远镜的公共数据运行该程序。此次搜索发现了 200 多个信号，其中 10 个来自先前确认的行星。找到那些已知的行星让邦德相信该程序可以找出他正在寻找的信号类型。

两颗星星脱颖而出。第一颗是 KIC 5689121，是天琴座一颗相对较冷的恒星，大小约为太阳的一半。 Codex 搜索发现亮度每 13.8 天就会下降一次。如果是一颗行星造成的，那么它阻挡的光量表明它的直径可能约为地球直径的 2.4 倍。

第二颗恒星 KIC 6691030 位于北方天空，光线昏暗。 Codex 搜索发现其亮度每 4.8 天就会下降一次，这与一颗比海王星小的行星一致。这是 SETI 研究所天文学家独立发现的两个信号。确认造成这些情况的原因可能需要数月或数年的时间。

“凯文的工作展示了配备人工智能的公民科学家如何帮助天文学家探索开普勒额外目录——开普勒原始目标之外的大量恒星。他的管道已经在传统搜索可能错过的数据中发现了有希望的候选者。我们的初步检查令人鼓舞，后续观察将告诉我们更多信息。”

伯德使用 Astra 设计了两次搜索。人们广泛地寻找系外行星候选者。另一个则关注恒星的宜居带。宜居带是指具有合适大气层的行星可以在其表面支持液态水的距离范围。

伯德随后要求阿斯特拉审查已发布的方法，构建搜索软件，并对有希望的信号进行初步检查。他的搜索借鉴了 NASA 于 2018 年发射的 TESS 和其他公共望远镜档案的观测结果。

Investing.com -- Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) and Tesla Inc (NASDAQ:TSLA) are working towards a potential $3.5 trillion merger, with five directors appointed to negotiate the terms of an all-stock combination that could create one of the world's largest corporate groups, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.

The companies have established separate special committees, comprising three directors from Tesla and two from SpaceX, to oversee negotiations and assess the proposed combination, people familiar with the process told Financial Times.

The directors are Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Jack Hartung from Tesla, and Roelof Botha and Randy Glein from SpaceX, according to the report.

The committees have appointed financial advisers to help determine the valuation and structure of the transaction. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs are advising SpaceX, while Evercore is working with Tesla. The parties are developing financial models and negotiating an appropriate exchange ratio for shareholders in what is expected to be an all-stock transaction, FT said.

The discussions are reportedly moving towards a potential year-end deadline, although people involved in the process cautioned that the committees were not yet close to reaching an agreement.

The proposed merger presents significant governance challenges because both companies share Chief Executive Elon Musk. The special committees are intended to provide independent oversight, with Musk barred from formally participating in active negotiations under applicable Texas corporate governance rules, although the committees can consult senior executives for information.

Shareholder approval will also be necessary. Tesla is expected to require a separate extraordinary shareholder meeting, with the deal needing more than 50% of all possible votes to pass. Abstentions and uncast votes would count against approval.

The transaction could also face regulatory scrutiny in the United States, China, Europe and the United Kingdom. Tesla's Chinese operations and SpaceX's rocket technology and Starlink satellite business could complicate approvals because of national security and geopolitical concerns.

The report noted that Musk controls about 84% of voting rights at SpaceX but around 20% at Tesla, meaning the merger could significantly reshape his control of the combined company.

Investing.com——据英国《金融时报》周二报道，太空探索技术公司（纳斯达克股票代码：SPCX）和特斯拉公司（纳斯达克股票代码：TSLA）正在努力进行一项价值 3.5 万亿美元的合并，并任命五名董事来谈判全股票合并的条款，该合并可能会创建世界上最大的企业集团之一。

我们的人工智能股票投资组合比标准普尔 500 指数高出 118%。发现我们正在购买的股票以及我们接下来关注的机会。雅虎独家！财经读者：黑色星期五可享受 55% 的折扣，结帐时可额外享受 15% 的折扣。今天就订阅吧！ »

知情人士告诉英国《金融时报》，两家公司已经成立了单独的特别委员会，由特斯拉的三名董事和 SpaceX 的两名董事组成，负责监督谈判并评估拟议的合并。

据报道，董事包括来自特斯拉的罗宾·丹霍姆、凯瑟琳·威尔逊·汤普森和杰克·哈同，以及来自 SpaceX 的罗洛夫·博塔和兰迪·格莱因。

委员会已任命财务顾问来帮助确定交易的估值和结构。摩根士丹利和高盛正在为 SpaceX 提供咨询服务，而 Evercore 正在与特斯拉合作。英国《金融时报》称，双方正在开发财务模型，并就预计全股票交易中股东的适当交换比例进行谈判。

股票已经上涨后，停止追逐股票。通过人工智能选股、收益见解和市场动态新闻寻找下一个投资机会。雅虎！财经读者在黑色星期五 55% 折扣的基础上还可享受额外 15% 的折扣。今天加入！ »

据报道，讨论正朝着可能的年底截止日期迈进，尽管参与这一过程的人士警告称，各委员会尚未接近达成协议。

拟议的合并带来了重大的治理挑战，因为两家公司都有共同的首席执行官埃隆·马斯克(Elon Musk)。特别委员会旨在提供独立监督，根据适用的德克萨斯州公司治理规则，马斯克被禁止正式参与积极谈判，尽管委员会可以向高级管理人员咨询信息。

还需要股东批准。预计特斯拉将需要召开单独的特别股东大会，该交易需要超过所有可能投票数的 50% 才能通过。弃权票和未投票的票将不计入批准。

该交易还可能面临美国、中国、欧洲和英国的监管审查。由于国家安全和地缘政治担忧，特斯拉的中国业务以及 SpaceX 的火箭技术和星链卫星业务可能会使审批变得复杂。

报告指出，马斯克控制着 SpaceX 约 84% 的投票权，但控制着特斯拉约 20% 的投票权，这意味着此次合并可能会极大地重塑他对合并后公司的控制权。

title: Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving
title_en: Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving
author: Elana Klein
article_content:
Sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude. “When I'm Googling, I type in ‘minus AI’ after every single search I do,” says the 27-year-old social work student, who lives in North Carolina. “I have deactivated Microsoft Copilot, all the things.”

The reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold. She worries about the degradation of critical thinking and cognitive functioning, some AI leaders’ alignment with the Trump administration, and the environmental impact of data centers, particularly on the water supply in nonwhite communities. Her perspective is born of strong ideological convictions: “My anti-AI stance is very deeply ingrained in my anti-capitalist beliefs,” she says.

Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a new mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.

The stark difference in opinion between Sophie and her relatives can make for some pretty tense family gatherings—something she’s dreading going into Thanksgiving. The topic “comes up every time” they get together. “I’m constantly anticipating frustration and being judged, being told that I am naive,” she says.

AI has been the focus of many an argument in Sophie’s family in recent years. (She and other interviewees chose to use pseudonyms or only first names to prevent further such conflict.) At a family get-together a couple of years ago, Sophie sent her résumé to her family members to get feedback, and the same cousin who uses ChatGPT for her babies’ meal schedule immediately fed the document to ChatGPT. “She didn't ask for my consent to use my intellectual property to train large learning language models,” Sophie says, which started a “huge conflict.” That cousin’s tech founder husband, she adds, asks snarky questions meant to poke holes in her stance, such as “Well, what about if it's a poor Black person in Africa using AI to create wealth for themselves?” And though Sophie successfully convinced a different cousin to stop using ChatGPT, that cousin immediately switched over to Claude, which Sophie describes as “a total white-liberal move to pick the better-branded version of the same evil tool.”

Over the past decade, the US’ chaotic, increasingly polarized political climate has put American families to the test: Trump, immigration, Israel and Palestine, the war in Iran, abortion, and LGBTQ rights are just a few issues that have turned holidays into yelling matches and siblings into strangers. This Thanksgiving, you might want to add AI to the list of topics to avoid bringing up around the table.

“It's the latest generational beef,” says Matt Lundquist, a psychologist and the founder and clinical director of Tribeca Therapy in New York City. He has found that arguments over AI are on the rise—especially among families.

Lundquist says the issue has “created a rupture,” even among people who are normally on the same page. This is the case for Lindsay, a 40-year-old romance novelist in Pennsylvania whose family is “very politically aligned.” Before AI became a hot-button issue, Lindsay says, her family “never had a conversation where you have to be like, ‘Nobody bring up politics. Nobody bring up Israel. Nobody bring up Trump.’” So she was surprised to find herself at odds with her uncle during Passover dinner when he began raving about what he believes are the wonders of ChatGPT.

As a professional writer, she was upset by her uncle's celebration of AI. Last year, Lindsay found out a book she wrote was used to train AI models. “I was like, ‘Do you understand that ChatGPT is not a magical device? It is being created by pirating work from actual writers.” She tried to convey the message that by using AI, “You're directly harming me.”

Her uncle was “befuddled” by her reaction and became “giggly and nervous.” This seemed to be the first time he’d heard that AI is trained on the intellectual property of real people left uncredited and uncompensated. “When I'm telling him this, I can see it's really not landing,” she says. “I can tell that he thinks this is a benevolent, harmless thing.”

Others in creative fields report running into similar arguments with older relatives, particularly those earlier in their careers. For John, a 20-year-old cinematography student in Chicago whose girlfriend works in animation, AI brings up fears around both his own career and the future of art. He says his dad, a civil and chemical engineer who works in the chemical plant industry, holds AI to a high regard and uses it to offload some of the work of managing plants around the country, organizing data—which makes his job more manageable.

“It can get heated,” says John. “I'll say, ‘Oh, this is potentially taking away my job.’ And his response will be like, ‘Well, I don't think that it'll get to that point.’ But then I'll say, ‘Oh, it's already doing that.’” From there, the discussion deteriorates: “Our positions are so ingrained,” he says.

“Folks under 30 are giving their parents shit about some of this stuff,” says Lundquist, who has found that anti-AI sentiment is resonant among young adults, particularly those new to the job market and who haven’t bought a home or raised children. This tracks with research from Pew published in August, which found that a majority of American adults under 30 describe themselves as more concerned than excited about AI—and 73 percent of the same group believe AI will result in fewer jobs. (At the same time, young people are still using AI. Axios reported in August that 61 percent of 18- to 34-year-old respondents to its poll said they'd used ChatGPT in the past month, while 48 percent said they’d used Gemini, and 20 percent had used Claude.)

Luke, a 23-year-old living in Toronto, says AI has become “the most debated topic in the household by far.” Luke just completed a degree in sports media and is struggling to find an entry-level job. Meanwhile, his dad, who has had a full career in computer science and web development, sees AI “as the next big step for every single person in the world.”

Debates over AI are “infecting all of our conversations,” Luke says. Last year, Luke remembers, at Canadian Thanksgiving, “what started off as just a discussion about my career and where I'm going next turned into a discussion about AI.”

“He wants what's best for me,” Luke says. He assumes his dad worries that taking an anti-AI stance could be “detrimental to my career and making a livelihood.”

In the family of Kaleigh, a 26-year-old living in Vermont and working toward a master’s degree in social work, disagreement about AI also falls along this parent-child fault line. The anti-AI stance of her and her younger brother is dismissed by her parents as “a young-person-exclusive take.”

When Kaleigh last returned to her parents’ house, her mother told her that ChatGPT had helped her redesign their backyard. This upset Kaleigh, as a close friend of hers is working toward a degree in landscape architecture. “It's an art form,” Kaleigh says. “It feels so out of touch or annoying to me to have somebody that has actual money not want to pay somebody to do something creative just because it's easier to access with this data thing.”

Lundquist has found that many older adults are “clueless” about how real the threat of AI feels to younger relatives. “I think if you own your second or third home with a 2.8 percent interest rate and you've already sent your kids to college, you're not worried about this stuff,” he says. “And so the fact that an AI bot can order your groceries for you is just kind of cool.”

His advice? Maybe avoid the topic altogether. “If it’s done in the genuine spirit of connection, learning, and exchanging ideas, that’s great,” he says. “If it’s done in the spirit of ‘This is going to be the 2026 Thanksgiving throwdown,’ that’s probably not very fruitful.”

If you do decide to go at it, he suggests getting in touch with what you’re actually fighting about. “When people are fighting about things like this, in reality they're probably fighting about other things,” he says. “The real beef is, ‘I’m mad about the pittance you and your generation have left for me. I’m mad about how the world seems to be not rewarding the kinds of things I anticipated it would and the things you anticipated it would as my parents.’”

Intergenerational fights about AI “hang on a desire to be understood,” he says. “So Dad picking up Claude and asking it for a sweet potato recipe burns in ways that feel like, ‘What the fuck, are you not paying attention?’”

article_content_zh:
Sophie 从未使用过 ChatGPT 或 Claude。 “当我在谷歌上搜索时，我每次搜索后都会输入‘减去人工智能’，”这位住在北卡罗来纳州的 27 岁社会工作学生说道。 “我已经停用了 Microsoft Copilot 等所有功能。”

她坚决反对人工智能的原因是多方面的。她担心批判性思维和认知功能的退化、一些人工智能领导者与特朗普政府的结盟，以及数据中心对环境的影响，特别是对非白人社区供水的影响。她的观点源于强烈的意识形态信念：“我的反人工智能立场在我的反资本主义信仰中根深蒂固，”她说。

尽管她的父母和兄弟姐妹或多或少意见一致，但人工智能在她的大家庭中的使用是“普遍的”。她担心她的阿姨可能“接近人工智能精神病”。她的一位表兄弟是双胞胎的新妈妈，她使用 ChatGPT 创建了她孩子的“整个喂养和睡眠时间表”，并投资了一款使用人工智能进行儿科医生评估的应用程序。

索菲和她的亲戚之间意见的巨大差异可能会导致一些相当紧张的家庭聚会——这是她在感恩节之前害怕的事情。他们“每次聚会都会出现”这个话题。 “我一直在期待着挫败感和被评判，被告知我很天真，”她说。

近年来，人工智能一直是苏菲一家争论的焦点。 （她和其他受访者选择使用化名或只使用名字，以防止进一步发生此类冲突。）在几年前的一次家庭聚会上，Sophie 将她的简历发送给家人以获取反馈，而使用 ChatGPT 为孩子制定膳食计划的表弟立即将文件发送给 ChatGPT。索菲说：“她没有征求我的同意使用我的知识产权来训练大型学习语言模型，”这引发了“巨大的冲突”。她补充道，那位表弟的科技创始人丈夫提出了尖锐的问题，意在戳破她的立场，比如“好吧，如果非洲的一个贫穷的黑人利用人工智能为自己创造财富呢？”尽管索菲成功说服了另一个表弟停止使用 ChatGPT，但那个表弟立即改用了克劳德，索菲将其描述为“完全是白人自由主义的举动，选择了同一个邪恶工具的更好品牌版本”。

过去十年，美国混乱、日益两极分化的政治气候让美国家庭面临考验：特朗普、移民、以色列和巴勒斯坦、伊朗战争、堕胎和 LGBTQ 权利等问题让假期变成了争吵，兄弟姐妹变成了陌生人。这个感恩节，你可能想将人工智能添加到主题列表中，以避免在餐桌上被提及。

“这是最新一代的牛肉，”纽约市翠贝卡疗法创始人兼临床主任、心理学家马特·伦德奎斯特 (Matt Lundquist) 说。他发现，关于人工智能的争论正在增加——尤其是在家庭之间。

伦德奎斯特表示，这个问题已经“造成了裂痕”，即使是那些通常意见一致的人也是如此。林赛 (Lindsay) 就是这种情况，她是宾夕法尼亚州的一位 40 岁的浪漫小说家，她的家庭“政治立场非常一​​致”。 Lindsay 说，在人工智能成为热点问题之前，她的家人“从来没有进行过这样的谈话：‘没有人提起政治。没有人提起以色列。没有人提起特朗普。’”因此，在逾越节晚餐期间，她惊讶地发现自己与叔叔发生了争执，当时他开始对他认为的 ChatGPT 奇迹赞不绝口。

作为一名职业作家，她对叔叔对人工智能的庆祝感到不安。去年，Lindsay 发现她写的一本书被用来训练人工智能模型。 “我当时想，‘你明白 ChatGPT 不是一个神奇的设备吗？它是通过盗版真实作家的作品而创建的。”她试图通过人工智能传达这样的信息：“你直接伤害了我。”

她的叔叔对她的反应感到“困惑”，变得“咯咯地笑着，紧张兮兮”。这似乎是他第一次听说人工智能是根据真实的人的知识产权进行训练的，而这些人的知识产权没有得到认可，也没有得到补偿。 “当我告诉他这一点时，我发现它确实没有着陆，”她说。 “我看得出来，他认为这是一件仁慈、无害的事情。”

其他在创意领域工作的人也曾与年长的亲戚发生过类似的争吵，尤其是那些职业生涯早期的亲戚。20岁的约翰是芝加哥一名电影摄影专业的学生，他的女朋友从事动画工作。对于他来说，人工智能让他对自己的职业生涯和艺术的未来感到担忧。他说，他的父亲是一名在化工厂工作的土木和化学工程师，他非常重视人工智能，用它来减轻管理全国各地工厂、组织数据的一些工作——这让他的工作更容易管理。

“它会变热，”约翰说。 “我会说，‘哦，这可能会夺走我的工作。’他的回答会是，‘好吧，我认为事情不会发展到那个地步。’但我会说，‘哦，它已经这么做了。’”从那时起，讨论就会恶化：“我们的立场是如此根深蒂固，”他说。

伦德奎斯特说：“30 岁以下的人对这些事情对他们的父母大骂。”他发现，反人工智能情绪在年轻人中引起共鸣，尤其是那些刚进入就业市场、没有买房或养育孩子的年轻人。这与皮尤研究中心 8 月份发布的研究结果相吻合，该研究发现，大多数 30 岁以下的美国成年人表示，他们对人工智能的担忧多于兴奋，而同一群体中 73% 的人认为人工智能将导致就业机会减少。 （与此同时，年轻人仍在使用人工智能。Axios 在 8 月份报告称，在其调查的 18 至 34 岁受访者中，61% 的人表示他们在过去一个月使用过 ChatGPT，而 48% 的人表示他们使用过 Gemini，20% 的人使用过 Claude。）

居住在多伦多的 23 岁卢克表示，人工智能已经成为“迄今为止家庭中争论最多的话题”。卢克刚刚完成体育媒体学位，正在努力寻找入门级工作。与此同时，他的父亲在计算机科学和网络开发领域拥有完整的职业生涯，他认为人工智能“是世界上每个人的下一个重要步骤”。

title: Xiaomi’s Sales Slip After Memory Shortages Weigh on Smartphones
title_en: Xiaomi’s Sales Slip After Memory Shortages Weigh on Smartphones
